items.name: Ohm's law and power
items.doc: Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance (U = R × I); the electrical power is P = U × I. Any two of the four values determine the other two.
items.source: Ohm's law and Joule's law (P = U·I); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Voltage divider
items.doc: Two resistors in series divide the input voltage: V_out = V_in × R2 / (R1 + R2). The output is unloaded; for a divider that drives a load use the loaded voltage divider. The current and power are those of the divider chain itself.
items.source: Voltage divider rule; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a passive divider can only attenuate.

items.name: Loaded voltage divider
items.doc: A voltage divider that drives a load R_L. The load is in parallel with R2, so V_out = V_in × R_P / (R1 + R_P) with R_P = R2 ∥ R_L. The unloaded output V_nl shows how much the load pulls the voltage down.
items.source: Voltage divider with a load (R2 in parallel with R_L); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a passive divider can only attenuate.
R_P must be smaller than R2; these values do not fit together (a load always pulls the lower resistance down).

items.name: Current divider
items.doc: Two resistors in parallel share the total current in inverse proportion to their resistance: I_1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2) and I_2 = I × R1 / (R1 + R2). The voltage across both is U = I_1 × R1. The two branch currents alone cannot fix the resistors, only their ratio.
items.source: Current divider rule (Kirchhoff's current law with Ohm's law); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2

items.name: Series and parallel resistors
items.doc: Resistors in series add up: R_S = R_1 + R_2 + …. Resistors in parallel combine as 1/R_P = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + …. Enter the values as a list, for example 4k7, 10k, 2k2.
items.source: Series and parallel resistor combination; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Decibel ratio
items.doc: The decibel expresses a ratio on a logarithmic scale: G = 20 × log10(A_2 / A_1) for voltages and currents (field quantities) and G = 10 × log10(A_2 / A_1) for power. Choose the quantity first: +20 dB is a factor of 10 for voltages but a factor of 100 for power.
items.source: Definition of the decibel (field quantities 20·log10, power quantities 10·log10), cf. IEC 60027-3 (logarithmic quantities and their units)

items.name: dB levels
items.doc: Absolute levels in decibels: dBm is relative to 1 mW, dBV to 1 V and dBu to 0.7746 V, the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 Ω. From a voltage and a load resistance the power follows; the derived values are shown as dBm, dBV and dBu.
items.source: Definitions: dBm = 10·log10(P / 1 mW), dBV = 20·log10(U / 1 V), dBu = 20·log10(U / 0.7746 V) with 0.7746 V = sqrt(0.6) V (1 mW in 600 Ω); decibel per IEC 60027-3

items.name: Wheatstone bridge
items.doc: A Wheatstone bridge is two voltage dividers side by side: R1 over R2 on the left and R3 over R4 on the right. The bridge voltage V_D between the two midpoints is V_D = V_S × (R2 / (R1 + R2) − R4 / (R3 + R4)). It is zero when R1 × R4 = R2 × R3; R_4b shows the R4 that balances the bridge.
items.source: Wheatstone bridge as two voltage dividers with the balance condition R1·R4 = R2·R3; e.g. C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits (resistance measurement with the Wheatstone bridge)

items.name: Star-delta transform
items.doc: Converts between a star (Y) network of three resistors R_A, R_B, R_C and the equivalent delta (Δ) network R_AB, R_BC, R_CA. Delta to star: R_A = R_AB × R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA), and cyclically. Star to delta: R_AB = (R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A) / R_C, and cyclically. Enter either the three delta or the three star resistors.
items.source: Wye-delta (star-delta) transformation; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2
formula: rab = (ra * rb + rb * rc + rc * ra) / rc

items.name: RMS, peak and average
items.doc: Converts between the RMS value, the peak value, the peak-to-peak value and the average of the rectified waveform for a sine, square or triangle wave. The crest factor is V_pk / V_rms and the form factor is V_rms / V_avg; for a sine wave they are √2 and π / (2√2) ≈ 1.1107. The average is the mean of the absolute value (the rectified average), not the mean of the signal, which is zero for a symmetric wave.
items.source: Standard waveform relations: sine rms = peak/√2 and rectified average = 2·peak/π; square rms = rectified average = peak; triangle rms = peak/√3 and rectified average = peak/2 (integration of the waveform); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (signals)

items.name: Charge and energy
items.doc: Charge Q in ampere-hours (1 Ah = 3600 C) and energy E in watt-hours (1 Wh = 3600 J) are related by the voltage: E = Q × U. A 2 Ah cell at 3.7 V holds 7.4 Wh. The nominal voltage is only an average; real batteries deliver less energy at high load.
items.source: Definitions of charge and energy: E = Q·U (1 C·V = 1 J), 1 Ah = 3600 C, 1 Wh = 3600 J; The International System of Units (SI Brochure, BIPM)

items.name: Standard-value combiner
items.doc: Finds resistor values from a standard E series (IEC 60063) that reach a target: the nearest single value, and pairs in series or in parallel whose combined value comes closest. Enter the target resistance and choose the series in the settings (E6 to E192); every combination shows its value and its deviation from the target. In series R = R_1 + R_2, in parallel R = R_1 × R_2 / (R_1 + R_2). Example: 5 kΩ from E12 gives 4.7 kΩ + 270 Ω (−0.6 %) or 10 kΩ parallel to 10 kΩ (exactly 5 kΩ).
items.source: IEC 60063 (preferred number series E3 to E192); series and parallel resistor combination: P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: ADC (voltage to code)
items.doc: An ideal N-bit analog-to-digital converter divides the reference range V_ref into 2^N steps of one LSB = V_ref / 2^N and outputs the code floor(V_in / LSB), limited to 0 … 2^N − 1 (straight binary, unipolar). The code is shown in decimal, hexadecimal and binary. Real converters add offset, gain and linearity errors, and some round to the nearest code instead of truncating; check the datasheet. Example: 12 bit with V_ref = 3.3 V has an LSB of 0.806 mV, and 1 V reads as code 1241 (0x4D9).
items.source: Ideal N-bit converter transfer function with LSB = V_ref/2^N (terminology of IEEE Std 1241 for analog-to-digital converters); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (A/D and D/A conversion)

checks.warn: V_in is at or above V_ref: the code is clamped to full scale (2^N − 1).
V_in is negative: a unipolar ADC reads code 0.
A resolution below 1 bit leaves a single code.

items.name: DAC (code to voltage)
items.doc: An ideal N-bit digital-to-analog converter outputs V_out = code × V_ref / 2^N for a code of 0 … 2^N − 1 (straight binary, unipolar). One LSB is V_ref / 2^N; the full-scale code gives V_ref − 1 LSB. From V_ref, N and a code the output voltage follows; from V_ref, N and a wanted V_out the nearest code is found (rounded, so the real output of that code differs slightly). The number of bits N must be entered, it cannot be computed. Real converters have offset, gain and linearity errors. Example: 12 bit, V_ref = 3.3 V and code 2048 give 1.65 V.
items.source: Ideal N-bit converter transfer function V_out = code·V_ref/2^N; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (A/D and D/A conversion)

checks.warn: The code does not fit the resolution: the largest code is 2^N − 1.

items.name: I²C pull-up resistors
items.doc: The pull-up resistor of an I²C line must be small enough to pull the line up within the allowed rise time and large enough for the driver to sink the current: R_max = t_r / (0.8473 × C_b) from the 30 % to 70 % rise of an RC network, and R_min = (V_DD − V_OL) / I_OL. t_r is the maximum rise time of the mode: 1000 ns (standard-mode), 300 ns (fast-mode) and 120 ns (fast-mode plus). Pick a standard value between R_min and R_max (the nearest E-series values are shown). The drivers of standard and fast-mode sink 3 mA at V_OL = 0.4 V, fast-mode plus drivers 20 mA: enter the value of your driver. Example: 3.3 V, 100 pF, standard-mode and 3 mA give 967 Ω ≤ R ≤ 11.8 kΩ (4.7 kΩ is a common choice).
items.source: NXP UM10204: I²C-bus specification and user manual (pull-up resistor sizing R_p(max) = t_r/(0.8473·C_b) and R_p(min) = (V_DD − V_OL(max))/I_OL; maximum rise times and bus capacitance of standard-mode, fast-mode and fast-mode plus)

checks.warn: R_min is not below R_max: no pull-up resistor meets both limits. Lower the bus capacitance, use a driver with a higher sink current, or choose a slower mode.
C_b exceeds the maximum bus capacitance of the selected mode (400 pF; 550 pF in fast-mode plus).

items.name: Level shifter (resistor divider)
items.doc: A resistor divider shifts a 5 V logic signal down to 3.3 V in one direction: V_out = V_in × R2 / (R1 + R2). The receiver sees a logic high only while V_out stays above its input-high threshold V_IH (take it from the datasheet: 2.0 V for 3.3 V LVTTL inputs, 0.7 × V_DD = 2.31 V is typical for CMOS inputs), and V_out must stay below the absolute maximum input voltage of the pin (often V_DD + 0.3 V). Enter the guaranteed high level of the driver as V_in. A divider loads the driver and slows the edges (R1 ∥ R2 with the pin capacitance); for fast or bidirectional signals such as I²C use a level-shifter IC or a MOSFET shifter. Example: 5 V into 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ gives 3.33 V, which is 1.33 V above V_IH = 2 V, at 1.67 mA.
items.source: Voltage divider rule; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (logic interfacing); the input threshold V_IH comes from the datasheet of the receiving device

checks.warn: V_out is below V_IH: the receiver may not see a logic high.
V_out is not below V_in: a passive divider can only attenuate.

items.name: UART baud rate error
items.doc: A UART derives its bit clock by dividing the peripheral clock: baud = f_clk / (N × divisor), with N = 16 samples per bit (normal) or 8 (double-speed mode) and a whole-number divisor, so the real baud rate differs from the wanted one. The divisor is rounded to the nearest integer and the error is (actual − wanted) / wanted. As a rule of thumb keep it below ±2 %: the errors of sender and receiver add up, and an 8N1 frame tolerates only a few percent in total. Some UARTs have a fractional divider and do better. On some chips the register holds the divisor minus one. Example: 16 MHz and 115 200 Bd with 16× sampling gives divisor 9, 111 111 Bd and −3.55 %; double speed (8×) gives divisor 17 and +2.12 %; an 11.0592 MHz crystal hits 115 200 Bd exactly.
items.source: UART baud-rate generator: baud = f_clk/(N·divisor) with N = 16 or 8 samples per bit; e.g. the USART chapter of the ATmega328P datasheet (Microchip), where the register holds the divisor minus one

checks.warn: The baud rate error is above ±2 %: the receiver may mis-sample bits (rule of thumb; the errors of both ends add up).

items.name: Number systems (dec, hex, bin, oct)
items.doc: Shows one whole number in decimal, hexadecimal, binary and octal. Type it into any field: hex takes an optional 0x, bin an optional 0b and oct an optional 0o prefix, and digits may be separated by _ or blanks. The value is limited to 0 … 2^53 − 1 (9 007 199 254 740 991), the range in which whole numbers stay exact in the calculator. Long hex and binary results are grouped for readability. Example: 255 = 0xFF = 0o377 (eight one bits in binary).
items.source: Positional number systems with radix 2, 8, 10 and 16; D. E. Knuth: The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 2 (Seminumerical Algorithms), ch. 4.1 (positional number systems)

items.name: RC debounce
items.doc: RC debouncing of a switch in front of a Schmitt-trigger input. The circuit has a pull-up R1 from V_DD to the switch node, the switch from that node to ground, a series resistor R2 from the node to the capacitor C, and the Schmitt-trigger input at the capacitor. After the switch opens, C charges through R1 + R2 until it reaches the rising threshold V_T+: t = −R × C × ln(1 − V_T+ / V_DD). After the switch closes, C discharges through R2 until it falls to the falling threshold V_T−: t = −R × C × ln(V_T− / V_DD). Choose the edge, then enter R = R1 + R2 for the rising edge or R = R2 for the falling edge, together with the threshold of that edge. Any four of the five values can be entered when the missing one is R, C, V_T or the time (the supply must be known). The defaults are the typical thresholds of a 74HC14 at a 4.5 V supply (V_T+ 2.5 V, V_T− 1.6 V, Texas Instruments SN74HC14 datasheet), applied to a 5 V supply for a rough design. For a guaranteed minimum delay use the worst-case thresholds of the datasheet: the lowest V_T+ for the rising edge and the highest V_T− for the falling edge give the shortest times. Contact bounce can only lengthen the delay, never shorten it, because every re-closing partly recharges or discharges the capacitor; make both times longer than the bounce time (Ganssle measured bounce mostly under 10 ms and designs for 20 ms). The formulas assume that the capacitor was fully charged or discharged before the switch changed (several time constants), an ideal switch and no input current into the gate; the capacitor tolerance and the threshold spread are large. The input must have hysteresis: an ordinary logic or microcontroller input without a Schmitt trigger gives no defined result from a slow RC edge. Example with the defaults: 10 kΩ × 2.2 µF with the threshold at half the supply gives 22 ms × ln 2 = 15.2 ms.
items.source: RC charge and discharge of a capacitor through a resistor, v(t) = V_DD·(1 − e^(−t/RC)) and v(t) = V_DD·e^(−t/RC), solved for the time of the threshold; J. G. Ganssle: A Guide to Debouncing (The Ganssle Group, 2004, rev. 3 2008), the RC debouncer with R1, R2 and a Schmitt-trigger gate; thresholds V_T+ and V_T− from the datasheet of the gate, e.g. Texas Instruments SN74HC14, document SCLS085L

vars.label: R
vars.name: Resistance R (rising edge: R1 + R2, falling edge: R2)

vars.label: V_T
vars.name: Gate threshold of the edge (V_T+ rising, V_T− falling)

vars.label: t
vars.name: Delay until the threshold is crossed

checks.warn: The threshold is not below the supply: the capacitor never reaches it.
Below 10 ms: many switches bounce for up to 10 ms; 20 ms is a conservative design value.

items.name: Data transfer time
items.doc: Time needed to send an amount of data at a given line rate: t = S × f / R, with the data size S, the line rate R in bits per second and the framing factor f (line bits per payload bit). Enter any two of size, rate and time. Sizes and rates accept bits and bytes with decimal and binary prefixes: 1 B = 8 bit; kB, MB, GB are powers of 1000 (1 MB = 10⁶ B) and KiB, MiB, GiB powers of 1024 (1 MiB = 2²⁰ B = 1 048 576 B), so 1 MiB is 4.86 % more than 1 MB. Many programs print binary sizes with the decimal symbols. Data rates are given in bits per second (Mbit/s), file sizes in bytes: the factor is 8. The framing choice covers an asynchronous serial line: with 8 data bits every byte is sent as one start bit, 8 data bits and the parity and stop bits, that is 10 line bits for 8N1 (f = 10/8 = 1.25) and 11 for 8E1 or 8N2 (f = 11/8 = 1.375); the UART baud rate counts line bits per second, so enter it as the rate. The net rate R / f and the efficiency 1 / f are shown. The result is a lower limit: characters are assumed to follow back to back, and protocol overhead (headers, checksums, USB or TCP/IP framing), pauses between characters, flow control and retransmissions make a real transfer slower. Example with the defaults: 100 MB at 100 Mbit/s take 8 s; 1 MiB through a 115 200 Bd UART with 8N1 takes 91.02 s.
items.source: BIPM, The International System of Units (SI), 9th edition (SI prefixes are powers of 10; the binary prefixes kibi Ki = 2^10, mebi Mi = 2^20, gibi Gi = 2^30 are described in IEC 80000-13, which was not read); NIST, Prefixes for binary multiples (1 B = 8 bit, 1 MB = 10^6 B, 1 MiB = 2^20 B); asynchronous frame of one start bit, 5 to 8 data bits, an optional parity bit and 1, 1.5 or 2 stop bits: Texas Instruments KeyStone Architecture UART User Guide, SPRUGP1 (data format)

items.name: Logic level compatibility
items.doc: Checks whether a logic output (driver) can drive a logic input (receiver). Noise margin HIGH NM_H = V_OH(min, driver) − V_IH(min, receiver), noise margin LOW NM_L = V_IL(max, receiver) − V_OL(max, driver); both must be at least 0 V. Each family is taken at its nominal supply. V_OH and V_OL are the data-sheet limits at light load (CMOS inputs: 20 µA for 74HC and 74HCT, 100 µA for 74LVC); the TTL, 74LS and RP2040 data sheets give them only at their rated output current, so those margins are conservative. 74HC at 5 V uses V_IH = 0.7 × V_CC = 3.5 V and V_IL = 0.3 × V_CC = 1.5 V; its data sheets list 4.5 V and 6 V only. The over-voltage check compares the driver's supply, the highest level its HIGH output can reach, with the highest input voltage the receiver allows in operation. The table logic_levels has the full data of the families. Example: 3.3 V LVCMOS (V_OH 3.2 V) does not reliably drive 74HC at 5 V (V_IH 3.5 V) but does drive 74HCT (V_IH 2.0 V).
items.source: Maker data sheets of the parts named in the options: Texas Instruments SDLS025D (SN7400, SN74LS00), SCLS181H (SN74HC00), SCLS062F (SN74HCT00), SCES212AC (SN74LVC1G00), SCES115G (SN74ALVC00) and the Logic Guide SDYU001AC; Fairchild DM74LS00 (DS006439); Diodes Incorporated 74HC00 (DS35319), 74HCT00 (DS35329), 74LVC1G00 (DS32196); Raspberry Pi RP2040 Datasheet (DC characteristics of the GPIO); Microchip ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P (DS40002061A, common DC characteristics)

derived.label: V_OH
derived.name: HIGH output level of the driver, V_OH(min)

derived.label: V_OL
derived.name: LOW output level of the driver, V_OL(max)

derived.label: V_IH
derived.name: HIGH input threshold of the receiver, V_IH(min)

derived.label: V_IL
derived.name: LOW input threshold of the receiver, V_IL(max)

derived.label: V_I,max
derived.name: Highest input voltage of the receiver

checks.warn: HIGH is not reliably recognised: V_OH(min) of the driver is below V_IH(min) of the receiver. Use a receiver with TTL-level inputs (such as 74HCT) or a level shifter.
LOW is not reliably recognised: V_OL(max) of the driver is above V_IL(max) of the receiver.
Over-voltage: the driver's HIGH level can reach its supply, which is above the highest input voltage the receiver allows. Use a level shifter or a 5-V-tolerant input (such as 74LVC).

items.name: Stepper motor steps per mm
items.doc: How many (micro)steps a stepper motor needs per millimetre of travel. Steps per revolution: full steps per revolution × microsteps per full step (200 × 16 = 3200 for a 1.8° motor at 1/16). Travel per revolution: for a toothed belt the belt pitch × the number of teeth of the driving pulley (GT2: 2 mm × 20 teeth = 40 mm); for a leadscrew the LEAD, that is the travel of the nut per screw revolution. The lead is the thread pitch multiplied by the number of starts: a T8 screw has 2 mm pitch and 4 starts, so the lead is 8 mm. Enter the lead, never the pitch of a multi-start screw: with 2 mm instead of 8 mm the result would be four times too high. For a single-start thread lead and pitch are equal (M8 rod: 1.25 mm); for inch screws the pitch is 25.4 mm divided by the threads per inch. Steps per mm = steps per revolution / travel per revolution; the travel per microstep is its reciprocal (80 steps/mm = 12.5 µm). The variable at 'Belt pitch / screw lead' means the belt pitch with the belt drive and the lead with the leadscrew; the tooth count is ignored for a screw and cannot be solved for. A gear stage between motor and pulley or screw is not included: multiply the result by the gear ratio (motor revolutions per output revolution). This is pure geometry without belt stretch, backlash or thread errors; calibrate with a measured move. The result is shown in steps per mm.
items.source: Klipper documentation, Rotation distance (rotation_distance = full steps per rotation × microsteps / steps per mm; belt: pitch × teeth; leadscrew: pitch × number of starts); Thomson Industries, What is the difference between screw pitch and lead? (lead = pitch × starts); RepRap wiki, Triffid Hunter's Calibration Guide (worked examples); LightBurn documentation, Steps per MM

items.name: Motor torque, speed and power
items.doc: The mechanical power at a rotating shaft is the torque times the angular velocity: P = M × ω = 2π × n × M, with the speed n in revolutions per second (in r/min: P = 2π × n × M / 60, about 0.1047 × n × M). Solved the other way, M = P / (2π × n) and n = P / (2π × M); with P in kW and n in r/min the torque is about 9549.3 × P / n. One r/min is 0.1047198 rad/s (NIST SP 811). Torque and speed must be those at the same point of the shaft; behind a gearbox use the output speed and output torque and include the efficiency of the gearbox. The rated power on a motor nameplate is the shaft power, not the electrical input. Example: 1500 r/min at 10 N·m is 1570.8 W; 1000 r/min at 0.5 N·m is 52.4 W. The speed is stored in 1/s and shown in rpm.
items.source: P = M × ω = 2π × n × M: Oriental Motor, AC Motor Glossary of Terms (entry Output Power) and Engineering Notes, Wattage Specification for Stepper Motors; FAULHABER, Motor Calculations for Coreless Brush DC Motors; conversion 1 r/min = 0.1047198 rad/s: NIST Special Publication 811, Appendix B.9

items.name: RC low-pass filter
items.doc: A first-order RC low-pass passes low frequencies and attenuates high ones. Cutoff frequency (−3 dB point): f_c = 1 / (2π × R × C). At the test frequency f the amplitude ratio is A_v = 1 / √(1 + (f / f_c)²), the gain is G = 20 × log10(A_v) and the output phase is φ = −arctan(f / f_c) (the output lags). Above f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. Example with the defaults: 10 kΩ and 10 nF give f_c ≈ 1.59 kHz; at 1 kHz the output is 84.7 % of the input (−1.45 dB) and lags by 32.1°. The formulas assume an unloaded output (load resistance much larger than R) and an ideal source.
items.source: First-order RC low-pass: f_c = 1/(2πRC), |H| = 1/√(1+(f/f_c)²), φ = −arctan(f/f_c); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC filters)

items.name: RC high-pass filter
items.doc: A first-order RC high-pass blocks low frequencies and passes high ones (a coupling capacitor with the input resistance behind it). Cutoff frequency (−3 dB point): f_c = 1 / (2π × R × C). At the test frequency f the amplitude ratio is A_v = (f / f_c) / √(1 + (f / f_c)²), the gain is G = 20 × log10(A_v) and the output leads the input by φ = arctan(f_c / f). Below f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. Example with the defaults: 10 kΩ and 100 nF give f_c ≈ 159 Hz; at 100 Hz the output is 53.2 % of the input (−5.48 dB) and leads by 57.9°. The formulas assume an ideal source and an unloaded output.
items.source: First-order RC high-pass: f_c = 1/(2πRC), |H| = (f/f_c)/√(1+(f/f_c)²), φ = arctan(f_c/f); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC filters)

items.name: LC resonance
items.doc: An ideal LC circuit resonates at the Thomson frequency f_0 = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)); there the reactances are equal, X_L = X_C = √(L / C) = Z_0, the characteristic impedance. Enter any two of L, C and f_0. Example with the defaults: 100 µH and 1 nF resonate at about 503 kHz (medium-wave band) with Z_0 ≈ 316 Ω. Real coils and capacitors have losses; the RLC calculator gives the quality factor and the bandwidth.
items.source: Thomson's resonance formula f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) and Z_0 = √(L/C); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (resonant circuits); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 14 (frequency response, resonance)

items.name: RLC circuit: Q and bandwidth
items.doc: Resonance of a series or a parallel RLC circuit. Both resonate at f_0 = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)). The quality factor is Q = √(L / C) / R for a series circuit (R in series with L and C) and Q = R / √(L / C) for a parallel circuit (R in parallel with L and C, for example a load); the −3 dB bandwidth is BW = f_0 / Q. In the formula the exponent s is +1 for the series and −1 for the parallel circuit. Enter three of the six values; the calculator solves the rest when they determine it (f_0, Q and BW alone do not, because BW = f_0 / Q). Example with the defaults (series circuit): R = 10 Ω, L = 100 µH and C = 1 nF give f_0 ≈ 503 kHz, Q ≈ 31.6 and BW ≈ 15.9 kHz (= R / (2π × L)). For the parallel circuit enter the parallel resistance, for example 10 kΩ, which gives the same Q and BW. A Q below 1 means that the bandwidth is larger than f_0.
items.source: Series and parallel RLC resonance: f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)); series Q = √(L/C)/R, parallel Q = R/√(L/C), BW = f_0/Q; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 14 (series and parallel resonance); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

checks.warn: Q is below 1: the bandwidth is larger than the resonant frequency, the circuit is hardly selective. (For a parallel circuit R is the resistance across the tank.)

items.name: Sallen-Key low-pass (unity gain)
items.doc: Second-order active low-pass in the Sallen-Key topology with unity gain (the op-amp is a voltage follower) and two equal resistors R. C_1 is the capacitor from the junction of the two resistors to the output (feedback), C_2 goes from the non-inverting input to ground. f_0 = 1 / (2π × R × √(C_1 × C_2)) and Q = ½ × √(C_1 / C_2). C_1 = 2 × C_2 gives Q = 0.707 (Butterworth, maximally flat); C_1b shows that C_1 for the present C_2. Enter any three independent values. Example with the defaults: R = 10 kΩ, C_1 = 22 nF and C_2 = 10 nF give f_0 ≈ 1.07 kHz and Q ≈ 0.742. The op-amp is assumed ideal; its bandwidth must be much higher than f_0 and the source impedance low.
items.source: Unity-gain Sallen-Key low-pass with equal resistors: f_0 = 1/(2πR√(C_1C_2)), Q = ½√(C_1/C_2), C_1 the feedback capacitor; R. P. Sallen, E. L. Key: A Practical Method of Designing RC Active Filters, IRE Transactions on Circuit Theory, 1955; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 6 (filters)

items.name: Twin-T notch filter
items.doc: Passive twin-T notch (band-stop) filter: two T networks in parallel between input and output, one of two resistors R with a capacitor 2C to ground, the other of two capacitors C with a resistor R/2 to ground. The transfer function has a zero at f_0 = 1 / (2π × R × C), so the output is (ideally) zero there; R/2 and 2C are the shunt parts. Example with the defaults: R = 31.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF give f_0 ≈ 50.4 Hz, a notch for 50 Hz mains hum (shunt parts 15.8 kΩ and 200 nF). The notch is only deep when the parts match closely (use 1 % resistors and matched capacitors). The passive filter has a low Q (a wide notch) and needs a source impedance much lower than R and a load impedance much higher than R.
items.source: Passive twin-T network (arms R-R-2C and C-C-R/2): transmission zero at f_0 = 1/(2πRC), obtained by nodal analysis; filter textbooks, e.g. P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 6 (filters)

items.name: Pi attenuator
items.doc: Matched resistive pi attenuator (π pad): one series resistor R_s between two equal shunt resistors R_p. Terminated with Z_0 it presents Z_0 at the other port and attenuates by A dB. With the voltage ratio K = 10^(A / 20): R_p = Z_0 × (K + 1) / (K − 1) and R_s = Z_0 × (K² − 1) / (2K). Enter any two of Z_0, A, R_s and R_p. Example with the defaults: 10 dB in a 50 Ω system need R_s ≈ 71.2 Ω and R_p ≈ 96.2 Ω. The power rating of the resistors must cover the dissipated power; this calculator does not size it.
items.source: Matched resistive pi attenuator (image-impedance design): K = 10^(A/20), R_p = Z_0(K+1)/(K−1), R_s = Z_0(K²−1)/(2K); Reference Data for Engineers, 9th ed. (Newnes), chapter on attenuators; formulas checked by two-port analysis

checks.warn: The attenuation must be greater than 0 dB.
R_p must be larger than Z_0 for a pi attenuator; these values do not fit together.

items.name: T attenuator
items.doc: Matched resistive T attenuator (T pad): two equal series resistors R_s with one shunt resistor R_p to ground between them. Terminated with Z_0 it presents Z_0 at the other port and attenuates by A dB. With the voltage ratio K = 10^(A / 20): R_s = Z_0 × (K − 1) / (K + 1) and R_p = 2 × Z_0 × K / (K² − 1). Enter any two of Z_0, A, R_s and R_p. Example with the defaults: 10 dB in a 50 Ω system need R_s ≈ 26.0 Ω and R_p ≈ 35.1 Ω. The power rating of the resistors must cover the dissipated power; this calculator does not size it.
items.source: Matched resistive T attenuator (image-impedance design): K = 10^(A/20), R_s = Z_0(K−1)/(K+1), R_p = 2Z_0K/(K²−1); Reference Data for Engineers, 9th ed. (Newnes), chapter on attenuators; formulas checked by two-port analysis

checks.warn: The attenuation must be greater than 0 dB.
R_s must be smaller than Z_0 for a T attenuator; these values do not fit together.

items.name: LC low-pass, 2nd-order Butterworth
items.doc: Passive second-order LC low-pass with a maximally flat (Butterworth) response: a series inductor L and a shunt capacitor C to ground, sized for the −3 dB cutoff frequency f_c. Two different normalisations exist for this same ladder, and choosing the wrong one halves or doubles C (L is the same in both). Source and load R (both ends): the generator has the internal resistance R and the load is R as well (prototype values g_1 = g_2 = √2): L = √2 × R / (2π × f_c) and C = √2 / (2π × f_c × R); the load then receives half of the source voltage in the pass band (−6 dB, the matched divider, not a loss of the filter) and f_c = √2 × f_0. Voltage source, load R: the source has zero impedance, as an amplifier output, a class-D output stage or a loudspeaker filter fed from a voltage source (g_1 = √2, g_2 = 1/√2): L = √2 × R / (2π × f_c) and C = 1 / (√2 × 2π × f_c × R), half the capacitance; here f_c = f_0. f_0 = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)) is the resonance of L and C alone, and √(L/C) is the ratio of the two reactances at that frequency. Enter any two of R, f_c, L and C. Example with the defaults: 50 Ω at both ends and f_c = 1 MHz give L = 11.25 µH and C = 4.50 nF (the published Stanford example). The parts are assumed ideal: the inductor's resistance lowers the pass band, and above its self-resonance (and with the capacitor's lead inductance) the stop-band attenuation collapses. The stop band falls by 12 dB per octave.
items.source: Butterworth prototype g-values for n = 2 (g_1 = g_2 = 1.4142, doubly terminated) and impedance scaling: M. Steer, Microwave and RF Design IV: Modules, section 2.7 (Butterworth and Chebyshev Filters); Stanford University EE133 handout Filters; voltage-source (singly terminated) case f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), L = √2·R/ω_0, C = 1/(√2·ω_0·R): Texas Instruments, LC Filter Design (SLAA701B), section 1.3.3

vars.label: R
vars.name: Load resistance (with both ends terminated also the source resistance)

derived.label: f_0
derived.name: Resonance of L and C alone

checks.warn: C is only a few pF: stray capacitance of the board and the inductor shifts the cutoff.
L is only a few nH: trace and lead inductance are of the same order.

items.name: Sallen-Key high-pass (unity gain)
items.doc: Second-order active high-pass in the Sallen-Key topology with unity gain (the op-amp is a voltage follower) and two equal capacitors C in series with the signal. R_1 is the feedback resistor, from the junction of the two capacitors to the output; R_2 is the resistor from the non-inverting input to ground. This mirrors the low-pass calculator, where C_1 is the feedback element and C_2 goes to ground. Mind the numbering: the sources differ. The Texas Instruments documents SLOD006B (Op Amps for Everyone) and SLOA024B call the resistor to ground R1, while SBOA225 and Wikipedia call the feedback resistor R1; here R_1 is always the feedback resistor. f_0 = 1 / (2π × C × √(R_1 × R_2)) and Q = ½ × √(R_2 / R_1). R_2 = 2 × R_1 gives Q = 0.707 (Butterworth, maximally flat), and then f_0 is the −3 dB cutoff; R_2b shows that R_2 for the present R_1. For other Q the −3 dB frequency differs from f_0, and at f_0 the gain equals Q. Enter any three independent values. Example with the defaults: R_1 = 11 kΩ, R_2 = 22 kΩ and C = 10 nF give f_0 ≈ 1.023 kHz and Q = 0.707. The op-amp is assumed ideal; being a high-pass, the circuit really is a band-pass whose upper edge the op-amp's bandwidth sets, so choose an op-amp with a gain-bandwidth product far above f_0. The source impedance must be low (it drives a capacitor) and the two capacitors must be equal.
items.source: Unity-gain Sallen-Key high-pass with equal capacitors: f_0 = 1/(2πC√(R_1R_2)), Q = ½√(R_2/R_1), R_1 the feedback resistor; Texas Instruments, Op Amps for Everyone (SLOD006B), chapter 16 (active filter design techniques); Texas Instruments, Analysis of the Sallen-Key Architecture (SLOA024B), high-pass circuit; Texas Instruments, Single-supply, 2nd-order, Sallen-Key high-pass filter circuit (SBOA225)

vars.label: R_2
vars.name: Resistor to ground (at the non-inverting input)

checks.warn: Q is above 0.707: the response rises above the pass-band gain near f_0 (at f_0 the gain is Q).
Q is below 0.5: the two poles are real and the corner is very soft (two cascaded RC high-passes do the same).

items.name: MFB band-pass (multiple feedback)
items.doc: Second-order active band-pass in the multiple-feedback (MFB) topology with one inverting op-amp and two equal capacitors C. The input resistor R_in leads from the signal to a junction; from that junction go the resistor R_gnd to ground and one capacitor to the output and the other capacitor to the inverting input; the feedback resistor R_fb connects the output to the inverting input; the non-inverting input is grounded. The resistors are named by their place, because the sources number them differently (what Texas Instruments calls R2 is the feedback resistor, what Analog Devices calls R2 is the resistor to ground). f_0 = √((R_in + R_gnd) / (R_in × R_gnd × R_fb)) / (2π × C), Q = π × f_0 × R_fb × C, G = R_fb / (2 × R_in) and the −3 dB bandwidth B = f_0 / Q = 1 / (π × R_fb × C). G is the gain at the centre frequency f_0 (the output is inverted there); Analog Devices' H is not this gain, the centre gain is H × Q. R_gnd shifts f_0 without changing B or G. For a design enter f_0, Q, G and C: R_fb = Q / (π × f_0 × C), R_in = R_fb / (2G) and R_gnd = G × R_in / (2Q² − G). R_gnd exists only for 2 × Q² > G; at 2 × Q² = G the resistor is left out, and a higher gain at that Q cannot be built with this circuit. Example with the defaults, the rounded values of the Texas Instruments example: 7.96 kΩ, 80.4 Ω, 31.8 kΩ and 100 nF give f_0 ≈ 1.0004 kHz, Q ≈ 9.99 and G ≈ 2.0. The op-amp is assumed ideal; its open-loop gain at f_0 should be at least 20 dB above the gain at f_0 (Analog Devices), and the circuit suits Q up to about 20.
items.source: Multiple-feedback band-pass, one op-amp, equal capacitors: f_0, Q = π·f_0·R_fb·C, G = R_fb/(2R_in), B = 1/(πR_fbC); Texas Instruments, Op Amps for Everyone (SLOD006B), chapter 16 (multiple feedback topology, Example 16-5); Analog Devices, Mini Tutorial MT-218 Multiple Feedback Band-Pass Design Example

vars.label: R_gnd
vars.name: Resistor from the junction to ground

checks.warn: Not realisable: R_gnd exists only for Q² > G / 2. Lower the gain or raise Q (at Q² = G / 2 the resistor R_gnd is left out).
Q above about 20: the single-op-amp MFB band-pass becomes very sensitive to tolerances and needs an op-amp with very high gain at f_0; a filter with two or three op-amps is better.

formula: f0 = sqrt((rin + rgnd) / (rin * rgnd * rfb)) / (2 * pi * c)

items.name: 2-way speaker crossover, 2nd order
items.doc: Passive second-order (12 dB per octave) crossover between an amplifier and two drivers. The woofer section is a series inductor L with a capacitor C in parallel with the driver, the tweeter section the dual: a series capacitor C with an inductor L in parallel with the driver. Both are fed from the amplifier, a voltage source, and the values below size each section for its own driver impedance R. They are the relations of the second-order low-pass driven from a voltage source into the load R: f = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)) and Q = R × √(C / L), hence L = R / (2π × f × Q) and C = Q / (2π × f × R). Butterworth uses Q = 0.707 (L = 0.2251 × R / f, C = 0.1125 / (f × R)), the section is 3 dB down at the crossover frequency and the summed response rises by 3 dB there. Linkwitz-Riley uses Q = 0.5 (L = 0.3183 × R / f, C = 0.07958 / (f × R)), each section is 6 dB down at f and the sum is flat. In a second-order crossover the two outputs are 180° apart, so the tweeter is connected with reversed polarity. Enter any two of R, f, L and C. Example with the defaults: 6 Ω and 3 kHz Linkwitz-Riley give L = 637 µH and C = 4.42 µF. The drivers are assumed to be pure resistances: use the impedance measured at the crossover frequency, not the nominal 4 Ω or 8 Ω (a real driver's impedance rises with frequency and has a resonance peak), otherwise crossover frequency and slope differ. Ideal parts and an amplifier with zero output impedance are assumed; the DC resistance of the inductor lowers the level of the woofer. Only the electrical filter is described: the drivers' own responses, sensitivities and mounting distance also shape the result.
items.source: Second-order low-pass driven from a voltage source into the load R (f = 1/(2π√(LC)), Q = R√(C/L)): Texas Instruments, LC Filter Design (SLAA701B), section 1.3.3; Q of the Butterworth (0.7071) and the Bessel alignment: Texas Instruments, Op Amps for Everyone (SLOD006B), chapter 16, Tables 16-4 and 16-5; Linkwitz-Riley alignment (two cascaded first-order sections, Q = 0.5, −6 dB at the crossover, one output inverted): D. Bohn, Linkwitz-Riley Crossovers: A Primer, RaneNote 160, Rane Corporation

vars.label: R
vars.name: Driver impedance at the crossover frequency (resistive)

vars.label: L
vars.name: Inductor (series at the woofer, parallel at the tweeter)

vars.label: C
vars.name: Capacitor (parallel at the woofer, series at the tweeter)

items.name: L-pad attenuator
items.doc: Loudspeaker L-pad: a series resistor R_s and a parallel resistor R_p across the driver lower the level of a driver (usually the tweeter) by A dB while the crossover still sees the driver's impedance Z. Two conditions fix the resistors: the input resistance R_s + (R_p ‖ Z) equals Z, and the divider ratio (R_p ‖ Z) / Z equals 1 / K. With the voltage ratio K = 10^(A / 20): R_s = Z × (K − 1) / K and R_p = Z / (K − 1). Enter any two of Z, A, R_s and R_p; from R_s and R_p alone Z = (R_s + √(R_s² + 4 × R_s × R_p)) / 2. Example with the defaults: 6 dB for an 8 Ω driver need R_s ≈ 3.99 Ω and R_p ≈ 8.04 Ω. The pad is constant-impedance only looking into it from the crossover (looking back from the driver the source resistance is no longer near zero), which is why L-pads belong on tweeters and not on woofers. It sits between the crossover and the driver, never in front of the crossover. The driver is treated as a pure resistance; the real impedance of a tweeter varies with frequency, which the parallel resistor reduces. This is the loudspeaker L-pad, not the RF L-pad that matches two different impedances. The calculator does not size the resistors' power: choose power ratings well above the power in this branch of the crossover, which is not the amplifier's rated power.
items.source: Constant-impedance loudspeaker L-pad: input resistance R_s + R_p‖Z = Z and divider ratio 1/K with K = 10^(A/20), derived by Ohm's law; the same design steps and a worked example: R. Elliott, Design of Passive Crossovers, Elliott Sound Products, section Attenuation Networks

checks.warn: No attenuation: no pad is needed (R_s = 0, R_p open).
R_s is not below Z: no constant-impedance pad exists with this series resistor.

items.name: Cable cross-section finder
items.doc: Finds the smallest standard cross-section of a cable for a design current Ib from the current-carrying capacity tables of IEC 60364-5-52 and DIN VDE 0298-4 (guide values; the standard is authoritative). Choose the conductor and insulation (copper or aluminium, PVC 70 °C or XLPE/EPR 90 °C), the installation method (A1 to F) and the number of loaded conductors (2 for single-phase or DC, 3 for three-phase). The table value, valid for 30 °C ambient air and one circuit, is multiplied by the ambient temperature factor kt (linear interpolation between the listed temperatures) and by the grouping factor kg of the number of circuits (bunched for A1 to B2, one layer on a wall for C, one layer on a perforated tray for E and F; a count between two listed counts takes the next larger listed one). The result is the first cross-section whose corrected capacity Iz = table value × kt × kg is at least Ib, so the table value must reach Ib / (kt × kg). Empty cells of the tables (method F below 25 mm², the 2.5 mm² cells of copper XLPE in A1 and B1, most aluminium cells and the bunched factor for 14 circuits have no value that two sources confirmed) are skipped by the search, and a combination without any cell is reported as not covered. The protective device (Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz), voltage drop and short-circuit limits are not checked. The row of the result is highlighted in the table. The defaults (20 A, 30 °C, one circuit, copper PVC, method B2, two loaded conductors) give 2.5 mm² with Iz = 23 A. Where IEC and DIN differ (1.5 mm² in A1 and A2, two loaded conductors) the IEC table value is used.
items.source: IEC 60364-5-52:2009 annex B (current-carrying capacity tables B.52.2 to B.52.5 and B.52.10 to B.52.13, ambient temperature factors B.52.14, grouping factors B.52.17) and DIN VDE 0298-4:2013-06; selection rule Iz = table value × kt × kg ≥ Ib

items.name: PCB conductor spacing finder (IPC-2221)
items.doc: Finds the minimum spacing between two conductors on a printed board for the voltage between them, from table 6-1 of IPC-2221B or IPC-2221C. Enter the DC voltage or the AC peak value, or choose AC RMS of a sine wave (the peak is then the RMS value times √2). Choose the revision and the column of the table for the board condition: B1 internal conductors, B2 external uncoated up to 3050 m, B3 external uncoated above 3050 m (C also in vacuum), B4 external with permanent polymer coating in B or solder mask in C, B5 external coated at any elevation or in vacuum (A5 with conformal coating in revision B), A6 to A8 component leads; A6 and A7 mean different things in the two revisions (revision B: A6 uncoated, A7 coated; revision C: A6 coated at any elevation or in vacuum, A7 uncoated up to 3050 m, A8 without conformal coating above 3050 m or in vacuum). The voltage bands use whole volts, so a voltage between two bands (15.5 V) takes the next band up. Above 500 V the spacing is the value of the 301 to 500 V band plus the per-volt increment of the table for every volt above 500 V. IPC-2221 gives functional spacing for the board, not safety isolation: for mains or SELV separation the creepage and clearance of IEC 60664-1 and IEC 62368-1 apply. The row of the result is highlighted in the table. The defaults (400 V, revision C, column B2) give 2.5 mm.
