items.name: Inverting amplifier
items.doc: The inverting op-amp amplifier: the input signal V_in reaches the inverting input through R_in, and the feedback resistor R_f returns part of the output to the same node. With an ideal op-amp this node is a virtual ground, so the gain is A_v = −R_f / R_in and V_out = A_v × V_in. The input resistance of the stage is R_in. Example with the defaults: R_in = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ give a gain of −10 (20 dB), so 0.1 V in gives −1 V out. The noise gain 1 + R_f / R_in = 11 sets the usable bandwidth (gain-bandwidth product divided by the noise gain). The output cannot exceed the supply rails.
items.source: Inverting amplifier with an ideal op-amp (virtual ground): A_v = −R_f / R_in; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

checks.warn: An inverting amplifier has a negative gain (−R_f / R_in): a positive gain is not possible with this circuit.

items.name: Non-inverting amplifier
items.doc: The non-inverting op-amp amplifier: the signal drives the non-inverting input, and the divider R_f / R_g in the feedback path sets the gain G = 1 + R_f / R_g, which is always 1 or more (V_out = G × V_in, same sign as the input). The input resistance is that of the op-amp input and very high. Example with the defaults: R_f = 10 kΩ and R_g = 1 kΩ give a gain of 11 (20.8 dB), so 0.1 V in gives 1.1 V out. For a gain of exactly 1 leave out R_g and replace R_f by a wire (voltage follower).
items.source: Non-inverting amplifier with an ideal op-amp: G = 1 + R_f / R_g; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

checks.warn: The gain must be above 1: a non-inverting amplifier cannot attenuate. For a gain of exactly 1 use a voltage follower (no R_g, R_f replaced by a wire).

items.name: Difference amplifier
items.doc: The classic op-amp difference amplifier with four resistors, R_3 = R_1 and R_4 = R_2: the signal V_1 reaches the inverting input through R_1, the signal V_2 reaches the non-inverting input through R_3 (which forms a divider with R_4 to ground), and R_2 is the feedback resistor. The output is V_out = (R_2 / R_1) × (V_2 − V_1): only the difference is amplified and a common-mode voltage is rejected, but only as well as the resistor ratios R_2 / R_1 and R_4 / R_3 match. The differential input resistance is 2 × R_1. Example with the defaults: R_1 = 10 kΩ and R_2 = 100 kΩ give a gain of 10, so V_2 − V_1 = 0.2 V gives 2 V out.
items.source: Difference amplifier with R_3 = R_1 and R_4 = R_2 (ideal op-amp): V_out = (R_2 / R_1) × (V_2 − V_1); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4; A. S. Sedra, K. C. Smith: Microelectronic Circuits (operational amplifiers)

items.name: Summing amplifier
items.doc: The inverting summing amplifier with equal input resistors R: every input V_k reaches the summing node through its own resistor R, the currents add, and the output is V_out = −(R_f / R) × (V_1 + V_2 + … + V_n). Every input has the same gain −R_f / R, and the inputs do not influence each other because the summing node is a virtual ground. With R_f = R / n the output is the inverted average of the n inputs. Enter the input voltages as a list, for example 1 V, 0.5 V, 0.25 V. Example with the defaults: inputs of 1 V, 0.5 V and 0.25 V with R = R_f = 10 kΩ give −1.75 V.
items.source: Inverting summing amplifier with an ideal op-amp: V_out = −R_f × Σ(V_k / R); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

derived.label: G_k
derived.name: Gain magnitude per input R_f / R

items.name: Integrator
items.doc: The ideal inverting integrator: a constant input V_in through R charges the feedback capacitor C with the current V_in / R, so the output ramps linearly, V_out = −V_in × t / (R × C), starting from zero at t = 0. For sine signals the gain falls as 1 / (2π f R C) and is 1 at the unity-gain frequency f = 1 / (2π R C). A real circuit needs a resistor in parallel with C or a reset switch, otherwise offset voltage and bias current drive the output into the supply rails. Example with the defaults: 1 V into R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF (R × C = 1 ms) gives −2 V after 2 ms.
items.source: Ideal inverting integrator: V_out = −(1 / RC) ∫ V_in dt; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

checks.warn: |V_out| is above 15 V: a real op-amp saturates at its supply rails long before this time.

items.name: Schmitt trigger
items.doc: Inverting Schmitt trigger with a reference: the input signal drives the inverting input, the non-inverting input sits between the reference V_ref (through R_1) and the output (through R_2, positive feedback). The output is at V_OH or V_OL, its saturation levels close to the supply rails (read them from the datasheet or measure them). The threshold at the non-inverting input is V_TH = V_ref + (V_OH − V_ref) × k with the output high and V_TL = V_ref + (V_OL − V_ref) × k with the output low, where k = R_1 / (R_1 + R_2). The output switches low when the input rises above V_TH and high when it falls below V_TL; the hysteresis is V_TH − V_TL = k × (V_OH − V_OL). For a design enter the four voltages and R_1 (or R_2) to get the other resistor and V_ref. Example with the defaults: a 5 V supply (V_OH = 5 V, V_OL = 0 V), V_ref = 2.5 V, R_1 = 10 kΩ and R_2 = 100 kΩ give V_TH ≈ 2.73 V, V_TL ≈ 2.27 V and a hysteresis of about 0.45 V.
items.source: Inverting Schmitt trigger with positive feedback through R_2 and a reference at R_1: V_TH, V_TL = V_ref + (V_O − V_ref) × R_1 / (R_1 + R_2); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4; A. S. Sedra, K. C. Smith: Microelectronic Circuits (bistable circuits)

checks.warn: V_OH must be above V_OL.

items.name: Instrumentation amplifier
items.doc: The classic instrumentation amplifier in the three-op-amp topology: two input buffer stages share one gain resistor R_G between their inverting inputs, and a unity-gain difference amplifier (four equal resistors) forms the output stage. The differential gain is G = 1 + 2R / R_G, where R is each of the two feedback resistors of the input stage (integrated types state the sum: G = 1 + 50 kΩ / R_G for the Texas Instruments INA128, G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / R_G for the Analog Devices AD620). Only the differential input V_diff = V+ − V− is amplified by G; a common-mode voltage passes the input stage with a gain of 1 and is rejected by the output stage. Without R_G the gain is 1. Example with the defaults: R = 25 kΩ and R_G = 500 Ω give G = 101 (40.1 dB), so 10 mV differential input gives 1.01 V.
items.source: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier, G = 1 + 2R / R_G (ideal op-amps, equal output-stage resistors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (instrumentation amplifiers); gain equations of the INA128 (Texas Instruments) and AD620 (Analog Devices) data sheets

derived.label: 2R
derived.name: Sum of the two feedback resistors 2R

checks.warn: The gain must be above 1: without R_G (open) the gain is exactly 1.

items.name: Differentiator
items.doc: The inverting op-amp differentiator: an input capacitor C and a feedback resistor R, so that V_out = −R × C × dV_in / dt. For a sine of frequency f the gain magnitude is A = 2π × f × R × C (rising 20 dB per decade, the output is inverted and lags a sine input by 90°) and it is 1 at the unity-gain frequency f_0 = 1 / (2π × R × C). The ideal circuit (without R_in) is fundamentally unstable and amplifies noise, so a real circuit adds a series resistor R_in at the input (the stop resistor): H = −s × R × C / (1 + s × R_in × C). Above the corner f_1 = 1 / (2π × R_in × C) the circuit stops differentiating and acts as an inverting amplifier with gain R / R_in. A_p is the gain with R_in at f: A / √(1 + (f / f_1)²), so at f = f_1 / 10 the amplitude is 99.5 % of the ideal value and at f_1 it is 70.7 %. Keep the highest signal frequency at least 3.5 times below f_1. A feedback capacitor across R (a second corner 1 / (2π × R × C_f)) is not modelled here. Fast input edges give R × C × dV / dt at the output and drive the op-amp into the supply rails, so check the largest slope. Example with the defaults: R = 100 kΩ, C = 10 nF and R_in = 1 kΩ give A = 6.28 at 1 kHz (f_0 = 159 Hz, f_1 = 15.9 kHz).
items.source: Inverting differentiator, V_out = −R·C·dV_in/dt, with a series input resistor: Texas Instruments, Differentiator Circuit, Analog Engineer's Circuit (SBOA276); Texas Instruments (Burr-Brown), Handbook of Operational Amplifier Applications (SBOA092B), differentiator with stop; J. M. Fiore: Operational Amplifiers and Linear Integrated Circuits: Theory and Application, chapter 10 (differentiators)

derived.label: A_p
derived.name: Gain magnitude with R_in at f

checks.warn: Without a series resistor (or a feedback capacitor, not modelled here) the differentiator is unstable and amplifies high-frequency noise.
R_in is not below R: there is no differentiating range left.
The signal frequency is closer than 3.5 times to the corner frequency f_1: the circuit no longer differentiates accurately (amplitude and phase error).

items.name: Closed-loop bandwidth from GBW
items.doc: Closed-loop −3 dB bandwidth of a voltage-feedback op-amp stage: BW = GBW / G_n, where G_n is the noise gain 1 + R_f / R_i. For a non-inverting stage the noise gain equals the signal gain G; for an inverting stage with gain −G it is G + 1, not G. This is the usual trap: an inverting stage with gain −1 has only half of GBW as bandwidth. Choose the configuration and enter the magnitude of the signal gain G. Enter any two of GBW, G and the bandwidth f. Example with the defaults: GBW = 1 MHz and a non-inverting gain of 10 give 100 kHz; the same gain inverting (noise gain 11) gives 90.9 kHz. The relation holds for an internally compensated voltage-feedback op-amp with one dominant pole (open-loop gain falling by 20 dB per decade through the crossover) and a resistive feedback network; it does not hold for current-feedback amplifiers. GBW varies from part to part and with temperature, so leave margin. The result is a small-signal bandwidth; large output swings are also limited by the slew rate (see the slew rate calculator), and the smaller of the two limits applies.
items.source: Closed-loop bandwidth BW = GBW / noise gain, noise gain = 1 + R_f/R_i: Texas Instruments, Analog Engineer's Pocket Reference (SLYW038D), section Op amp bandwidth; J. M. Fiore: Operational Amplifiers and Linear Integrated Circuits: Theory and Application, section 5.3 (gain-bandwidth product); Texas Instruments, Cascading Precision Op Amp Stages for Optimal AC and DC Performance (SBOA356)

derived.label: G_n
derived.name: Noise gain (G for non-inverting, G + 1 for inverting)

checks.warn: A non-inverting amplifier cannot have a gain below 1.

items.name: Slew rate and full-power bandwidth
items.doc: Full-power bandwidth: the highest sine frequency an amplifier can deliver at a given output amplitude before its slew rate distorts the signal. A sine V_p × sin(2π f t) is steepest at the zero crossing, where dV/dt = 2π × f × V_p; the slew rate limit is reached when this equals SR, so f = SR / (2π × V_p). Enter any two of SR, V_p and f. V_p is the PEAK voltage (the amplitude) at the output. Two published forms differ only in this convention: Texas Instruments uses the peak value with 2π, Microchip the peak-to-peak value with π (f = SR / (π × V_pp)); V_pp is shown so that you can compare. Using the peak-to-peak value with 2π gives a result too small by a factor of 2, and the RMS value one too large by √2. Example with the defaults: 0.5 V/µs and 10 V peak give 7.96 kHz. Distortion begins gradually below this frequency, so for low distortion choose a slew rate several times higher. The small-signal bandwidth (GBW divided by the noise gain) must also be sufficient; the smaller of the two limits applies. Datasheet slew rates are typical values for a large step, and the formula is an upper limit: measured full-power curves use a distortion criterion and lie lower.
items.source: Full-power bandwidth f = SR/(2π·V_p) with V_p the peak value: Texas Instruments, Analog Engineer's Pocket Reference (SLYW038D), section Full power bandwidth; Texas Instruments (National Semiconductor), Predicting Op Amp Slew Rate Limited Response (Linear Brief 19, SNOA852); equivalent form SR/(π·V_pp): Microchip, Operational Amplifier AC Specifications and Applications (AN723)

items.name: Capacitive reactance
items.doc: A capacitor opposes an alternating current with the reactance X_C = 1 / (2π × f × C). It falls as the frequency or the capacitance rises: a capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies. The current through an ideal capacitor leads the voltage by 90°. Example: 100 nF at 1 kHz has X_C ≈ 1.59 kΩ. ESR, ESL and dielectric losses are ignored.
items.source: Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ωC) with ω = 2πf; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors)

items.name: Inductive reactance
items.doc: An inductor opposes an alternating current with the reactance X_L = 2π × f × L. It rises with the frequency or the inductance: an inductor passes DC and blocks high frequencies. The current through an ideal inductor lags the voltage by 90°. Example: 10 mH at 1 kHz has X_L ≈ 62.8 Ω. Winding resistance and self-capacitance are ignored.
items.source: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL with ω = 2πf; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors)

items.name: Series impedance (RC, RL, RLC)
items.doc: The impedance of a resistor R in series with an inductor L, a capacitor C or both, at the frequency f. The reactances are X_L = 2π × f × L and X_C = 1 / (2π × f × C); the net reactance is X = X_L − X_C, the magnitude |Z| = √(R² + X²) and the phase φ = arctan(X / R) (positive: inductive, negative: capacitive). Choose the circuit first; the component that is not used is dimmed. At resonance X = 0 and |Z| = R. Example: 100 Ω, 10 mH and 1 µF at 1 kHz give X ≈ −96.3 Ω, |Z| ≈ 138.8 Ω and φ ≈ −43.9°.
items.source: Impedance of series RC, RL and RLC circuits (Z = R + jX, X = ωL − 1/(ωC)); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Parallel impedance (RC, RL, RLC)
items.doc: The impedance of a resistor R in parallel with an inductor L, a capacitor C or both, at the frequency f. The admittance is Y = 1/R + j × B with the susceptance B = 2π × f × C − 1 / (2π × f × L); the magnitude is |Z| = 1 / √((1/R)² + B²) and the phase φ = arctan(R × (1 / (2π × f × L) − 2π × f × C)) (positive: inductive, negative: capacitive). ECalc has no unit for a susceptance, so it shows the equivalent parallel reactance X_p = −1 / B instead; at resonance B = 0, the LC branch is an open circuit and X_p is infinite (shown as –). Choose the circuit first; the component that is not used is dimmed. Example: 100 Ω, 10 mH and 1 µF in parallel at 1 kHz give |Z| ≈ 72.0 Ω and φ ≈ +43.9°.
items.source: Impedance of parallel RC, RL and RLC circuits (admittance Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)), Z = 1/Y); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1
formula: z = 1 / sqrt(1 / r^2 + (uc * 2 * pi * f * c - ul / (2 * pi * f * l))^2)
phi = atan(r * (ul / (2 * pi * f * l) - uc * 2 * pi * f * c))

items.name: RC time constant
items.doc: A capacitor C charges or discharges through a resistor R with the time constant τ = R × C. In general V_C = V_f + (V_i − V_f) × e^(−t/τ) with the initial voltage V_i and the final voltage V_f. Charging towards the supply voltage V_0 means V_i = 0 and V_f = V_0, so V_C = V_0 × (1 − e^(−t/τ)); discharging from the initial voltage V_0 means V_i = V_0 and V_f = 0, so V_C = V_0 × e^(−t/τ). After 1 τ the capacitor has covered 63.2 % of the way, after 5 τ 99.3 %. Example: 10 kΩ and 100 µF have τ = 1 s; charging from a 5 V supply, V_C is 3.16 V after 1 s. The chart shows V_C from 0 to 5 τ.
items.source: First-order RC step response V_C(t) = V_f + (V_i − V_f)·e^(−t/RC); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC circuits); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 7 (first-order circuits)

checks.warn: V_C is at or beyond the final voltage V_f (V_0 when charging, 0 V when discharging). The capacitor only approaches V_f, so no finite time reaches it.
V_C lies on the far side of the initial voltage V_i: the capacitor starts at V_i and moves towards V_f, so this value would need a negative time.

items.name: Series and parallel capacitors
items.doc: Capacitors in parallel add up: C_P = C_1 + C_2 + …. Capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel: 1/C_S = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + …, so the total is smaller than the smallest capacitor. In series the voltage divides in inverse proportion to the capacitance; polarised capacitors in series need balancing resistors. Enter the values as a list, for example 4.7µ, 10µ, 22µ.
items.source: Series and parallel capacitor combination; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Series and parallel inductors
items.doc: Inductors in series add up: L_S = L_1 + L_2 + …. Inductors in parallel combine like resistors in parallel: 1/L_P = 1/L_1 + 1/L_2 + …, so the total is smaller than the smallest inductor. This holds only while the coils do not couple magnetically; mutual inductance is ignored. Enter the values as a list, for example 1m, 2.2m, 4.7m.
items.source: Series and parallel inductor combination (no mutual coupling); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Capacitor energy and charge
items.doc: The energy stored in a capacitor is E = ½ × C × U² and its charge is Q = C × U; also E = ½ × Q × U = Q² / (2 × C). Any two of the four values determine the other two. Example: 1000 µF at 12 V stores 72 mJ and 12 mC. Large or high-voltage capacitors can keep a dangerous charge long after switch-off: discharge them through a suitable resistor before touching them.
items.source: Energy stored in a capacitor E = ½CU² and charge Q = CU; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Air-core coil (Wheeler)
items.doc: Inductance of a single-layer, close-wound air-core coil (solenoid) by Wheeler's formula: L [µH] = N² × r² / (9 × r + 10 × ℓ), with the mean coil radius r and the winding length ℓ both in inches. In the SI units used here this is L = N² × D² / (50800 × (9 × D + 20 × ℓ)) with the mean diameter D (to the centre of the wire) and the length ℓ in metres. It is accurate to about 1 % for ℓ ≥ 0.8 × r (a coil at least 0.4 diameters long) and becomes rough for shorter coils; it assumes an air core and a wire much thinner than the coil. The wire length is the helix at the mean diameter without leads. Example: 25 turns on a 20 mm diameter, 30 mm long winding give about 6.3 µH.
items.source: H. A. Wheeler: Simple Inductance Formulas for Radio Coils, Proceedings of the IRE, vol. 16, no. 10, October 1928 (single-layer coil L = N²r²/(9r + 10ℓ) in inches and microhenries, accurate to about 1 % for ℓ > 0.8r)

checks.warn: The coil is shorter than 0.4 × its diameter: Wheeler's formula is only a rough estimate here (it is accurate to about 1 % from a length of 0.8 × the radius).

items.name: Toroid inductance (A_L)
items.doc: The inductance of a winding on a ferrite or powdered-iron core follows from the inductance factor A_L of the core: L = A_L × N². Data sheets print A_L in nH per turn² (1 nH/N² corresponds to 1 mH per 1000 turns); enter it with the unit prefix, for example 250n for 250 nH. N counts the turns through the centre of the core. A_L holds for small signals below saturation and is stated with a tolerance, so the result is only as exact as the core. N_w is the turn count rounded up to whole turns. Example: A_L = 250 nH and 20 turns give 100 µH.
items.source: Definition of the inductance factor A_L of a magnetic core, L = A_L·N² (A_L in nH/N² as printed in the data sheets of ferrite and powdered-iron core makers)

items.name: Wire resistance
items.doc: DC resistance of a straight conductor: R = ρ(T) × ℓ / A with ρ(T) = ρ20 × (1 + α × (T − 20 °C)). ρ20 and the temperature coefficient α are those of the selected material at 20 °C: annealed copper per IEC 60028 (ρ20 = 0.017241 Ω·mm²/m, α = 0.00393 1/K); aluminium per IEC 60889, hard-drawn aluminium wire (ρ20 = 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m, the 61 % IACS value, α = 0.00403 1/K); silver is a typical handbook value. Values of real wires vary with purity and alloy. The cross-section can be entered in mm², AWG (ASTM B258) or kcmil. For a two-wire run use twice the one-way length. The linear temperature model is reliable only in a moderate range around 20 °C. Example: 10 m of 1.5 mm² copper at 20 °C have 0.115 Ω.
items.source: R = ρ·ℓ/A with ρ(T) = ρ20·(1 + α·(T − 20 °C)); annealed copper ρ20 = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (rounded to 0.017241) and α20 = 0.00393 1/K per IEC 60028; aluminium ρ20 = 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m (the 61 % IACS value) and α = 0.00403 1/K per IEC 60889 (hard-drawn aluminium wire for overhead line conductors); silver 15.9 nΩ·m with α ≈ 0.0038 1/K as typical handbook values (e.g. CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics); AWG per ASTM B258

checks.warn: The temperature is far from 20 °C (below −50 °C or above 150 °C): the linear temperature model loses accuracy there.

formula: r = rho20 * (1 + tcr * dt) * len / a

items.name: Transformer turns ratio
items.doc: An ideal transformer: the voltages are in the ratio of the turns, U_s / U_p = N_s / N_p, the currents are in the inverse ratio, I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s, and the apparent power is the same on both sides, S = U_p × I_p = U_s × I_s. The turns ratio is defined here as n = N_p / N_s, so n > 1 is a step-down transformer (some datasheets state the inverse). An impedance on the secondary appears at the primary multiplied by n²: Z_p = n² × Z_L, which is how a transformer matches a source to a load (n = √(Z_p / Z_L)). Any four of the six values N_p, N_s, U_p, U_s, I_p, I_s that fix both ratios determine the rest. The model is ideal: winding resistance, leakage inductance, core losses and magnetising current are ignored. A real small transformer gives a higher voltage unloaded and a lower one at full load, draws a magnetising current with no load and has an efficiency below 100 %. It works with alternating voltage only (RMS values); a transformer does not pass direct current. The defaults (1000 : 52 turns on 230 V with 2 A on the secondary) give 11.96 V, 0.104 A and n = 19.23.
items.source: Ideal transformer U_s / U_p = N_s / N_p, I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s, Z_p = (N_p / N_s)² × Z_L: T. R. Kuphaldt: Lessons in Electric Circuits, vol. II (AC), ch. 9 (Transformers); J. Kirtley: Introduction to Electric Power Systems (MIT), ch. 3, section 3.4 (Transformers)

checks.warn: The number of turns must be greater than zero.

items.name: LM317 output voltage
items.doc: The adjustable regulator LM317 holds its reference voltage V_ref (about 1.25 V) between the OUT and ADJ pins. R_1 from OUT to ADJ and R_2 from ADJ to ground set the output voltage: V_out = V_ref × (1 + R_2 / R_1) + I_adj × R_2. The adjustment-pin current I_adj (typically 50 µA) also flows through R_2. About 240 Ω is the usual value for R_1. V_ref and I_adj are typical datasheet values and vary from part to part (V_ref from 1.2 V to 1.3 V). The defaults R_1 = 240 Ω and R_2 = 720 Ω give 5.036 V. The input voltage must stay above V_out by at least the dropout voltage of the regulator.
items.source: LM317 datasheets (Texas Instruments, STMicroelectronics): V_OUT = V_REF × (1 + R2 / R1) + I_ADJ × R2 with the typical V_REF = 1.25 V and I_ADJ = 50 µA

checks.warn: V_out is below the reference voltage: the LM317 cannot regulate lower than about 1.25 V.

formula: vout = vref * (1 + r2 / r1) + iadj * r2

items.name: LM317 constant-current source
items.doc: The LM317 as a constant-current source: the regulator keeps V_ref (about 1.25 V) across the resistor R between its OUT and ADJ pins, so R carries V_ref / R. The load sits between the ADJ pin and ground and also receives the adjustment-pin current I_adj (typically 50 µA): I = V_ref / R + I_adj. The resistor dissipates V_ref² / R. The default R = 10 Ω gives 125 mA with about 156 mW in the resistor. The input voltage must exceed the load voltage plus V_ref plus the dropout voltage of the regulator.
items.source: LM317 datasheets (Texas Instruments, STMicroelectronics): constant-current connection with the resistor between OUT and ADJ, I = V_REF / R + I_ADJ (V_REF = 1.25 V and I_ADJ = 50 µA typical)

checks.warn: The load current is above the rated output current of the LM317 (1.5 A).
The load current must be larger than the adjustment-pin current I_adj; no resistor can set it.

items.name: Linear regulator power loss
items.doc: A linear regulator turns the voltage difference between input and output into heat: P = (V_in − V_out) × I_out + V_in × I_q, where I_q is the quiescent current the regulator draws from the input in addition to the load current. The efficiency is η = V_out × I_out / (V_in × (I_out + I_q)). The defaults (12 V to 5 V at 500 mA with 5 mA quiescent current) dissipate 3.56 W at an efficiency of 41 %; this heat has to be removed with a heat sink, or the input voltage has to be lowered.
items.source: Power balance of a series (linear) regulator: P = (V_in − V_out) × I_out + V_in × I_q; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a linear regulator needs an input voltage above the output voltage (plus its dropout voltage).

items.name: Buck converter (step-down)
items.doc: An ideal step-down (buck) converter in continuous conduction: the duty cycle is D = V_out / V_in and the peak-to-peak inductor ripple current is ΔI_L = V_out × (V_in − V_out) / (V_in × f_sw × L). The inductor current swings between I_out − ΔI_L / 2 and I_out + ΔI_L / 2, so the inductor and the switch must handle the peak current I_pk = I_out + ΔI_L / 2. Assumptions: lossless components, constant input and output voltages, continuous conduction (the valley current stays above zero); I_out is the average output current. A ripple of 20 % to 40 % of I_out is a common design target. The defaults (12 V to 5 V, 1 A, 100 kHz, 100 µH) give D = 41.7 %, ΔI_L = 0.29 A and I_pk = 1.15 A. V_out and I_out are always inputs (V_out cannot be solved from the ripple current, because two output voltages give the same ripple).
items.source: Ideal continuous-conduction buck converter (D = V_out / V_in, ΔI_L = (V_in − V_out) × D / (f_sw × L)); R. W. Erickson, D. Maksimović: Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a buck converter can only step down.
The ripple current exceeds twice the output current: the inductor current falls to zero and the converter leaves continuous conduction, so these formulas no longer apply.

items.name: Boost converter (step-up)
items.doc: An ideal step-up (boost) converter in continuous conduction: the duty cycle is D = 1 − V_in / V_out, the average inductor current (equal to the input current) is I_L = I_out × V_out / V_in, and the peak-to-peak ripple current is ΔI_L = V_in × (V_out − V_in) / (V_out × f_sw × L). The inductor and the switch must handle the peak current I_pk = I_L + ΔI_L / 2. Assumptions: lossless components, constant input and output voltages, continuous conduction (the valley current stays above zero); I_out is the average output current. The defaults (5 V to 12 V, 0.5 A, 100 kHz, 100 µH) give D = 58.3 %, I_L = 1.2 A, ΔI_L = 0.29 A and I_pk = 1.35 A. V_in and I_out are always inputs (V_in cannot be solved from the ripple current, because two input voltages give the same ripple).
items.source: Ideal continuous-conduction boost converter (D = 1 − V_in / V_out, I_L = I_out / (1 − D), ΔI_L = V_in × D / (f_sw × L)); R. W. Erickson, D. Maksimović: Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

checks.warn: V_out is not above V_in: a boost converter can only step up.
The ripple current exceeds twice the average inductor current: the inductor current falls to zero and the converter leaves continuous conduction, so these formulas no longer apply.

items.name: Smoothing capacitor
items.doc: The capacitor behind a rectifier supplies the load between the charging peaks. The peak-to-peak ripple is approximately ΔV = I / (m × f × C), where f is the mains frequency and m the number of charging peaks per mains cycle: 1 for a half-wave rectifier, 2 for a full-wave (bridge) rectifier. The estimate takes the whole period between the peaks as the discharge time and neglects the short charging time, so the real ripple is slightly lower. The defaults (1 A, 50 Hz, 1 V ripple, full wave) need 10 mF (10 000 µF). The drawing shows the bridge; for half-wave use a single diode.
items.source: Capacitor-input filter ripple estimate ΔV = I / (m × f × C) with m = 1 (half-wave) or 2 (full-wave), charging time neglected; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

items.name: Battery runtime
items.doc: The runtime of a battery follows from its capacity and the load current: t = Q × usable fraction / I. The usable fraction is the part of the rated capacity you can actually draw; the cut-off voltage, ageing, low temperature and high discharge currents reduce it. The defaults (a 2500 mAh cell, 250 mA load, 80 % usable) run for 8 hours. The calculation assumes a constant load current; the rated capacity is only valid for the discharge rate stated in the cell's datasheet.
items.source: Definition of charge Q = I × t (1 Ah = 3600 C, SI Brochure, BIPM) with a usable-capacity fraction; background: D. Linden, T. B. Reddy (eds.): Handbook of Batteries, 3rd ed. (capacity depends on discharge rate and temperature)

checks.warn: A usable fraction above 100 % is not possible: more energy is drawn than the battery holds.

items.name: Battery charge time
items.doc: The charge time follows from the capacity and the charge current: t = Q / (I × η). The charge efficiency η is the share of the supplied charge that ends up stored; the rest is lost. With a constant-current/constant-voltage charger the current also tapers off near the end, which lengthens the real time further. The default of 80 % is a planning assumption, not a datasheet value; use the charge figure of the battery's datasheet where there is one. The defaults (2500 mAh, 1 A, 80 %) give 3.125 h (3 h 7.5 min).
items.source: Definition of charge Q = I × t (1 Ah = 3600 C, SI Brochure, BIPM) with a charge efficiency; background: D. Linden, T. B. Reddy (eds.): Handbook of Batteries, 3rd ed. (charging of secondary cells)

checks.warn: A charge efficiency above 100 % is not possible: more charge would be stored than supplied.

items.name: Battery pack (series/parallel)
items.doc: A pack of N_s cells in series and N_p such strings in parallel: the pack voltage is N_s × the cell voltage, the pack capacity is N_p × the cell capacity, and the stored energy is the product of both. The defaults (3S2P with 3.7 V, 2500 mAh cells) give 11.1 V, 5 Ah and 55.5 Wh. The cell voltage is the nominal voltage: a fully charged lithium-ion cell is higher (about 4.2 V), an empty one lower. Real packs also need cell balancing and protection.
items.source: Series connection adds voltages, parallel connection adds capacities, E = U × Q (1 Wh = 3600 J); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 and 9

checks.warn: The number of cells in series must be a whole number.
The number of strings in parallel must be a whole number.

items.name: Cable voltage drop
items.doc: Voltage drop of a copper or aluminium cable: ΔU = b × ρ × L × I × cos φ / A with the resistivity ρ at the conductor temperature, the one-way cable length L and the conductor cross-section A. b is 2 for direct current and single-phase AC (outgoing and return conductor) and √3 for three-phase AC (drop between the lines); cos φ does not apply to DC. The percentage is related to the nominal voltage U_n. Resistivity at 20 °C: copper 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028), aluminium 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60889); it rises with the temperature coefficient 0.00393 /K for copper (IEC 60028) and 0.00403 /K for aluminium (IEC 60889). The cable reactance is neglected, which is acceptable for small cross-sections; it adds to the drop at large cross-sections. The defaults (copper, single-phase 230 V, 20 m, 16 A, 2.5 mm², cos φ = 1, 70 °C) give about 5.3 V (2.3 %). Safety: mains voltage is dangerous. The results are guide values only; the design of a mains installation must follow the installation standard (for example DIN VDE 0100-520 or IEC 60364-5-52) and the local rules, and must be done and checked by a qualified electrician.
items.source: Resistive voltage drop of a conductor ΔU = b × ρ × L × I × cos φ / A; cf. IEC 60364-5-52 and DIN VDE 0100-520 (voltage drop in consumers' installations); resistivity at 20 °C of annealed copper 1/58 Ω·mm²/m with α = 0.00393 /K (IEC 60028) and of hard-drawn aluminium 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m with α = 0.00403 /K (IEC 60889)

checks.warn: The voltage drop is above 5 %: check the permissible value in the installation standard, and use a larger cross-section or a shorter run.
cos φ cannot be larger than 1.

formula: du = b * rho_t * l * i * cosphi / a

items.name: Power triangle (P, Q, S, cos φ)
items.name_en: Power triangle (P, Q, S, cos φ)
items.doc: The power triangle of a single-phase AC load with sinusoidal voltage and current: the real (active) power P and the reactive power Q are the legs and the apparent power S is the hypotenuse, S² = P² + Q². The power factor is cos φ = P / S, and the phase angle is φ = arctan(Q / P). With RMS voltage U and current I the powers are S = U × I, P = U × I × cos φ and Q = U × I × sin φ. Any two of P, Q, S and cos φ determine the others. The calculator works with magnitudes: it does not say whether the load is inductive (current lags) or capacitive (current leads). The values hold for sinusoidal voltage and current only; with harmonic currents (rectifiers, switch-mode supplies) the true power factor P / S is lower than cos φ. For a balanced three-phase load use the three-phase power calculator. With cos φ = 0 no real power is transferred, so S cannot be found from P. The defaults (230 V × 10 A = 2300 VA at cos φ = 0.8) give P = 1840 W, Q = 1380 var and φ = 36.87°.
items.source: Power triangle S² = P² + Q², cos φ = P / S, P = U × I × cos φ, Q = U × I × sin φ: Schneider Electric, Electrical Installation Guide, chapter L (Power Factor Correction), definition of reactive power; T. R. Kuphaldt: Lessons in Electric Circuits, vol. II (AC), ch. 11 (Power Factor); J. M. Fiore: AC Electrical Circuit Analysis: A Practical Approach, section 7.3 (Power Triangle)

checks.warn: The power factor must be between 0 and 1.
Real power cannot exceed apparent power; check the values.
Reactive power cannot exceed apparent power; check the values.

items.name: Three-phase power
items.doc: Power of a balanced three-phase load from the line-to-line voltage U, the line current I and the power factor cos φ of each phase: P = √3 × U × I × cos φ, S = √3 × U × I and Q = √3 × U × I × sin φ. The formulas are the same for a star and a delta load; the connection only decides how voltage and current split between the line and one leg: in a star the leg voltage is U / √3 and the leg current equals the line current, in a delta the leg voltage equals U and the leg current is I / √3. The result S = 3 × U_ph × I_ph is the same for both. U is the voltage between two line conductors (400 V in a 230/400 V system), not the voltage to the neutral conductor: entering 230 V gives a result that is too small by √3. The values hold for a balanced load and a symmetrical sinusoidal supply only; for an unbalanced load the three phases must be calculated separately. φ is the angle between voltage and current of each leg. With cos φ = 0 no real power is transferred, so the current cannot be found from P. The defaults (400 V, 10 A, cos φ = 0.8) give P = 5.543 kW, S = 6.928 kVA and Q = 4.157 kvar.
items.source: Balanced three-phase load P = √3 × U × I × cos φ, S = √3 × U × I, star U_ph = U / √3, delta I_ph = I / √3: Schneider Electric, Electrical Installation Guide, chapter L (Power Factor Correction), useful formulae; TDK Electronics, Product Profile Power Quality Solutions, PFC basic formulas; J. M. Fiore: AC Electrical Circuit Analysis: A Practical Approach, section 9.3 (Three-Phase Connections); T. R. Kuphaldt: Lessons in Electric Circuits, vol. II (AC), ch. 10 (Polyphase AC Circuits)

checks.warn: The power factor must be between 0 and 1.

items.name: Power-factor correction capacitor
items.doc: A capacitor in parallel with an inductive load supplies reactive power and raises the power factor from cos φ₁ to cos φ₂ while the real power P stays the same: Q_C = P × (tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) with tan φ = √(1 − cos²φ) / cos φ. A capacitor C at the voltage U_C across it has the reactive power Q = U_C² × 2π × f × C. A single-phase capacitor gives Q_C = U² × 2π × f × C, so C = Q_C / (2π × f × U²). In a three-phase star bank at the line-to-line voltage U the three capacitors together give the same expression, so each has the same C (a star leg sees only U / √3, but there are three legs). In a delta bank each of the three capacitors sees U and supplies a third of Q_C, so C = Q_C / (3 × 2π × f × U²): a star bank needs three times the capacitance of a delta bank for the same reactive power. In the three-phase case the value is that of each of three equal capacitors, and U is the line-to-line voltage. The calculation assumes sinusoidal voltage, a linear load, an inductive (lagging) load and unchanged P; cos φ₂ = 1 is full compensation, and a larger Q_C over-compensates (the power factor becomes leading, and the calculator then shows the magnitude of cos φ₂). The result is the capacitance at the fundamental frequency: in networks with harmonics plain capacitors can resonate with the supply and detuned banks (with series reactors) are needed. Use only capacitors rated for mains voltage and frequency, with discharge resistors; the design of a mains installation belongs to a qualified electrician. The defaults (10 kW from 0.7 to 0.95 at 400 V, 50 Hz) need Q_C = 6.915 kvar, that is 137.6 µF per capacitor in star or 45.86 µF in delta.
items.source: Q_C = P × (tan φ₁ − tan φ₂): Schneider Electric, Electrical Installation Guide, chapter L (Power Factor Correction), theoretical principles to improve power factor; TDK Electronics, Product Profile Power Quality Solutions, PFC basic formulas (Q = U² × ω × C). The capacitance of a star and of a delta capacitor follows from Q = U_C² × 2π × f × C per capacitor with the star voltage U / √3 and the delta voltage U (see also J. M. Fiore: AC Electrical Circuit Analysis: A Practical Approach, section 9.4, Power Factor Correction)

checks.warn: The power factors must be greater than 0 and at most 1.
The capacitor over-compensates: the power factor becomes leading (capacitive).
The target power factor must be higher than the present one; no capacitor is needed.

formula: qc = p * (sqrt(1 - pf1^2) / pf1 - sqrt(1 - pf2^2) / pf2)

items.name: Energy consumption and cost
items.doc: The energy a device uses and what it costs: E = P × t with the total time t = hours per day × number of days, and cost = E in kWh × price per kWh (1 kWh = 3.6 MJ). The price is a plain number in your own currency per kWh; no currency is assumed, and the default 0.30 is only a placeholder, not a tariff. Every quantity can be solved for: the power from a measured energy, the hours per day or the number of days from an energy, or the price from a bill. P is the average power while the device is switched on. Devices that cycle on and off (refrigerator, thermostat-controlled heater, compressor) use less than nameplate power × time, and the nameplate usually states the maximum rather than the typical draw. Standby consumption outside the hours of use is not included. The price is the energy rate per kWh: fixed monthly charges, demand charges and time-of-use tariffs are not covered. The defaults (100 W, 3 hours a day, 365 days at 0.30 per kWh) give 109.5 kWh and a cost of 32.85.
items.source: E = P × t and 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J: NIST Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI), appendix B.9; the cost estimate (watts × hours per day × days ÷ 1000 × price per kWh): Virginia Cooperative Extension, publication 2901-9014 (BSE-301NP), Estimating Appliance and Home Electronic Energy Use

checks.warn: A day has only 24 hours.
Power, time, days and price must not be negative.

items.name: LED strip supply (WS2812)
items.doc: Current, power and end-of-strip voltage of an addressable LED strip (WS2812 and similar) fed from one end. The total current is I = N × I_led, the power P = V × I. The strip is a long conductor loaded along its whole length, so the voltage drop to the far end is half of the current times the resistance of both rails: ΔV = I × R_s / 2 (a load spread uniformly along the line, as treated for distribution feeders in the lecture notes Purdue University ECE 595, Lecture 3 Approximate Feeder Analysis, and Iowa State University EE 455, Approximate Method of Analysis). The estimate assumes every pixel draws the same current whatever its local voltage; for N pixels the exact sum is larger by the factor (1 + 1 / N). The check compares the voltage at the far end with the lowest supply voltage the pixels accept. Current per pixel: the default of 36 mA is 3 × 12 mA, the working current per colour of the WS2812B-V5/W datasheet with red, green and blue at full brightness; the WS2812 datasheet gives 18.5 mA per colour (55.5 mA), the 2013 WS2812B datasheet states no current at all, and the common figure of 60 mA per pixel is a rounded worst case from Adafruit's NeoPixel Überguide (about 20 mA is typical for mixed animations). The minimum voltage default of 4.5 V is the lower end of the supply range for which the 2013 WS2812B datasheet specifies its electrical characteristics (4.5 to 5.5 V); take the value from the datasheet of your part. The rail resistance R_s (both rails together, whole strip) is not in the LED datasheets: the default 0.2 Ω is only a placeholder for about a metre, so measure it (short the far end and measure from + to − at the feed). The cable from the supply is not included. If the far end falls too low, feed the strip from both ends or inject power at several points (Adafruit advises a power connection within about a metre of every pixel); this calculator gives no number for that. Size the supply with generous headroom.
items.source: Datasheets of Worldsemi: WS2812 (18.5 mA per colour), WS2812B-V5/W (12 mA working current per colour), WS2812B (2013, supply range 4.5 to 5.5 V); Adafruit NeoPixel Überguide, Powering NeoPixels (60 mA worst case, 20 mA typical per pixel); voltage drop ΔV = I × R / 2 of a uniformly distributed load: Purdue University, ECE 595 Power Distribution System Analysis, Lecture 3 Approximate Feeder Analysis; Iowa State University, EE 455 Introduction to Energy Distribution Systems, 03 Approximate Method of Analysis

vars.label: R_s
vars.name: Resistance of both rails, whole strip

vars.label: V_min
vars.name: Lowest supply voltage of the pixels

derived.label: ΔV
derived.name: Voltage drop to the far end (fed from one end)

checks.warn: The voltage at the far end is below the lowest supply voltage of the pixels: feed the strip from both ends or inject power at more points.
The number of pixels must be a whole number.

items.name: Supercapacitor hold-up time
items.doc: How long a supercapacitor can supply a load while its voltage falls from the start voltage V₁ to the cut-off voltage V₂ at which the load stops working. With a constant current I the voltage falls linearly and t = C × (V₁ − V₂) / I. With a constant power P (for example a DC/DC converter) the current rises as the voltage falls and t = C × (V₁² − V₂²) / (2 × P). The usable energy is E = ½ × C × (V₁² − V₂²). Choose the load type: the value that the type does not use is dimmed. The equivalent series resistance (ESR) is ignored: it makes the real time shorter, because the voltage step I × R_ESR at the start and the loss in the ESR use up part of the voltage swing (with a high ESR or a large current this is not small, and the supercapacitor may not deliver the constant power at all near V₂). Capacitance also falls and ESR rises with age and at low temperature, the capacitance depends on voltage and discharge rate, and leakage is ignored, so add margin. For cells in series enter the values of the whole stack (C = C_cell / n) and never exceed the rated cell voltage. The defaults (1 F from 5 V to 3 V) last 200 s at 10 mA or 160 s at 50 mW.
items.source: Discharge of a capacitor, constant current t = C × (V₁ − V₂) / I, constant power t = C × (V₁² − V₂²) / (2 × P), E = ½ × C × (V₁² − V₂²): Würth Elektronik, support note SN009b, How to Use Supercapacitors? A Brief Guide to the Design-In Process; Abracon, application note Designing with Supercapacitors; Analog Devices, Analog Dialogue RAQ Issue 179, Energy Storage Using Supercapacitors: How Big Is Big Enough?

derived.label: E
derived.name: Usable energy between V₁ and V₂

checks.warn: The cut-off voltage must be below the start voltage.

items.name: Inverting buck-boost converter
items.doc: An ideal inverting buck-boost converter makes a negative output voltage from a positive input voltage and works for any ratio of the two magnitudes. In continuous conduction the duty cycle is D = |V_out| / (V_in + |V_out|), the average inductor current is I_L = I_out / (1 − D) = I_out × (1 + |V_out| / V_in), the peak-to-peak ripple current is ΔI_L = V_in × D / (f_sw × L), and the inductor and switch carry the peak I_pk = I_L + ΔI_L / 2 (valley current I_L − ΔI_L / 2). The input draws on average I_in = I_out × |V_out| / V_in. The regulator IC, switch and diode must withstand V_in + |V_out|. Enter |V_out| as a positive number. The inductor current is larger than the load current by 1 / (1 − D), so a buck regulator used as an inverter delivers much less than its rated current; the worst case is the lowest input voltage for the currents and the highest for the ripple. Continuous conduction needs a positive valley current, that is I_out > ΔI_L × (1 − D) / 2; below that a diode rectifier runs discontinuous and these formulas no longer apply (the calculator warns). Losses are not modelled: an efficiency below 100 % and the diode drop raise the duty cycle and the currents. Not covered: the right-half-plane zero, output ripple and capacitor currents. The defaults (+12 V to −5 V, 1 A, 400 kHz, 22 µH) give D = 29.4 %, I_L = 1.417 A, ΔI_L = 0.401 A and I_pk = 1.617 A. V_in or |V_out| can be found from the ripple current when the other is known.
items.source: Inverting buck-boost power stage in continuous conduction (D = |V_out| / (V_in + |V_out|), I_L = I_out / (1 − D), ΔI_L = V_in × D / (f_sw × L)): Texas Instruments SLVA059B, Understanding Inverting Buck-Boost Power Stages in Switch Mode Power Supplies; Texas Instruments SNVA856B, Working With Inverting Buck-Boost Converters; Texas Instruments SLYT286, Using a buck converter in an inverting buck-boost topology (Analog Applications Journal 4Q 2007); discontinuous-mode limit I_out = ΔI_L × (1 − D) / 2: Texas Instruments SLVA059B and Analog Devices AN-1083, Designing an Inverting Buck Boost Using the ADP2300 and ADP2301 Switching Regulators

derived.label: V_max
derived.name: Voltage stress on switch, diode and IC

checks.warn: The inductor current reaches zero: with a diode rectifier the converter runs in discontinuous mode and these formulas do not apply. Use a larger inductance or a higher load current.

formula: dil = vin * vout / ((vin + vout) * f * l)

items.name: Wavelength
items.doc: The wavelength of an electromagnetic wave is λ = c × VF / f, with the speed of light c = 299 792 458 m/s (exact) and the velocity factor VF of the medium (1 in free space, about 0.66 in coax with a solid polyethylene dielectric). Any two of f, VF and λ determine the third; the half and the quarter wavelength are shown too. Example: 145 MHz in free space gives λ = 2.068 m.
items.source: Wave relation λ = c/f with the exact speed of light c = 299 792 458 m/s (SI Brochure, BIPM); the velocity factor VF = v/c is the ratio of the propagation speed in the medium to c

checks.warn: A velocity factor above 1 is not physical: the wave would be faster than light in vacuum.

items.name: Half-wave dipole length
items.doc: A resonant half-wave dipole is slightly shorter than half a free-space wavelength because of the end effect: L = K × c / (2 f), with a shortening factor K of about 0.95 for a wire dipole (the familiar 468 / f(MHz) feet corresponds to K ≈ 0.952). The quarter-wave length is half of L: one leg of the dipole, or a quarter-wave vertical over a ground plane. Example: 7.1 MHz (40 m band) gives L = 20.06 m. Trim for the lowest SWR; height, wire diameter and surroundings shift the resonance.
items.source: Half-wave dipole L = K·c/(2f) with the end-effect shortening factor K (about 0.95); the rule of thumb 468/f(MHz) feet is widely published, e.g. The ARRL Antenna Book (dipole antennas) and J. D. Kraus: Antennas

checks.warn: A shortening factor above 1 is unusual: the end effect makes a resonant dipole shorter than half the free-space wavelength.

items.name: Microstrip impedance
items.doc: Characteristic impedance of a surface microstrip line on a PCB by the IPC-2141 approximation: Z_0 = 87 / √(ε_r + 1.41) × ln(5.98 h / (0.8 w + t)), with the dielectric thickness h, the trace width w and the copper thickness t. The formula is usually quoted for 0.1 < w/h < 2.0 and 1 < ε_r < 15; outside that range the result is only a rough guide and a warning appears. Use it for a first design and have critical lines checked with a field solver or the impedance data of the board maker. Example: a 3 mm trace on 1.6 mm FR-4 (ε_r ≈ 4.3, 1 oz copper) gives about 49.8 Ω. ε_r depends on the laminate and the frequency: use the datasheet value.
items.source: IPC-2141 (design guide for high-speed controlled impedance circuit boards), surface microstrip approximation Z0 = 87/√(εr+1.41)·ln(5.98h/(0.8w+t)), as commonly quoted for 0.1 < w/h < 2.0 and 1 < εr < 15

checks.warn: w/h is below 0.1: outside the range the IPC-2141 approximation is quoted for (0.1 to 2.0), expect a larger error.
w/h is above 2.0: outside the range the IPC-2141 approximation is quoted for (0.1 to 2.0), expect a larger error.
ε_r is outside the range 1 to 15 the approximation is quoted for.

items.name: Coaxial cable impedance
items.doc: Characteristic impedance of a lossless coaxial line: Z_0 = (η_0 / 2π) / √ε_r × ln(D / d), with η_0 / 2π = 59.958 Ω (η_0 = μ_0·c ≈ 376.73 Ω), the inner diameter D of the shield, the diameter d of the inner conductor and the relative permittivity ε_r of the dielectric. This is the same as the familiar 138 / √ε_r × log10(D / d). The velocity factor is 1 / √ε_r. Example: solid polyethylene (ε_r = 2.25) with D / d = 3.5 gives about 50 Ω (VF 0.667). PTFE has ε_r ≈ 2.1.
items.source: Lossless coaxial line Z0 = (η0/2π)·ln(D/d)/√εr with η0 = μ0·c ≈ 376.73 Ω; D. M. Pozar: Microwave Engineering, ch. 2 (transmission line theory)

checks.warn: The inner conductor diameter d must be smaller than the inner diameter D of the shield.

items.name: SWR and return loss
items.doc: A mismatch reflects part of the wave. With the magnitude of the reflection coefficient |Γ|: SWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 − |Γ|), return loss RL = −20 log10 |Γ| (larger means a better match) and mismatch loss = −10 log10 (1 − |Γ|²), the power lost to reflection. |Γ|² is the reflected fraction of the power. Enter any one of SWR, |Γ| or RL. Example: SWR 2:1 gives |Γ| = 0.333, RL = 9.54 dB, a mismatch loss of 0.51 dB and 11.1 % reflected power.
items.source: Reflection coefficient Γ, standing wave ratio, return loss and mismatch loss (definitions); D. M. Pozar: Microwave Engineering, ch. 2 (transmission line theory)

checks.warn: An SWR below 1 is not possible: the SWR is at least 1 (a perfect match).
|Γ| above 1 is not possible for a passive load: it cannot reflect more than it receives.

items.name: RF power and voltage (dBm, dBµV)
items.doc: Converts between power, voltage and the logarithmic RF levels of a sine wave across a resistance R (usually 50 Ω): P = V_rms² / R and V_pp = 2√2 × V_rms. dBm is relative to 1 mW (10 log10 (P / 1 mW)), dBµV to 1 µV (20 log10 (V / 1 µV)); across 50 Ω dBµV = dBm + 107. Enter two of P, R, V_rms and V_pp (V_rms and V_pp alone are not enough). To enter a level in dBm choose dBm in the unit menu of the power field. Example: 0 dBm (1 mW) into 50 Ω is 223.6 mV rms, 632.5 mV peak to peak and 107 dBµV.
items.source: Definitions: dBm = 10·log10(P / 1 mW), dBµV = 20·log10(V / 1 µV), P = V_rms²/R and V_pp = 2√2·V_rms for a sine wave; decibel per IEC 60027-3

items.name: Free-space path loss
items.doc: Free-space path loss between two isotropic antennas in the far field: FSPL = 20 log10 (4π d f / c) in dB, with the distance d, the frequency f and c = 299 792 458 m/s. Each doubling of the distance or the frequency adds 6.02 dB. It is the loss of the path alone, without antenna gains, cable loss or obstacles. Example: 1 km at 2.4 GHz gives 100.05 dB. The formula holds in the far field only (d much larger than λ); for d < λ / (4π) it would turn negative.
items.source: Friis free-space transmission formula (H. T. Friis, 1946), FSPL = (4πdf/c)²; ITU-R Recommendation P.525 (calculation of free-space attenuation)

checks.warn: A negative loss: the distance is shorter than λ / (4π), far outside the far-field range of the formula.

items.name: Skin depth
items.doc: The skin depth δ = √(ρ / (π f μ_0 μ_r)) is the depth at which the current density of an alternating current in a good conductor has fallen to 1/e (about 37 %) of its surface value. Most of the current flows within a few δ of the surface, which raises the AC resistance of thick wires; R_s = ρ / δ is the surface resistance per square. Copper, silver, gold and aluminium are non-magnetic (μ_r = 1). The resistivities are values for 20 °C and change by about 0.4 % per kelvin; real wire and plating differ from the pure metal. Example: copper at 1 MHz has δ = 66.1 µm.
items.source: Skin depth δ = √(ρ/(π f μ0 μr)) in a good conductor (D. M. Pozar: Microwave Engineering, ch. 1) with μ0 = 4π·10^-7 H/m; resistivity at 20 °C: copper 1.7241e-8 Ω·m (annealed copper standard, 58 MS/m, IEC 60028), silver 1.587e-8, gold 2.214e-8 and aluminium 2.65e-8 Ω·m (pure-metal handbook values, e.g. CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics)

items.name: Thermal (Johnson) noise
items.doc: A resistor R at the absolute temperature T generates a white noise voltage: v_n = √(4 × k × T × R × B) (RMS, open circuit) in the noise bandwidth B, with the Boltzmann constant k = 1.380 649 × 10⁻²³ J/K (exact in the SI). The same noise seen as a short-circuit current is i_n = v_n / R. The voltage density e_n = √(4kTR) is shown as a voltage: it is the value in V per √Hz, so 1 kΩ at 290 K gives about 4 nV/√Hz. The available noise power is P_n = k × T × B. It is what the resistor delivers into a matched, noiseless load, it does not depend on R, and at 290 K in 1 Hz it is −173.975 dBm (the familiar −174 dBm/Hz). Do not compute it as v_n² / R: that value is 6 dB too high, only v_n² / (4R) equals kTB. Choose the display unit dBm for P_n and dBV for v_n. B is the noise bandwidth, not the −3 dB frequency: for a first-order low-pass it is 1.57 times the corner frequency, for higher orders it approaches the corner frequency. Enter any three of R, T, B and v_n. Values are RMS; real resistors add current-dependent excess noise at low frequencies and an amplifier adds its own noise. Example: 1 kΩ, 290 K and 1 Hz give e_n = 4.002 nV/√Hz.
items.source: Thermal noise v_n = √(4kTRB) of a resistor: Texas Instruments, Noise Analysis in Operational Amplifier Circuits (SLVA043B), Thermal Noise, and Analog Dialogue 24-2, Ask the Applications Engineer—7: Op-amp Noise; available noise power P = kTB: Rohde & Schwarz, dB or not dB? (application note 1MA98), section Noise; Boltzmann constant k = 1.380 649e-23 J/K exact: SI Brochure, 9th edition (BIPM)

items.name: L-network matching
items.doc: Two reactive parts, one in series and one in parallel, transform a load resistance to a different source resistance at one frequency, for maximum power transfer. With R_hi the larger and R_lo the smaller of the two resistances the Q is fixed by their ratio: Q = √(R_hi / R_lo − 1). The series reactance is X_s = Q × R_lo (on the low-resistance side) and the parallel reactance is X_p = R_hi / Q (across the high resistance), so X_s × X_p = R_hi × R_lo. Low-pass variant (passes DC, attenuates harmonics): L = X_s / (2π f) in series, C = 1 / (2π f X_p) in parallel. High-pass variant (blocks DC): C = 1 / (2π f X_s) in series, L = X_p / (2π f) in parallel. The part values depend only on R_hi and R_lo, so source and load can be swapped, but the network must then be mirrored: the series element always sits on the low-resistance side and the shunt element across the high-resistance side. The drawing shows R_S < R_L (series element next to the source); with R_S > R_L put the series element next to R_L and the shunt element across R_S. Example: 100 Ω to 1 kΩ at 100 MHz gives Q = 3, X_s = 300 Ω, X_p = 333 Ω, so L = 477 nH and C = 4.77 pF (low-pass). Valid for purely resistive source and load, ideal lossless parts and one frequency; reactive parts of the source or load must be compensated first. With lumped parts this works up to roughly 1 to 2 GHz. The calculator gives no bandwidth: the Q of an L-network is fixed by the ratio and is not the loaded Q of a resonator, so the rule bandwidth = f / Q must not be used. For another Q use a three-element network.
items.source: Two-reactance (L) matching network, Q = √(R_hi/R_lo − 1), X_s = Q·R_lo, X_p = R_hi/Q with the shunt reactance across the larger resistance: NXP (Motorola/Freescale) application note AN721, Impedance Matching Networks Applied to RF Power Transistors, section Two-Reactance Matching Networks; M. Steer, Microwave and RF Design III: Networks, section The L Matching Network

derived.name: Q of the network (fixed by the ratio)

checks.warn: Source and load are equal: no matching network is needed.
R_S is larger than R_L: the values are right, but mirror the drawn network (series element next to R_L, shunt element across R_S).

formula: l = if(lp, xs, xp) / (2 * pi * f)
c = if(lp, 1 / xp, 1 / xs) / (2 * pi * f)

items.name: EIRP and ERP
items.doc: The equivalent isotropically radiated power (EIRP) is the power supplied to the antenna times the antenna gain relative to an isotropic radiator, in the direction of that gain. In decibels: EIRP [dBm] = P_TX [dBm] − L_c [dB] + G [dBi], with the transmitter output power P_TX, the loss L_c of the cable, connectors and filters between transmitter and antenna, and the antenna gain G in dBi. Any three of P_TX, L_c, G and EIRP give the fourth, for example the highest transmitter power for an EIRP limit: P_TX = EIRP − G + L_c. The effective radiated power (ERP) refers to a half-wave dipole instead: ERP = EIRP − 2.15 dB (a factor of 1.64 in watts), because the ideal half-wave dipole has 2.15 dBi. A gain given in dBd is converted with G [dBi] = G [dBd] + 2.15 dB. Display the powers in dBm or in watts as you prefer. EIRP and ERP are regulatory quantities: check which of the two a limit refers to (for example e.r.p. for short-range devices below 1 GHz, e.i.r.p. for 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz WLAN). The gain must be that of the antenna as installed, and the loss must include everything between the point where P_TX is specified and the antenna; mismatch loss is not included. The calculator does not compute the field strength. Example: 20 dBm, 3.35 dB cable loss and a 21 dBi dish give 37.65 dBm = 5.82 W EIRP.
items.source: e.i.r.p. and e.r.p. as defined in the ITU Radio Regulations (Nos. 1.161 and 1.162, quoted in ITU-R Recommendation BS.561-2) and in 47 CFR § 2.1; half-wave dipole gain 2.15 dBi: ITU-R Recommendation P.341-7, Table 1; EIRP = transmitter power − cable loss + antenna gain (dBm, dB, dBi): Cisco, RF Power Values (document 23231)

vars.name: Antenna gain (dBi, relative to an isotropic radiator)

items.name: Coax stub / electrical length
items.doc: The physical length ℓ of a coaxial line with a given electrical length θ follows from the frequency f and the velocity factor VF of the cable: ℓ = θ / 360° × λ_g with the wavelength in the cable λ_g = c × VF / f and c = 299 792 458 m/s (exact). 90° is a quarter-wave section, 180° a half-wave section. Any three of f, VF, θ and ℓ give the fourth: from a stub trimmed to resonance you can find the true velocity factor of a cable. The free-space wavelength and the wavelength in the cable are shown. VF = 1 / √ε_r holds only for a line that is completely filled with one solid dielectric (solid polyethylene, ε_r ≈ 2.3, gives 0.66); foam cables are an air and plastic mixture, so use the velocity factor from the cable datasheet. The electrical length is exact at one frequency only: the same piece has θ proportional to f. Datasheet velocity factors are nominal and real cables deviate by a few per cent, so cut stubs and phasing lines slightly long and trim them while measuring; connectors and the open or shorted end add length. A quarter-wave line turns a short into an open and the reverse, a half-wave line repeats the impedance. Example: a quarter-wave section for 145 MHz in 0.66 coax is 0.341 m long.
items.source: Electrical length θ = β·ℓ with a wavelength of 360° and λ = v_p/f: M. Steer, Microwave and RF Design II: Transmission Lines, section Transmission Line Theory; velocity factor VF = 1/√ε_r of a solid-dielectric coax line (RG-59 with polyethylene, ε_r = 2.25, about 67 % of c): S. W. Ellingson, Electromagnetics Vol. 1, section Coaxial Line; speed of light c = 299 792 458 m/s exact (SI Brochure, BIPM)

checks.warn: The velocity factor must lie between 0 and 1 (enter 66 % as 0.66).
More than one wavelength: the line behaves like one shortened by whole wavelengths, but only at this frequency.

items.name: Cascaded noise figure (Friis)
items.doc: The overall noise figure of three stages in a row (amplifiers, cables, mixers, filters) follows from the Friis formula with the linear noise factors F_i = 10^(NF_i / 10) and power gains g_i = 10^(G_i / 10): F = F_1 + (F_2 − 1) / g_1 + (F_3 − 1) / (g_1 × g_2), and NF = 10 × log10(F). Enter every noise figure and gain in dB; the conversion to linear values is done inside (adding the dB values of the noise figures is the classic mistake). The chain is fixed at three stages: for two stages enter NF_3 = 0 dB, which removes the third term. The gain of the last stage does not matter. The first stage dominates: a loss in front of the first amplifier adds directly to the noise figure, and a stage with high gain makes the following stages count less. A passive, lossy stage at 290 K (cable, attenuator, filter) has a noise figure equal to its loss and a gain equal to the negative loss, both in dB. From the overall noise figure, the required NF_1 or the required gain G_1 of the first stage can be found; if the later stages alone already exceed the target, the answer is impossible (NF_1 below 0 dB, or no result). The equivalent input noise temperature is T_e = 290 K × (F − 1). Noise figures refer to a source at 290 K. Example: an LNA with 1 dB and 12 dB gain, a second LNA with 3 dB and 15 dB gain and an ADC with a noise figure of 20 dB give 1.8 dB.
items.source: Friis formula for cascaded stages F = F1 + (F2−1)/G1 + (F3−1)/(G1·G2) and Te = 290 K·(F−1): Agilent Technologies, Fundamentals of RF and Microwave Noise Figure Measurements (Application Note 57-1); worked three-stage example: Texas Instruments, How the ADC noise figure impacts RF receiver designs (SLYT839, Analog Design Journal 3Q 2023), Table 3

items.name: LED series resistor
items.doc: An LED needs a series resistor that takes up the part of the supply voltage the LEDs do not use: R = (V_S − n × V_F) / I_F for a string of n LEDs in series. Parallel strings each get their own resistor, so the supply delivers m × I_F in total; never let several parallel strings share one resistor. Example with the defaults: a 12 V supply and two strings of three red LEDs (V_F ≈ 2 V) at 20 mA need 300 Ω per string; the supply delivers 40 mA (0.48 W), and half of that power is lost in the resistors. Take V_F from the datasheet for the chosen current; it varies with colour, current and temperature.
items.source: Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law for an LED string (the LED as a diode with a forward voltage); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (LEDs and diode circuits)

derived.label: η
derived.name: Share of the power in the LEDs

checks.warn: The supply voltage does not exceed the forward voltage of the string: no resistor can set the current.
The number of LEDs per string and the number of strings must be whole numbers.
The resistor dissipates more than 0.25 W: use a resistor with a higher power rating.

items.name: Zener regulator
items.doc: A shunt regulator: a series resistor R feeds a Zener diode in parallel with the load. R must pass the maximum load current I_L plus the minimum Zener current I_Z(min) that keeps the Zener in regulation: R = (V_in − V_Z) / (I_L + I_Z(min)). Without load the whole current flows through the Zener, so its power is V_Z × I_R at no load, the worst case. The Zener is treated as ideal (dynamic resistance neglected). Use the lowest input voltage to size R and check the powers with the highest. Example with the defaults: 12 V to 5.1 V at 20 mA load and 5 mA minimum Zener current needs 276 Ω (270 Ω is the nearest E24 value); the Zener then dissipates about 0.13 W without load.
items.source: Zener shunt regulator (series resistor R = (V_in − V_Z) / (I_L + I_Z) with an ideal Zener); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (Zener diode regulators)

checks.warn: V_in must be above V_Z: otherwise no current flows through the series resistor.
The resistor cannot supply the load current plus the minimum Zener current (one of the currents comes out negative).
The Zener dissipates more than 0.5 W without load: a 500 mW Zener is not enough.
The series resistor dissipates more than 0.25 W: use a resistor with a higher power rating.

items.name: Transistor switch
items.doc: An NPN transistor as a saturated low-side switch: the base resistor must pass enough base current to drive the collector current I_C into saturation. The minimum base current is I_C / h_FE; the overdrive factor multiplies it (a factor of 2 to 10 is common) so that the transistor stays saturated despite spread and temperature: I_B = overdrive × I_C / h_FE and R_B = (V_in − V_BE) / I_B. Use the minimum h_FE from the datasheet at this collector current, not the typical value. Example with the defaults: a 5 V logic output switching 100 mA with h_FE = 100 and an overdrive of 5 needs 5 mA of base current and R_B = 860 Ω. The forced gain h_FE / overdrive is the ratio I_C / I_B the circuit actually uses.
items.source: Saturated BJT switch (R_B = (V_in − V_BE) / I_B with I_B = overdrive × I_C / h_FE); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2

checks.warn: V_in does not exceed V_BE: no base current can flow.
Overdrive below 1: the base current is smaller than I_C / h_FE, so the transistor does not saturate.

items.name: BJT divider bias
items.doc: DC operating point of a common-emitter stage with voltage-divider bias (four resistors). The divider R1 / R2 is replaced by its Thevenin equivalent, V_TH = V_CC × R2 / (R1 + R2) with R_TH = R1 ∥ R2, and the base current is taken into account: I_B = (V_TH − V_BE) / (R_TH + (β + 1) × R_E), I_C = β × I_B, I_E = (β + 1) × I_B, V_E = I_E × R_E, V_B = V_E + V_BE and V_CE = V_CC − I_C × R_C − I_E × R_E. The model assumes the forward-active region; this calculator is forward-only (enter all seven values). Example with the defaults: 12 V, R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, R_C = 4.7 kΩ and β = 100 give I_C ≈ 1.29 mA and V_CE ≈ 4.66 V. The warning for a soft divider appears when R_TH exceeds a tenth of (β + 1) × R_E: then I_C depends noticeably on β.
items.source: Voltage-divider bias with the Thevenin base circuit and (β + 1) × R_E; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2; A. S. Sedra, K. C. Smith: Microelectronic Circuits (BJT biasing)

checks.warn: V_TH does not exceed V_BE: the transistor is off and the model does not apply.
V_CE is below 0.2 V, a typical saturation voltage: the transistor is saturated and the active-region result is not valid.
The base divider is soft: R_TH is more than a tenth of (β + 1) × R_E, so I_C depends noticeably on β.

items.name: MOSFET losses
items.doc: Estimated losses of a MOSFET that switches the current I_D against the voltage V_DS at the frequency f_sw with the duty cycle D. Conduction loss: P_cond = D × I_D² × R_DS(on). Switching loss with linear, overlapping voltage and current transitions: P_sw = ½ × V_DS × I_D × (t_r + t_f) × f_sw. Gate-drive loss, output-capacitance loss, reverse-recovery and body-diode loss are not included, and R_DS(on) rises with temperature, so enter the value at operating temperature from the datasheet. The calculator is forward-only. Example with the defaults: 10 A at 12 V, R_DS(on) = 10 mΩ, D = 50 %, t_r = t_f = 20 ns and 200 kHz give 0.5 W conduction plus 0.48 W switching, 0.98 W in total.
items.source: Conduction loss D·I²·R_DS(on) and the linear-transition switching loss ½·V·I·(t_r + t_f)·f_sw; R. W. Erickson, D. Maksimović: Fundamentals of Power Electronics (switching loss); N. Mohan, T. M. Undeland, W. P. Robbins: Power Electronics (power MOSFET losses)

checks.warn: The duty cycle must be between 0 % and 100 %.
The switching times take more than half of the period: the linear switching-loss model does not apply.

items.name: Heatsink
items.doc: Steady-state thermal model of a power device: a chain of thermal resistances from the junction to the ambient air, T_J = T_A + P × (R_thJC + R_thCS + R_thSA), with junction-to-case, case-to-heatsink (insulator, grease) and heatsink-to-ambient resistance. Every stage drops P × R degrees. Enter the maximum junction temperature of the datasheet as T_J (for example 125 °C or 150 °C) together with the power and the other resistances to find the heatsink resistance R_thSA you need; a result of zero or below means no heatsink is good enough. Example with the defaults: 10 W at 25 °C ambient with 1.5 + 0.5 + 3 °C/W gives a junction temperature of 75 °C.
items.source: Steady-state thermal resistance network (the thermal analogue of Ohm's law: ΔT = P × R_th); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (heat and power design)

checks.warn: The junction temperature is above 150 °C, a common absolute maximum for silicon power devices: check the datasheet limit.

items.name: Optocoupler resistors (CTR)
items.doc: Two resistors for a phototransistor optocoupler. The LED series resistor is R_F = (V_in − V_F) / I_F; use the maximum forward voltage when the current must be guaranteed. The pull-up on the output is the smallest value for which the transistor still saturates: the collector current the coupler can guarantee is I_C = I_F × CTR, and the pull-up must not ask for more than that, so R_L = (V_CC − V_CE(sat)) / (I_F × CTR). Enter in CTR the minimum current transfer ratio after derating, not the typical value: the CTR printed in the datasheet is a minimum at one test point (for example I_F = 5 mA, V_CE = 5 V, 25 °C), it falls with temperature and age, it is lower in saturation than at the test point, and it varies from part to part. Both manufacturer application notes derate the datasheet minimum by factors read from the datasheet curves (Toshiba: 5 mA × 2.3 × 0.5 × 0.7 × 0.75 = 3.02 mA for 10 mA LED current and a 100 % minimum; Vishay application note 45: 100 % × 0.71 × 0.8 × 0.75 = 42.6 %), and Toshiba designs for a 50 % CTR loss over ten years. With the typical CTR, the output may not reach the low level in the worst case. The saturation voltage V_CE(sat) is an input: use the low level the load needs, which is usually larger than the V_CE(sat) of the datasheet, measured at a small collector current. A larger pull-up saturates more safely but switches off more slowly. Keep the LED current well below the absolute maximum of the part. Example: 5 V, V_F = 1.2 V (PC817), 10 mA and a derated CTR of 20 % give R_F = 380 Ω, I_C = 2 mA and R_L = 2.3 kΩ for a low level of 0.4 V.
items.source: LED resistor R = (V − V_F)/I_F and the smallest pull-up R_L = (V_CC − V_CE(sat))/(I_F × CTR_min) from the derated minimum CTR: Toshiba, Basic Characteristics and Application Circuit Design of Transistor Output Photocouplers (application note), sections 2.1 and 2.4; Vishay Semiconductors, How to Use Optocoupler Normalized Curves (application note 45, document 83706); PC817 values: Sharp, PC817X series datasheet

vars.name: LED forward voltage at I_F (maximum for a guaranteed current)

vars.name: Required low level at the output

items.name: MOSFET gate drive
items.doc: Gate-drive estimates for a power MOSFET from its gate charge. Power and current use the total gate charge Q_g, read from the gate-charge curve at your gate voltage and drain voltage, never the input capacitance C_iss: a charge of 98 nC at 10 V is an effective 9.8 nF, while the C_iss of the same part is only 2.6 nF, so C_iss × V² × f underestimates the drive power several times (Microchip AN799, Toshiba). The gate-drive power is P_g = Q_g × V_drv × f and the average current from the driver supply is I_avg = Q_g × f; the same power is lost in the driver and the gate resistances whatever their value, it only moves between them. The switching time is a first-order estimate with a constant gate current: t = Q_gd / I_g. It uses the gate current on the Miller plateau, I_g = (V_drv − V_pl) / (R_int + R_g), not the peak current, and the switching charge Q_gd (gate-drain charge) of the drain-voltage edge, which is the charge delivered while the drain voltage changes. The peak current at the start of the edge with the gate at 0 V is V_drv / (R_int + R_g). R_int is the sum of the driver output resistance (pull-up for turn-on, pull-down for turn-off) and the internal gate resistance of the MOSFET; R_g is the external gate resistor. Give any two of Q_gd, R_g and t: for example the resistor for a wanted voltage fall time is R_g = t × (V_drv − V_pl) / Q_gd − R_int. A larger R_g slows the edges (less ringing and EMI, more switching loss). Source inductance, the driver's own rise time and current limit and non-linear capacitances change real edges; measured transients can deviate by 16 % to more than 100 % from such a calculation (Vishay AN608A). The power covers charging and discharging the gate only; quiescent and cross-conduction losses of the driver come on top. Example: Q_gd = 12 nC, 12 V drive, V_pl = 4.5 V and 6 Ω in total give a plateau current of 1.25 A and 9.6 ns.
items.source: Gate-drive power P = Q_g·V_drv·f and average current Q_g·f: Microchip, AN799 Matching MOSFET Drivers to MOSFETs, and Texas Instruments, Fundamentals of MOSFET and IGBT Gate Driver Circuits (SLUA618A); switching time from the gate-drain charge and the plateau current t = Q_gd·R/(V_G − V_pl): Toshiba, MOSFET Gate Drive Circuit (application note), section 1.2, and Vishay Siliconix, Power MOSFET Basics: Understanding Gate Charge and Using it to Assess Switching Performance (AN608A)
