items.name: NTC thermistor (B equation)
items.doc: An NTC thermistor lowers its resistance as it warms up. The B (beta) equation describes it with the resistance R_0 at a reference temperature T_0 (normally 25 °C) and the B value of the datasheet: R = R_0 × exp(B × (1/T − 1/T_0)). The temperatures are absolute (the page converts °C and °F to kelvin) and B is in kelvin. Rearranged, the equation gives the temperature from a measured resistance, B from two points and R_0 from one point. Limit of the model: B is not constant. The equation is exact only at T_0 and at the second temperature that defines B (85 °C for B25/85) and drifts away from them; TDK calls it suitable only for a restricted range around the rated temperature, and common materials have B between 2000 K and 5000 K. Compared with the Vishay NTCLE100E3 10 kΩ table (B = 3977 K) the model is about 0.8 K off at 0 °C, 0.3 K at 50 °C and 0.4 K at 100 °C, but about 2.3 K at −25 °C, 3.6 K at −40 °C, 1.4 K at 125 °C and 2.8 K at 150 °C: within roughly 0 … 100 °C the error stays near 1 K for this material, outside it grows quickly (other materials differ). Tolerances of R_0 and B come on top. For precise work use the R/T table of the datasheet or the Steinhart–Hart equation. The measuring current must not heat the thermistor. Example: 100 kΩ with B = 3977 K at 100 °C is 6.849 kΩ.
items.source: B equation of NTC thermistors, R = R25 × exp(B × (1/T − 1/298.15 K)): Vishay BCcomponents application note NTC Thermistors (document 29053), section Material constant B; Texas Instruments application note SBAA338A, Monitoring NTC Thermistor Circuit With Single-Ended ADC; EPCOS/TDK, NTC Thermistors – General technical information (validity range and B range)

checks.warn: Unusual B value: common NTC materials lie between 2000 K and 5000 K.

items.name: NTC voltage divider
items.doc: An NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor R_fix form a voltage divider that turns the temperature into a voltage for an ADC. With the NTC on the low side (to ground) V_out = V_cc × R_NTC / (R_fix + R_NTC) and the voltage falls as it gets warmer; with the NTC on the high side (to the supply) V_out = V_cc × R_fix / (R_fix + R_NTC) and it rises. The NTC resistance follows the B equation R_NTC = R_0 × exp(B × (1/T − 1/T_0)) with absolute temperatures and B in kelvin (see the calculator NTC thermistor for the accuracy of that model: it is best between about 0 and 100 °C). Enter the measured voltage to get the temperature back, or enter the NTC resistance from the R/T table of the datasheet instead of using the B equation. The ratio k = V_out / V_cc is what a ratiometric ADC reads when it uses the same supply as its reference. The result is for an unloaded divider: a low-impedance ADC input or a long cable changes it. Close to a rail (k below 0.05 or above 0.95) little resolution is left per kelvin; choose another R_fix. P_NTC is the power the NTC dissipates and heats itself with: (V_cc / (R_fix + R_NTC))² × R_NTC. Example: 3.3 V, R_fix = 100 kΩ and a 100 kΩ NTC (B = 3977 K) at 100 °C give 0.2115 V on the low side.
items.source: Voltage divider of two resistors (Ohm's law) with the B equation of the NTC: Texas Instruments application note SBAA338A, Monitoring NTC Thermistor Circuit With Single-Ended ADC (NTC on the ground side, published ADC values); EPCOS/TDK, NTC Thermistors – General technical information, section 3.2.2 (constant voltage with series resistor); Microchip application note AN685, Thermistors in Single Supply Temperature Sensing Circuits

checks.warn: The reading is close to a rail: little resolution is left per kelvin. Choose a different fixed resistor.
Unusual B value: common NTC materials lie between 2000 K and 5000 K.

items.name: Pt100/Pt1000 resistance thermometer (IEC 60751)
items.doc: A platinum resistance thermometer (Pt100: 100 Ω at 0 °C, Pt1000: 1000 Ω) follows the Callendar–Van Dusen equation with the coefficients of IEC 60751 (α = 0.00385 /°C): for t ≥ 0 °C R = R_0 × (1 + A·t + B·t²), for t < 0 °C R = R_0 × (1 + A·t + B·t² + C·(t − 100)·t³), with t in °C, A = 3.9083·10⁻³ /°C, B = −5.775·10⁻⁷ /°C² and C = −4.183·10⁻¹² /°C⁴, valid from −200 °C to +850 °C. The temperature from a resistance uses the closed-form root of the quadratic for R ≥ R_0 (0 °C and above); below 0 °C the quartic term is included by two explicit Newton steps that start from that root, so no iteration is needed (the error is below 3·10⁻⁹ K over −200 … 0 °C). The page shows t in °C or °F. The coefficients are those printed in the Texas Instruments application note SBAA275A and the WIKA data sheet IN 00.17 and match the IEC table (100 °C: 138.5055 Ω, printed 138.51 Ω; −200 °C: 18.52 Ω; 850 °C: 390.48 Ω); the standard itself was not read, and tolerance classes are not part of this calculator. The equation is for IEC 60751 platinum only: sensors to JIS (0.003916) or the US curve (0.00392) have other coefficients. With a 2-wire connection the lead resistance adds to R (about 2.6 °C per ohm for a Pt100, 0.26 °C per ohm for a Pt1000, from R_0 × A = 0.39 Ω/°C); use 3-wire or 4-wire connection for accuracy. Table values are rounded to 0.01 Ω, so a table resistance gives the temperature only within about ±0.013 °C.
items.source: IEC 60751 (DIN EN 60751) industrial platinum resistance thermometers, Callendar–Van Dusen equation with A = 3.9083e-3, B = −5.775e-7, C = −4.183e-12, as printed in Texas Instruments application note SBAA275A, A Basic Guide to RTD Measurements, and WIKA technical information IN 00.17; the resistance table of the standard as reproduced by Isothermal Technology, Industrial Platinum Resistance Thermometer Tables; the standard itself was not read

checks.warn: Outside the range of the IEC 60751 equation (−200 … +850 °C).

formula: r = r0 * (1 + cva * t + cvb * t^2)

items.name: 4–20 mA current loop
items.doc: A 4–20 mA loop sends a process value as a current: 4 mA stands for the lower range value (LRV, the value at 4 mA), 20 mA for the upper range value (URV), and the 16 mA span is linear in between (live zero: 0 mA means a broken loop). I = 4 mA + 16 mA × (PV − LRV) / (URV − LRV); the percent of span is (I − 4 mA) / 16 mA. PV, LRV and URV share any unit (°C, bar, psi, …), may be negative, and URV may be smaller than LRV (reverse acting); LRV = URV has no span. A burden resistor at the receiver turns the current into a voltage, V = I × R: 250 Ω gives 1 … 5 V, a 249 Ω shunt 0.996 … 4.98 V, and it dissipates P = I² × R (0.1 W for 250 Ω at 20 mA). The burden is an input, not a fixed value. A current outside 4 … 20 mA means under range, over range or a fault; fault limits such as NAMUR NE 43 are not applied here. The calculator assumes a linear transmitter (not a square-root flow signal). The loop supply must also cover the minimum voltage of the transmitter plus the drop across the burden and the wires at 20 mA; take that minimum voltage from the transmitter datasheet (values from 7.5 V to 12 V are common). Example: 100 … 300 °F at 200 °F gives 12 mA.
items.source: 4–20 mA scaling: University of Alaska Fairbanks, PRT 140 Industrial Process Instrumentation I, lesson 10 (Control Loops, Sensors, and Transmitters); T. R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, vol. I, chapter 9 (Electrical Instrumentation Signals), section Current Signal Systems; burden resistor and loop voltage: NI, 4-20 mA Current Loop Fundamentals, System Design, and Setup

checks.warn: Outside the 4–20 mA span: under or over range, or the transmitter signals a fault. Near 0 mA the loop is open.
The value at 4 mA and the value at 20 mA are equal: there is no span.

items.name: Shunt current measurement
items.doc: A shunt (sense resistor) turns the current into a small voltage, V = I × R, and dissipates P = I² × R. A current-sense amplifier with the gain G scales that voltage to V_out = G × V, which should stay inside the output swing and the ADC range at the maximum current: G ≤ V_fs / (I × R), where V_fs is the ADC full scale or the usable output swing of the amplifier (enter it as V_out to get the largest gain). The largest shunt for a power budget P_max is R ≤ P_max / I². A larger shunt gives more signal and less relative offset error but more loss and more voltage burden; a milliohm shunt needs a four-terminal (Kelvin) connection so that solder joints and traces do not add to R, and the amplifier inputs go as close to the shunt as possible. Example (Texas Instruments INAx180): 40 A on 0.5 mΩ gives 20 mV and 0.8 W, and a gain of 200 gives 4 V. Low-side sensing (shunt between load and ground) is simple, but lifts the load off ground and does not see a short of the load to ground. High-side sensing (shunt between supply and load) keeps the load grounded and detects such shorts, but the amplifier must handle the supply as common-mode voltage. The values are for DC or slow currents; with fast edges the inductance of the shunt matters, and a varying current needs the RMS value for P.
items.source: Ohm's law and P = I²R for the shunt; gain and power-budget limits (R < P_max / I², I × R × G < V_swing): Texas Instruments datasheet INAx180 (SBOS741), section RSENSE and Device Gain Selection and its design example; Microchip application note AN1332, Current Sensing Circuit Concepts and Fundamentals (low-side and high-side sensing)

items.name: NE555 astable (oscillator)
items.doc: Astable multivibrator with an NE555 timer: the capacitor charges through R_1 + R_2 up to 2/3 of the supply and discharges through R_2 down to 1/3. The high time is t_H = ln 2 × (R_1 + R_2) × C (ln 2 ≈ 0.693), the low time t_L = ln 2 × R_2 × C, the frequency f = 1 / (t_H + t_L) = 1.44 / ((R_1 + 2 R_2) × C) and the duty cycle D = t_H / (t_H + t_L) = (R_1 + R_2) / (R_1 + 2 R_2), which is always above 50 %. Enter any three independent values (for example f, D and C to design the resistors). Example with the defaults: R_1 = 1 kΩ, R_2 = 68 kΩ and C = 10 nF give about 1.05 kHz at 50.4 % duty cycle (t_H ≈ 478 µs, t_L ≈ 471 µs). With the control pin not driven the result does not depend on the supply voltage; real parts add the tolerances of R and C, leakage and switching delays, so very high frequencies and very small resistors deviate.
items.source: NE555 datasheet (Texas Instruments NE555 / SE555 precision timer), astable operation: f = 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)·C), t_H = ln 2·(R_A + R_B)·C, t_L = ln 2·R_B·C; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 7 (timers)

checks.warn: The duty cycle is not above 50 %: a standard NE555 astable cannot do that (R_1 would be zero or negative). A diode across R_2 allows lower duty cycles.

items.name: NE555 monostable (one-shot)
items.doc: Monostable (one-shot) with an NE555 timer: a trigger pulse at pin 2 starts the output pulse, during which the capacitor charges through R from 0 up to 2/3 of the supply. The pulse width is t = R × C × ln 3 ≈ 1.0986 × R × C (the datasheet rounds this to 1.1 × R × C). Enter any two of R, C and t. Example with the defaults: 100 kΩ and 10 µF give a pulse of about 1.1 s. The trigger pulse must be shorter than the output pulse; the real width varies with the capacitor tolerance and leakage (use film or low-leakage capacitors for long times).
items.source: NE555 datasheet (Texas Instruments NE555 / SE555 precision timer), monostable operation: t_w = 1.1·R_A·C, exactly ln 3·R_A·C (charging from 0 to 2/3 V_CC); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 7 (timers)

items.name: Crystal load capacitors
items.doc: Load capacitors for a parallel-resonant quartz crystal in a Pierce oscillator: two capacitors C_1 = C_2 from the crystal pins to ground. The crystal sees the load capacitance C_L = C_1 × C_2 / (C_1 + C_2) + C_stray, where C_stray is the pin, trace and board capacitance (a few pF as a rough estimate, 2 to 5 pF). With C_1 = C_2 = C this gives C = 2 × (C_L − C_stray). Take C_L from the crystal datasheet. Example with the defaults: C_L = 18 pF and C_stray = 4 pF give C_1 = C_2 = 28 pF (use the nearest standard value, 27 pF).
items.source: Load capacitance of a parallel-resonant crystal in a Pierce oscillator: C_L = C_1·C_2/(C_1 + C_2) + C_stray (series connection of the two capacitors plus stray capacitance); the crystal datasheet states C_L; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 7 (crystal oscillators)

checks.warn: C_stray is not below C_L: the board already provides the load capacitance, no load capacitors are needed (or the crystal needs a lower load capacitance).

items.name: Frequency, period and duty cycle
items.doc: Converts between the frequency f, the period T = 1 / f and the duty cycle D of a rectangular signal: t_high = D × T and t_low = T − t_high. Enter any two independent values (the frequency and the period alone do not fix the duty cycle). Example with the defaults: 1 kHz at a duty cycle of 30 % is a period of 1 ms with 300 µs high and 700 µs low.
items.source: Definitions: frequency f = 1/T (hertz = 1/s, SI Brochure, BIPM) and duty cycle D = t_high/T of a periodic rectangular signal

checks.warn: The duty cycle must be between 0 % and 100 %.

items.name: PWM average voltage
items.doc: Average and RMS value of a rectangular PWM signal that switches between V_low and V_high with the duty cycle D: V_avg = V_low + D × (V_high − V_low) (a low-pass filter, or the inertia of a motor, LED or heater, turns the PWM into this DC voltage) and V_rms = √(D × V_high² + (1 − D) × V_low²) (the heating effect in a resistive load). Enter any three of D, V_high, V_low and V_avg. Example with the defaults: 25 % duty cycle between 0 V and 5 V gives V_avg = 1.25 V and V_rms = 2.5 V.
items.source: Average and RMS value of a rectangular two-level waveform over one period (integration of the waveform); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (signals)

checks.warn: The duty cycle must be between 0 % and 100 %.

items.name: Crystal drift (ppm ↔ s/day)
items.doc: Converts the frequency tolerance of a crystal in ppm (parts per million, 1 ppm = 10⁻⁶) into the error of a clock that counts its oscillator, and back. The relative error is δ = Δf / f₀, so a clock that runs δ too fast gains δ × t_elapsed: Δt = δ × 86 400 s per day. One ppm is 0.0864 s per day. Because the length of a month or a year is a convention, the derived values are labelled with their days: 30 days (2 592 000 s) and 365 days (31 536 000 s). The frequency error is Δf = δ × f₀ at the nominal frequency. Enter the error in ppm or the time error per day (and the nominal frequency for Δf). The result is the magnitude of the error: the sign (a crystal that is too fast makes the clock gain, one that is too slow makes it lose) is not kept. The conversion is exact while δ stays constant over the interval. Temperature, aging and the load capacitance change δ in real life and are not part of this calculator: the value is a tolerance from the datasheet, not the error of a particular day. Example with the defaults: 20 ppm are 1.728 s per day, 51.84 s per 30 days (about a minute per month) and 630.72 s per 365 days, and 0.655 Hz at 32 768 Hz.
items.source: Definition of the relative frequency error δ = Δf/f₀ in parts per million and of the time error Δt = δ·t (1 ppm = 10⁻⁶); published figures for comparison: Analog Devices (Maxim) note on crystal considerations for real-time clocks (20 ppm is about one minute per month); Seiko Epson RX8900SA/CE application manual ETM45E-10 (frequency characteristics in seconds of month deviation); Texas Instruments SLAA322D, MSP430 32-kHz crystal oscillators (frequency tolerance in Hz at 32 768 Hz)

derived.label: Δf
derived.name: Frequency error at the nominal frequency

checks.warn: More than 10 000 ppm (1 %) is not a crystal tolerance; check the unit.

items.name: AVR timer compare value (CTC)
items.doc: Compare value OCR of an AVR timer (ATmega328P family) in CTC mode (clear timer on compare match). The counter runs from 0 up to OCR and starts again, so one cycle takes OCR + 1 timer clocks of f_clk / N (N = prescaler). A toggled output pin needs two compare matches per period: f = f_clk / (2 × N × (1 + OCR)). The compare-match interrupt (or the cycle rate) runs twice as fast: f = f_clk / (N × (1 + OCR)); this rate follows from the same counting sequence, the datasheet prints the equation for the toggled pin. Enter f_clk (normally F_CPU) and the wanted frequency, and choose the mode and the counter width (8 bit: Timer0 and Timer2, TOP = 255; 16 bit: Timer1, TOP = 65 535). The calculator rounds the exact value f_clk / (k × N × f) to the nearest whole number of timer clocks (k = 2 or 1), subtracts the 1 and shows the real frequency and its error. The prescaler is either picked automatically (the smallest of 1, 8, 64, 256 and 1024 whose OCR fits the counter; if even 1024 is too small the warning says so) or fixed. The list 1, 8, 64, 256, 1024 is valid for Timer0 and Timer1 and also exists on Timer2; Timer2 additionally has the prescalers 32 and 128, which are not offered here. Forgetting the +1 makes the period one timer clock too long: with a 32.768 kHz crystal, prescaler 1024 and an interrupt every second the correct value is OCR = 31 (32 clocks); OCR = 32 gives 33 clocks, 1.03125 s. OCR is assumed static and the timer clock to be the I/O clock (a Timer2 in asynchronous mode runs from the crystal frequency instead). Example with the defaults: 16 MHz and 1 kHz on a toggled pin (8 bit) pick prescaler 64 and OCR = 124: 16 000 000 / (2 × 64 × 125) = 1000 Hz.
items.source: Microchip (Atmel) ATmega328P datasheet 7810D-AVR-01/15: CTC mode of Timer/Counter0, Timer/Counter1 and Timer/Counter2, toggled output f_OCnx = f_clk_I/O / (2·N·(1 + OCRnx)) with the prescalers N = 1, 8, 64, 256, 1024 (Timer2 also 32 and 128); the compare-match interrupt rate f_clk_I/O / (N·(1 + OCR)) follows from the same counting sequence 0 … OCR; the rounding of OCR to the nearest value is the choice of this calculator

derived.label: f_clk/(k·f)
derived.name: Exact timer clocks per period (N × (1 + OCR), unrounded)

checks.warn: The compare value does not fit the timer; choose a larger prescaler or the 16-bit timer.
The target frequency is above the maximum for this prescaler (f_clk / (k × N)).

items.name: PCB trace width (IPC-2221)
items.doc: Current-carrying capacity of a printed-circuit trace after the IPC-2221 equation I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725, with the current I in A, the temperature rise ΔT in °C and the copper cross-section A in mil² (1 mil = 25.4 µm). The constant k is 0.048 for traces on external layers and 0.024 for internal layers. The cross-section is the copper thickness times the trace width; 1 oz copper is a layer of about 35 µm. The defaults (2 A, 10 °C rise, 1 oz, external) need a trace about 0.78 mm (31 mil) wide. The IPC-2221 curves cover temperature rises of about 10 °C to 100 °C and currents up to about 35 A. The result is a guide value for a single trace: neighbouring copper, vias and the board thickness change the real temperature rise, and the newer IPC-2152 gives more detailed data for critical designs.
items.source: IPC-2221 (generic standard on printed board design), current-carrying capacity equation I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725 with k = 0.048 (external) and k = 0.024 (internal layers); see also IPC-2152

checks.warn: The current is above the range of the IPC-2221 curves (about 35 A); the result is an extrapolation.
The temperature rise is above the range of the IPC-2221 curves (about 100 °C); the result is an extrapolation.

items.name: PCB trace resistance
items.doc: Resistance of a copper trace: R = ρ × L / (W × T), with the resistivity at the trace temperature ρ = ρ_20 × (1 + α × (θ − 20 °C)). For copper ρ_20 = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (17.24 nΩ·m) and α = 0.00393 /K (annealed copper, IEC 60028). The voltage drop is R × I and the dissipated power R × I². The sheet resistance R_sq = ρ / T is the resistance of a square of any size. The defaults (0.25 mm wide, 35 µm thick, 50 mm long, 25 °C, 1 A) give about 0.1 Ω, so 0.1 V and 0.1 W. Enter the temperature of the trace, not of the room: at the temperature rise of a heavily loaded trace the resistance is noticeably higher.
items.source: Resistance of a prismatic conductor R = ρ × L / A; annealed copper ρ_20 = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m and α = 0.00393 /K per IEC 60028; resistivity at temperature ρ = ρ_20 × (1 + α × (θ − 20 °C))

items.name: Via current capacity
items.doc: Estimate for a plated through-hole via. The copper barrel is a tube of length H (the board thickness) with the finished hole diameter D and the plating thickness T_p, so its copper cross-section is A = π × T_p × (D + T_p) and its resistance at 20 °C is R = ρ × H / A with ρ = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028). The IPC-2221 equation is written for traces; applying it to a via barrel is a common engineering approximation, not a rule of the standard. Here the barrel cross-section is used with the constant for internal layers: I = 0.024 × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725 (A in mil²), which is the lower of the two IPC-2221 constants. Several vias in parallel share the current. The defaults (0.3 mm finished hole, 25 µm plating, 1.6 mm board, 10 °C rise) give A = 0.0255 mm², R = 1.08 mΩ and I = 0.95 A.
items.source: Tube cross-section A = π × T_p × (D + T_p) and R = ρ × H / A with ρ = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028); current from the IPC-2221 equation I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725 with the internal-layer constant k = 0.024 applied to the barrel as an approximation

derived.label: I
derived.name: Current for the temperature rise (IPC-2221, internal)

checks.warn: The temperature rise is above the range of the IPC-2221 curves (about 100 °C); the result is an extrapolation.

items.name: AWG wire size conversion
items.doc: American Wire Gauge: the diameter of the gauge n is d = 0.005 in × 92^((36 − n) / 39) (ASTM B258), a factor of about 1.123 per gauge step and about 2 for every 6 steps. The cross-section is A = π / 4 × d². Enter the diameter in AWG, mm, mil or inch, or the cross-section in AWG, mm², kcmil or mil²; a circular mil is the area of a circle 1 mil in diameter, so 1 kcmil = 0.5067 mm². The gauges 0000, 000 and 00 are −3, −2 and −1. The default AWG 10 is 2.588 mm in diameter and 5.261 mm² (ASTM B258 lists 2.588 mm). The resistance of 1 km is for annealed copper at 20 °C (1/58 Ω·mm²/m).
items.source: ASTM B258 (standard nominal diameters and cross-sectional areas of AWG sizes of solid round wires): d = 0.005 in × 92^((36 − n) / 39); 1 circular mil = π / 4 mil²; copper resistivity 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028)

items.name: SMD chip sizes (resistors, capacitors)
items.doc: Sizes of SMD chip resistors and capacitors: EIA (inch) and metric size codes, body length and width, and the typical rated power and working voltage of thick-film chip resistors with the values of three makers.
items.notes: Ratings are for general-purpose thick-film chip resistors at 70 °C ambient; above 70 °C derate linearly to zero at the maximum film temperature (155 °C for most series, 125 °C for Yageo RC0075–RC0201 and Panasonic ERJ-XG/1G). The continuous working voltage is the lower of √(P·R) and the maximum working voltage. The typical columns show the value that most makers share for the standard type; where the makers differ (power at 0402, voltage at 2010 and 2512, body size of 2512) the maker columns and the remark show the spread. Capacitor (MLCC) bodies use the same size codes, but thickness and tolerances are maker-specific. Panasonic marks some sizes and parts NRFND (not recommended for new designs). Beware of mixed-up codes: 0402 and 0603 exist in both systems (imperial 0402 = metric 1005, metric 0402 = imperial 01005; imperial 0603 = metric 1608, metric 0603 = imperial 0201).
items.source: Yageo RC_L series product specification (V.11); Vishay Dale D/CRCW e3 datasheet (document 20035); Panasonic ERJ precision thick film chip resistors; KEMET C0G/X7R and TDK MLCC size code tables

items.name: Cable current ratings, copper, PVC (70 °C)
items.doc: Current-carrying capacity of copper conductors with PVC insulation (70 °C) for the installation methods A1 to F, with two or three loaded conductors, at 30 °C ambient air and one circuit (IEC 60364-5-52, DIN VDE 0298-4).
items.notes: Reference conditions: one circuit, 30 °C ambient air, continuous operation, AC 50/60 Hz or DC. Installation methods (IEC 60364-5-52): A1 insulated conductors or single-core cables in conduit in a thermally insulated wall; A2 multi-core cable in conduit in a thermally insulated wall; B1 insulated conductors or single-core cables in conduit on or in a wall; B2 multi-core cable in conduit on or in a wall; C cable fixed directly on or in a wall or on an unperforated tray; E multi-core cable in free air or on a perforated tray, at least 0.3 d from the wall; F single-core cables touching in free air (2 loaded: flat, 3 loaded: trefoil). Multiply by the ambient temperature factor and the grouping factor (see the tables Ambient temperature factors and Grouping factors for cables). Method F has no values below 25 mm². IEC and DIN differ in two cells: DIN VDE 0298-4 (2013) gives 15.5 A for 1.5 mm² in A1 and A2 with two loaded conductors; this table carries the IEC values 14.5 A and 14 A. BS 7671 gives 20 A for 2.5 mm² in method A with two cables, IEC and DIN give 19.5 A (the table follows IEC and DIN).
items.source: IEC 60364-5-52:2009 annex B (tables B.52.2, B.52.4, B.52.10) = DIN VDE 0298-4:2013-06 table 3, as reproduced in the ABB SACE Electrical Installation Handbook (6th ed. 2010, table 8), BS 7671:2018 appendix 4 (tables 4D1A, 4D2A), the Schneider Electrical Installation Guide (figure G20), ABB Stotz-Kontakt 2CDC400027D0104 (table 2) and Engineering ToolBox

Multiply by the ambient temperature factor and the grouping factor (see the tables Ambient temperature factors and Grouping factors for cables). Method F has no values below 25 mm². The four cells for 2.5 mm² in A1 and B1 are empty: they were found in the ABB handbook only. 90 °C values may only be used if terminals, devices and accessories are rated for 90 °C; in building installations DIN VDE 0298-4 usually limits the conductor temperature to 70 °C, so use the PVC table there.

Multiply by the ambient temperature factor and the grouping factor (see the tables Ambient temperature factors and Grouping factors for cables). Method F has no values below 25 mm². Aluminium conductors from 16 mm² (IEC also lists 2.5 to 10 mm²). Only the columns with three loaded conductors in A1, A2, B1, B2 and C are confirmed by a second source; the columns with two loaded conductors and the methods E and F are empty (ABB handbook only). items.doc: Current-carrying capacity of aluminium conductors with XLPE/EPR insulation (90 °C) for the installation methods A1 to F, with two or three loaded conductors, at 30 °C ambient air and one circuit (IEC 60364-5-52, DIN VDE 0298-4).

Installation methods (IEC 60364-5-52): A1 insulated conductors or single-core cables in conduit in a thermally insulated wall; A2 multi-core cable in conduit in a thermally insulated wall; B1 insulated conductors or single-core cables in conduit on or in a wall; B2 multi-core cable in conduit on or in a wall; C cable fixed directly on or in a wall or on an unperforated tray; E multi-core cable in free air or on a perforated tray, at least 0.3 d from the wall; F single-core cables touching in free air (2 loaded: flat, 3 loaded: trefoil). items.name: Ambient temperature factors for cables in air
items.name_en: Ambient temperature factors for cables in air
items.doc: Correction factors for the current-carrying capacity of cables in air at an ambient temperature other than 30 °C, for conductors rated 60 °C (rubber cords), 70 °C (PVC) and 90 °C (XLPE, EPR) (IEC 60364-5-52 table B.52.14, DIN VDE 0298-4 table 17).
items.notes: Multiply the current-carrying capacity for 30 °C by k. An empty cell means that the insulation is not permitted at that ambient temperature. The 65 °C value of the 70 °C column (0.35) comes from DIN VDE 0298-4; IEC stops at 60 °C. The 60 °C column (DIN VDE 0298-4 only, for rubber cords) is empty from 10 to 25 °C and the 90 °C value at 85 °C is omitted, because they were found in one source only. For cables in the ground other factors apply (reference 20 °C, IEC table B.52.15). In Germany 25 °C is common practice; the factor for 70 °C is then 1.06.
items.source: IEC 60364-5-52:2009 table B.52.14 and DIN VDE 0298-4:2013-06 table 17, as reproduced in the Schneider Electrical Installation Guide (figure G12), the ABB SACE Electrical Installation Handbook vol. 2 (4th ed., table 4), ABB Stotz-Kontakt 2CDC400027D0104 (table 5) and Lapp T12 (table 12-2)

items.name: Grouping factors for cables
items.doc: Reduction factors for the current-carrying capacity of cables in groups of several circuits (one multi-core cable, or one group of 2 or 3 single-core cables, counts as one circuit), by the arrangement of the cables (IEC 60364-5-52 table B.52.17, DIN VDE 0298-4 table 21).
items.notes: The standard lists the arrangements as rows and the numbers of circuits as columns; here they are swapped so that the number of circuits is the key. The factors apply to cables of similar size that are equally loaded and touch each other, unless stated otherwise; the sizes may differ by at most three adjacent standard sizes (IEC) or one size step (DIN). No factor is needed when the horizontal clearance exceeds twice the cable diameter or when a cable carries less than 30 % of its grouped rating. For single-layer arrangements there is no further reduction above nine circuits (IEC), so the factors for 10 to 20 circuits repeat the value for nine. The two spaced arrangements come from DIN VDE 0298-4 only. Empty cells are not listed in the standard or were found in one source only (the bunched factor for 14 circuits and the spaced factors for 5, 8, 12 and 14 circuits). If the number of circuits is not listed, use the next larger listed number.
items.source: IEC 60364-5-52:2009 table B.52.17 and DIN VDE 0298-4:2013-06 table 21, as reproduced in the Schneider Electrical Installation Guide (figure G16), the ABB SACE Electrical Installation Handbook vol. 2 (4th ed., table 5), ABB Stotz-Kontakt 2CDC400027D0104 (table 7) and Lapp T12 (table 12-6)

items.notes: Apply the factor to the current-carrying capacity for three loaded conductors. items.notes: US view; for IEC and DIN installations use the cable current-rating tables. The columns are the temperature rating of the insulation (60, 75 and 90 °C); the temperature rating of the terminals (usually 60 °C or 75 °C) limits which column may be used. Aluminium means aluminium or copper-clad aluminium. The overcurrent device for 14, 12 and 10 AWG copper is limited to 15, 20 and 30 A (NEC 240.4(D)) whatever the table says; the last column marks these rows. items.doc: Minimum spacing between conductors on a printed board by the voltage between them (DC or AC peak), for internal and external conductors and component leads (IPC-2221B table 6-1, the same table as in IPC-2221A).
items.notes: IPC-2221 spacing is functional spacing for printed boards; for mains or safety isolation use the creepage and clearance of IEC 60664-1 and IEC 62368-1. items.name: PCB copper weight and thickness
items.doc: Copper weight of printed-circuit copper layers in ounces per square foot with the area weight and the thickness by several conventions (physical density, IPC-4562A, commercial designation, 1.37 mil rule).
items.notes: A copper weight of 1 oz is an area weight (1 ounce of copper spread over 1 square foot), not an exact thickness: 34.2 µm (density of pure copper), 34.3 µm (IPC-4562A nominal), 34.8 µm (1.37 mil rule) and 35 µm (designation) are all in use. ECalc's unit oz uses 35 µm. The area weight follows from the unit definitions (1 oz/ft² = 305.1517 g/m²); the physical thickness assumes 8.935 g/cm³. Finished copper after processing is thinner (about 30 µm for 1 oz). The designations of 1/4 and 3/8 oz are names and not exact fractions of 1 oz. The rows for 1/4, 3/8 and 4 oz of the 1.37 mil rule are arithmetic extensions. Typical values; empty cells have no published value.
items.source: NIST SP 811 appendix B.9 (oz/ft² to kg/m²); copper density 8.935 g/cm³ (Wikipedia); IPC-4562A nominal thicknesses as quoted by B. Hargin (Siemens EDA, 2025); Denkai TOB-III data sheet (IPC-4562 table 1-1 designations); 1.37 mil rule per JLCPCB and AIVON

items.name: SI prefixes
items.doc: The 24 SI prefixes from quetta (10^30) to quecto (10^-30): name, symbol and factor.
items.notes: Prefix symbols are case-sensitive (M = mega, m = milli). Prefixes are never combined (write nm, not mµm). The kilogram is the only base unit with a prefix in its name, so prefixes are applied to the gram (mg, not µkg). The symbol µ is the micro sign (U+00B5); ECalc input also accepts u for µ and K for k. Ronna, ronto, quetta and quecto were added by the CGPM in 2022.
items.source: BIPM, The International System of Units (SI), 9th edition (2019, V4.01), Table 7 "SI prefixes"; BIPM, 27th CGPM (2022), Resolution 3 (ronna, ronto, quetta, quecto)

items.name: SI units
items.doc: The seven SI base units, the 22 units with special names and common coherent derived units, with their expression in SI base units.
items.notes: The radian and steradian are the coherent units of plane and solid angle; they are dimensionless (1) but keep their names for clarity. The hertz is only for periodic phenomena, the becquerel only for stochastic processes (radioactive decay). The electric potential difference is also called voltage. A temperature difference has the same numerical value in K and °C. The order of the base-unit symbols follows the 9th edition of the SI Brochure (newton = kg·m·s⁻²).
items.source: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition (V4.01), Tables 2, 4, 5 and 6; German names: Einheitenverordnung (EinhV) Anlage 1 and de.wikipedia "Liste physikalischer Größen"

items.name: Physical constants
items.doc: 30 physical constants for electronics: the seven SI defining constants, electromagnetic constants, particle masses and derived constants, with the CODATA 2022 values and uncertainties.
items.notes: CODATA 2022 values as printed by NIST, shown as text with every printed digit. Since the 2019 SI revision h, e, k and N_A are exact; µ0 and ε0 are measured (µ0 is about 4π × 10⁻⁷ N/A², to about 1 part in 10¹⁰). Constants marked exact (derived) are computed from the exact ones; NIST prints their digits truncated, so compute them from h, e, k and N_A when you need more digits. Uncertainties are standard uncertainties (1σ) in the unit of the value; exact constants have none. The thermal voltage kT/e is 25.852 mV at 300 K and 25.693 mV at 25 °C (computed from exact constants).
items.source: NIST, Fundamental Physical Constants, complete listing, 2022 CODATA adjustment; exact values per the BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, Table 1
rows: electron mass energy equivalent in MeV

items.name: Greek alphabet
items.doc: The 24 letters of the Greek alphabet with their variant forms, English and German names and typical uses of the letters as symbols in electrical engineering.
items.notes: Uses are typical, not normative, and vary between fields and countries (conductivity is σ internationally, often γ or κ in German electrical engineering): check the symbol definitions of the document you are reading. Letters without an entry have no common use in electronics. The micro sign µ (U+00B5) and the Greek small mu μ (U+03BC) look alike; the ohm sign (U+2126) is canonically equivalent to the Greek capital omega Ω (U+03A9).

items.notes: The two numerals are independent: IPX7 does not imply IPX5 or IPX6 (immersion is not a jet test); a product tested for both is marked e.g. IPX6/IPX7. items.name: ISM and SRD bands
items.doc: The ITU ISM bands (6.78 MHz to 245 GHz) and the EU short-range-device (SRD) bands around 433, 868 MHz, 2.4 and 5.8 GHz, with band edges, legal basis and the allowed transmit power and duty cycle.
items.notes: ISM bands are designated for industrial, scientific and medical RF energy (e.g. microwave ovens); radio services there must accept interference from ISM equipment. Short-range devices (SRD) are licence-exempt only under the EU and national conditions (power, duty cycle or listen-before-talk with adaptive frequency agility, LBT/AFA). Radio use always needs the national frequency assignment (in Germany the general assignments of the Bundesnetzagentur). Duty cycle is the share of transmit time: 1 % is 36 s per hour. SRD limits per Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/180; check EUR-Lex for later amendments. The further rows of that decision (for example wideband data and voice) are not listed. The ITU footnote numbers (RR 5.138 and 5.150) are taken from Wikipedia, the Radio Regulations themselves were not read. The EU-only band at 169 MHz is not listed. Frequencies are rounded to the significant digits set in the ECalc settings.

items.name: Amateur radio bands in Germany (AFuV)
items.doc: The 45 frequency ranges of Annex 1 of the German Amateur Radio Ordinance (AFuV): band edges, primary or secondary status, maximum power per licence class A, E and N and the additional conditions.
items.notes: Only the current AFuV and the decisions of the Bundesnetzagentur are binding; temporary toleration rules (e.g. for the 70 MHz band) are not part of Annex 1 and are not listed. P = the amateur service is primary, S = secondary. PEP = peak envelope power, ERP = effective radiated power. An empty class cell means the band is not available to that class. The band names are conventional and not part of the regulation. Row 45 covers every frequency above 275 GHz (the lower edge is not included). General rule (Annex 1 (1)): remote-controlled and automatic terrestrial stations above 30 MHz may use at most 50 W ERP (except remote operation). Additional conditions (part B): 1 max. occupied bandwidth 800 Hz; 2 sites must be notified to the BNetzA; 3 max. bandwidth 2.7 kHz; 4 max. bandwidth 7 kHz below 29 MHz, 40 kHz above; 5 no interference to broadcasting and wind-profiler radars, horizontal polarisation only, fixed stations only (50 to 52 MHz); 6 max. bandwidth 40 kHz; 7 max. 2 MHz (AM TV 7 MHz); 8 max. 2 MHz (AM and digital TV 7 MHz, FM TV 18 MHz); 9 max. 10 MHz (TV 20 MHz); 10 no remote-controlled stations except remote operation, no contests; 11 1247 to 1263 MHz max. 3.05 W ERP, no remote-controlled or automatic stations; 12 automatic stations max. 50 W ERP; 13 also usable for the amateur-satellite service (see the regulation for primary and secondary details); 14 bands above 275 GHz usable without protection; 15 weekends on 1850 to 2000 kHz: class A 750 W PEP, class E 100 W PEP, contests allowed; 16 max. bandwidth 12 kHz; 17 links of remote-controlled and automatic stations up to 1000 W ERP in justified cases. Frequencies are rounded to the significant digits set in the ECalc settings.
items.source: Amateurfunkverordnung (AFuV) Anlage 1, BGBl. 2024 I Nr. 175, gesetze-im-internet.de; checked row by row against buzer.de and against the DARC summary "Amateurfunkverordnung – Änderungen zum 24.06.2024"

items.name: Logic levels
items.doc: Input and output voltage limits of TTL, 74LS, 74HC, 74HCT, 5 V CMOS and 3.3, 2.5 and 1.8 V LVCMOS logic: VIH, VIL, VOH, VOL, load currents and switching threshold.
items.notes: Interfacing rule: a driver fits a receiver when VOH(min) of the driver is at least VIH(min) of the receiver and VOL(max) of the driver is at most VIL(max) of the receiver. Example: a 3.3 V LVCMOS output (VOH at least 2.4 V) drives 74HCT (VIH 2.0 V) but not 74HC at 5 V (VIH 3.15 V at 4.5 V). Noise margin high = VOH(min) − VIH(min); noise margin low = VIL(max) − VOL(max). The VIH and VIL columns are the limits at the nominal supply; for the CMOS rules 0.7 and 0.3 × VCC (5 V) and 0.65 and 0.35 × VCC (1.8 V) the numbers are the values at that supply. The VOH and VOL columns show a / b for the two load currents of the next column; "VCC − 0.1" is the light-load value. Values are the limits of real parts (−40 to 85 °C) from the data sheets named in the source, not the JEDEC standards (not read); output levels depend strongly on load current and temperature, so check the data sheet of the actual part. The switching threshold Vt is read from the TI Logic Guide figures and is approximate.

items.name: RS-232, RS-485 and LVDS signal levels
items.name_en: RS-232, RS-485 and LVDS signal levels
items.doc: Voltage levels, thresholds and loads of the serial interfaces RS-232 (TIA-232-F), RS-485 (TIA/EIA-485-A) and LVDS (TIA/EIA-644-A): minimum, typical and maximum values with the test condition.
items.notes: The unit of the Min, Typ and Max values is in the Unit column (the rows use different units). RS-232 uses negative logic on the data lines: logic 1 (mark, idle) is negative, logic 0 (space) is positive; control lines are active when positive. RS-485 and LVDS are differential: the receiver evaluates VA − VB, and the line is terminated with its characteristic impedance (RS-485 typically 120 Ω at both ends, LVDS 100 Ω at the receiver). Noise margin RS-485 = 1.5 V − 0.2 V = 1.3 V; RS-232 = 5 V − 3 V = 2 V. The TIA standards themselves were not read; the values come from maker documents that cite them and from Wikipedia. Typical per the named maker document, one source each: the RS-232 load of 3 to 7 kΩ, input impedance and slew rate of 30 V/µs (TI SLLA037A), the RS-485 unit load of about 12 kΩ (TI SLLA272D), and the LVDS output voltage limits of 247 and 454 mV and the offset voltage limits of 1.125 and 1.375 V (TI SN65LVDS31 data sheet, a part that meets TIA/EIA-644; its typical output voltage is 340 mV, the 350 mV shown is the nominal value of the TI LVDS Owner's Manual).

items.name: ASCII table
items.doc: The 128 ASCII codes (0 to 127) in decimal and hexadecimal with the character or control-character abbreviation, RFC 20 class, Ctrl notation and name.
items.notes: ASCII is a 7-bit code (0 to 127). Codes 128 to 255 are not ASCII; their meaning depends on the code page (e.g. ISO 8859-1, Windows-1252) or on UTF-8 multi-byte sequences. The code column can be shown in decimal, hexadecimal, binary or octal with its unit selector. SP is the space (code 32). Line ends: Unix and Linux LF (0x0A), Windows CR LF (0x0D 0x0A), classic Mac OS CR (0x0D). Upper and lower case letters differ only in bit 5 (0x20): A = 0x41, a = 0x61. The Ctrl notation of a control character is the code XOR 0x40 (Ctrl+key); DEL is ^?. RFC 20 classes: CC communication control, FE format effector, IS information separator. English names are those of RFC 20 (modern names in brackets where the 1969 name is archaic); RFC 20 notes that several characters should not be used in international interchange without agreement between sender and recipient.
items.source: RFC 20 (USAS X3.4-1968), rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc20.txt; German control-character names: de.wikipedia "Steuerzeichen"

items.name: Resistivity of conductor and resistance materials
items.name_en: Resistivity of conductor and resistance materials
items.doc: Resistivity at 20 °C and temperature coefficient of common conductor, contact, resistance and solder materials, for estimates of wire resistance and voltage drop.
items.notes: Typical values at 20 °C. Real conductors differ with purity, alloy content and temper (cold work raises the resistivity). The linear model ρ(T) = ρ20 · (1 + α · (T − 20 °C)) holds only in a moderate range around 20 °C; for iron, nickel and tungsten the error grows quickly with temperature. Annealed copper (IEC 60028) and hard-drawn aluminium wire (IEC 60889) are the standard values of the wire calculators; the other rows come from handbooks and maker data sheets, and the columns for the lowest and highest resistivity show how far the sources spread. For constantan and manganin the makers specify a band for α instead of a single value (columns α lower and upper limit); inside that band the resistance is practically constant. α is left empty where the sources disagree or only one source was found: gold, nickel, iron, unalloyed steel, stainless steel and nichrome (the row note names the spread). The only α found for phosphor bronze was not confirmed from a primary document and is left empty too, and the resistivity of tin is only reliable to two digits. The sources give no α for the solders. 1 Ω·mm²/m = 1 µΩ·m = 100 µΩ·cm; % IACS = 1.7241 µΩ·cm / ρ × 100.
items.source: IEC 60028 (annealed copper) and IEC 60889 (hard-drawn aluminium wire); CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 84th ed., section 12 (pure metals); Wikipedia, HyperPhysics and Engineering ToolBox (textbook values after Giancoli and Serway); Isabellenhütte and Kanthal data sheets (manganin, constantan, nichrome); Deutsches Kupferinstitut, Aurubis and Bikar data sheets (brass, phosphor bronze); Elgin and Lamineries Matthey data sheets (steels); NIST solder database, Kester and Indium Corporation (solders)

items.name: Relative permittivity and loss tangent of dielectrics
items.name_en: Relative permittivity and loss tangent of dielectrics
items.doc: Relative permittivity εr and loss tangent tan δ of circuit board laminates, cable insulation, glass and ceramic substrates, with the frequency of the measurement.
items.notes: Typical values. εr and tan δ depend on frequency, temperature, humidity and, for laminates, on resin content and glass weave; always state the frequency with the value. For impedance design use the board maker's stack-up data (Rogers: the design Dk). The lowest and highest columns show the range between sources or grades. For Rogers laminates εr is the process value at 10 GHz and the design Dk is the value to use for line impedances. Several loss tangents come from a single data sheet (polyethylene, PVC, borosilicate glass, Kapton, alumina 99.5 %), and the generic FR-4 row is a collection of values from application notes, not one maker. The upper ends of the ranges for alumina 96 % (Kyocera values) were not confirmed from a primary document and are left empty. tan δ is the ratio of the loss to the stored energy per cycle; the dielectric attenuation of a line grows with √εr · tan δ · f.
items.source: Rogers Corporation data sheets (RO4003C, RO4350B, RT/duroid 5880); Isola 370HR data sheet; DuPont Teflon PTFE properties handbook and Kapton HN data sheet K-15345-2; Lapp ÖLFLEX catalogue appendix T15 and myElectrical (cable insulation); SCHOTT BOROFLOAT 33; CoorsTek ceramic properties chart; Wikipedia (FR-4, relative permittivity) and Engineering ToolBox
rows: Depends on resin content and glass style; ask the board maker for the stack-up value.
Same laminate at 100 MHz: εr 4.24 / tan δ 0.0150.
FR-4 losses rise with frequency (2 GHz: εr 4.04 / tan δ 0.0210).
εr 3.38 ± 0.05 is the process (clamped stripline) value; use the design Dk 3.55 (8–40 GHz) for line impedance.
εr 3.48 ± 0.05 process value; design Dk 3.66 (8–40 GHz).
εr is almost independent of frequency and temperature. tan δ is an upper limit: DuPont gives below 0.0001 from 60 Hz to 2 GHz, other sources up to 0.0004.
3.4 for 25–50 µm and 3.5 for 75–125 µm film; tan δ rises from 0.0018 (25 µm) to 0.0026 (125 µm).
Very low loss; solid-PE coax has a velocity factor of about 0.66.
High loss; not suitable as an RF dielectric. The source gives tan δ as 0.04 to 0.1; 0.05 is a representative value.
For most calculations εr = 1. No source gives a loss tangent; air is practically lossless.
Other glasses range from about 3.7 to 10.
The upper ends of the ranges are left empty: the higher values found (Kyocera A476: 9.4 and 0.0004) were not confirmed from a primary document.

items.name: Thermocouple types (IEC 60584)
items.doc: The standard thermocouple types B, E, J, K, N, R, S and T: conductor materials, temperature range of the reference function, tolerance classes 1 and 2, thermoelectric voltage and sensitivity, and the colours of thermocouple cables.
items.notes: The thermoelectric voltage is defined with the reference (cold) junction at 0 °C; at another reference temperature subtract the voltage of the same type at that temperature. The sensitivity changes with temperature, so use the reference function or table, not a constant, for accurate work. Voltages and sensitivities are taken from the NIST ITS-90 tables, whose reference functions equal those of IEC 60584-1. Tolerance: the larger of the fixed value (°C) and the proportional value (factor × |t|) applies; for types R and S the class 1 limit above 1100 °C is ±[1 + 0.003·(t − 1100)] °C, and class 1 is not defined for type B (class 3 exists but is not listed). The tolerance classes are transcribed from three agreeing maker tables, not from the IEC table itself. IEC 60584-1:2013 limits the type K reference function to 1300 °C (the NIST tables go to 1372 °C). Colours follow IEC 60584-3:2007 (the positive core in the type colour, the negative core white, intrinsically safe circuits with a blue sheath); the 2021 edition, which also adds types C and A, was not checked. The IEC name of the type E colour is violet, makers write purple. The IEC colours of type B are weakly sourced and left empty. ANSI MC96.1: the negative core is always red; the thermocouple-grade jacket is not established for types R, S and B. For type B the mean sensitivity between 0 and 100 °C is not meaningful (the output is almost zero below about 50 °C). Older national colour codes (DIN 43714, BS 1843, JIS, NF) differ: check the colours of an existing installation before connecting.
items.source: IEC 60584-1:2013 (conductors and reference-function ranges); tolerance classes after SAB Bröckskes, Thermosense and TC Direct (IEC 60584-1 classes); thermoelectric voltages after the NIST ITS-90 Thermocouple Database; colours after IEC 60584-3:2007 (TC Direct, Tempco, EPIC Sensors) and ANSI MC96.1 (Thermometrics, Omega)
rows: Above 760 °C the iron leg changes; the lower range may then no longer stay within tolerance.
Most common general-purpose type. IEC 60584-1:2013 limits the reference function to 1300 °C.
Good for low temperatures; tightest class 1 tolerance. The range ends at 400 °C, so there is no value at 1000 °C.
Highest output of the standard types. 1000 °C is the end of the range, so there is no sensitivity at that point.
More stable than type K at high temperature.
Noble-metal type for high temperatures; low output. Class 1 above 1100 °C: ±[1 + 0.003·(t − 1100)] °C. The ANSI colours are those of the compensating cable.
Noble-metal type for high temperatures; low output. Class 1 above 1100 °C: ±[1 + 0.003·(t − 1100)] °C. The ANSI colours are those of the compensating cable.
Output is almost zero near room temperature; use above 600 °C. Class 1 is not defined; the IEC colours are weakly sourced and left empty.

items.name: Solder alloys
items.doc: Common soft solder alloys for electronics: composition, ISO 9453 designation, melting range, density and typical use.
items.notes: Typical values from maker data sheets. Non-eutectic alloys are pasty between solidus and liquidus; eutectic alloys melt at one temperature. Use the maker's data sheet for the soldering profile. Lead-containing solders (Sn63Pb37, Sn60Pb40) are restricted by RoHS in the EU; use them only where an exemption applies (for example repairs of old equipment). The liquidus of SAC405 is left empty because the sources give 217, 219 and 225 °C, and no ISO 9453 number of SAC405 was found. The number 703 for Sn96.5Ag3.5 rests on a single weak source and is left empty. The ISO 9453 numbers 401 (Sn99.3Cu0.7) and 301 (Sn42Bi58) come from one maker catalogue. The densities are typical values and differ by up to about 2 % between makers.
items.source: ISO 9453:2006 (alloy numbers and designations, after the Stannol catalogue and the iTeh preview); Kester alloy temperature chart and technical data on soft solders; Indium Corporation solder alloy directory and Indalloy 256 data sheet; DKL Metals E-Qual data sheet; NIST database for solder properties
rows: Hand, wave and reflow soldering of electronics (leaded)

Lead-free reflow soldering and BGA solder spheres

items.name: Capacitor codes
items.doc: Capacitor markings: the picofarad code (104 = 100 nF), R and RKM notation (4R7, 4p7, 2n2), tolerance letters and the two-character rated-voltage codes (1H = 50 V). Several parts of one marking can be read together ("104K 1H").
items.source: IEC 60062:2016 (capacitance codes and tolerance letters); the voltage codes are a convention of the part-numbering systems of TDK, Nichicon, Panasonic and Murata, not of IEC 60062; KEMET and Vishay ceramic capacitor datasheets

voltages.note: Murata lists 3F as 3.15 kV, TDK as 3 kV.
voltages.note_en: Murata lists 3F as 3.15 kV, TDK as 3 kV.

notes: Ceramic and film capacitors: the code is in picofarads - 104 = 100 000 pF = 100 nF. Aluminium electrolytic part numbers use microfarads (101 = 100 µF); that reading is not offered.
Below 10 pF tolerance letters mean absolute pF (C = ±0.25 pF), from 10 pF up they mean percent.
Voltage codes come from maker part-numbering systems and are not part of IEC 60062; some makers deviate (Murata writes YA for 35 V).
Codes and letters that only one source lists are not decoded; the decoder says so.

items.name: Ceramic capacitor temperature codes
items.doc: EIA-198 temperature characteristics of ceramic capacitors: class 1 codes such as C0G or U2J (temperature coefficient and tolerance in ppm/K) and class 2 codes such as X7R or Y5V (category temperature range and capacitance change), in both directions.
items.source: EIA-198 code letters as printed in the Vishay general information on ceramic disc capacitors and in the Murata, KEMET and TDK ceramic capacitor catalogues

notes: C0G (NP0) is the most stable class 1 dielectric: 0 ± 30 ppm/K.
Class 2 codes describe only the temperature range and the change over temperature; DC bias and ageing reduce the capacitance further.
Y5V and Z5U are class 2 here; some manufacturers call them class 3.
Letters and digits that only one source lists are not decoded; the decoder says so.

items.name: Inductor colour code
items.doc: Colour bands of inductors in microhenries: the four-band EIA style and the five-band military style (wide silver first band, gold as the decimal point), read and written in both directions.
items.source: Bourns colour-code markings for inductors (EIA and military tables) and MIL-PRF-15305 for RF coils; IEC 60062 defines no inductor colour code; E-series from IEC 60063

notes: Inductor colour codes are maker and military conventions; IEC 60062 only covers resistors. Values are in µH.
A wide silver first band marks a military (MIL-PRF-15305) coil; gold inside the value bands is then the decimal point.
Without the wide silver band (EIA style), gold in the third band means ×0.1 and silver ×0.01.
Only gold (±5 %) and silver (±10 %) are decoded as tolerance; other tolerance colours are not cross-checked in the sources.

items.name: Resistor colour code
items.doc: Colour bands of resistors per IEC 60062: 3 to 6 bands read and written in both directions (two or three significant figures, multiplier, tolerance and temperature coefficient). Writing a value picks the nearest standard value of the series that fits the tolerance.
items.source: IEC 60062:2016 (marking codes for resistors and capacitors) with COR1:2016 and AMD1:2019, Table 1; the older tolerance colours from the resistor colour-code notes of Panasonic and TT Electronics; E-series from IEC 60063

notes: Read from the end where the bands start; the tolerance band is at least 1.5 times as wide as the others (IEC 60062, corrigendum 2016). Gold, silver and pink never stand first.
Older charts use grey = ±0.05 % and give orange and yellow no tolerance; IEC 60062:2016 uses grey ±0.01 %, orange ±0.05 % and yellow ±0.02 %. Check the datasheet of precision resistors.
Pink (×0.001) is new in IEC 60062:2016 for very low resistances.
A single black band marks a zero-ohm jumper.
The temperature coefficient band only exists together with three significant figures (six bands).
Displayed colours are illustrations only.

items.name: SMD inductor codes
items.doc: Value marking of SMD inductors, three characters: three digits are microhenry (two significant digits and the number of zeros, 101 = 100 µH), R is the decimal point in µH (4R7 = 4.7 µH, R47 = 0.47 µH) and N is the decimal point in nH (4N7 = 4.7 nH, 47N = 47 nH). A fourth letter is the tolerance. Only the tolerance letters that two makers state in the same way are read (C, G, H, J, K, M); the others differ between makers (D is ±0.5 nH at Murata but ±0.3 nH at Bourns) or are stated by one maker only, and are not decoded. Small chip inductors are often printed with no value at all.
items.source: Murata part numbering for RF inductors (LQ series); Bourns CE1005Q and SRR1260 datasheets; Vishay Dale IHLP2020AB-A1 (document 34711); TDK inductor marking FAQ (read as a DigiKey copy)

notes: 3 digits are microhenry: the last digit is the number of zeros, so 100 = 10 µH and 101 = 100 µH.
R marks the decimal point in µH (4R7 = 4.7 µH, R47 = 0.47 µH); N marks the decimal point in nH (4N7 = 4.7 nH, 47N = 47 nH).
Tolerance letters are not the same at every maker: D is ±0.5 nH at Murata but ±0.3 nH at Bourns, and ±30 % is N at Vishay but Y at Bourns. Those letters are not decoded; check the datasheet.
Small chip inductors are often not printed with a value at all.

items.name: SMD resistor codes
items.doc: Markings of chip resistors: the 3-digit and 4-digit codes, the R notation (4R7, R47, 1L5) and the EIA-96 code (two digits for the E96 value plus a multiplier letter). The input is auto-detected; writing a value lists every marking that can express it.
items.source: IEC 60062:2016 (RKM code, three- and four-character codes); EIA-96 marking tables of Yageo, Bourns, Venkel and TT Electronics; E96 values from IEC 60063

notes: The two EIA-96 digits are an index, not the value: 01 means 100, 68 means 499.
3-digit codes: the last digit is the number of zeros, so 100 = 10 Ω, not 100 Ω.
R (and L for milliohm) marks the decimal point: 4R7 = 4.7 Ω, R47 = 0.47 Ω, 1L5 = 1.5 mΩ.
Very small chips (0402 and smaller) are usually unmarked.
Some makers use R, S or H as extra EIA-96 letters with conflicting meanings; they are not decoded - check the datasheet.

items.name: 3.5 mm jack, stereo (TRS)
items.doc: The common 3.5 mm stereo plug of headphones and line cables, shown from the side with the tip at the left.
items.notes: Left and right on tip and ring apply to headphones and stereo line signals. Balanced studio TRS jacks use the same contacts for positive, negative and ground instead.
items.source: Texas Instruments TS3A225E datasheet SCDS329A, table 2; Rane Note 102 (Rane Corporation), section on phone jacks; Wikipedia, Phone connector (audio)

items.name: 3.5 mm headset jack (TRRS)
items.doc: The four-contact plug of headsets with a microphone. Tip and first ring stay left and right; microphone and ground sit on the last two contacts, in an order that depends on the variant.
items.notes: CTIA (also called AHJ) and OMTP differ only in that microphone and ground are swapped, so a headset of the other kind gets the two the wrong way round. The Android headset specification requires the CTIA order and treats OMTP as optional.
items.source: Android Open Source Project, 3.5 mm headset accessory and jack specifications; Texas Instruments TS3A225E datasheet SCDS329A, table 2; Wikipedia, Phone connector (audio)

items.name: XLR, 3-pin (balanced audio)
items.doc: The three-pin XLR connector of balanced microphone and line signals.
items.notes: Pin 2 hot is the wiring of IEC 268 and AES14-1992; older equipment can differ, so check its manual if polarity matters. Pins 1 and 2 lie level with the centre and pin 3 straight below it, so the pattern is a T, not an equal triangle. The notch in the drawing marks the latch at 12 o'clock; a small polarising rib also sits at the upper right of the male face.
items.source: Neutrik drawings ST-NC3MAH and 3102 St 18 19 (NC3FAV1); Amphenol Entertainment Interconnect Catalogue, AX series standard data; ITT Cannon Audio XL catalogue; Rane Note 102; Shure SM58 user guide; Mackie 1620 manual, appendix B

items.name: MIDI (DIN-5, 180°)
items.doc: The 5-pin 180° DIN connector of MIDI 1.0. Only pins 2, 4 and 5 are used: 4 and 5 carry a 5 mA current loop at 31.25 kBd, 2 the cable shield.
items.notes: The contacts follow the arc in the order 1, 4, 2, 5, 3. On the solder side of a jack that order is mirrored, which matches the plug view of this drawing, not the jack view. Pin 2 is grounded at MIDI Out and Thru only; at MIDI In it has no DC path to ground. The cable shield goes to pin 2 only, never to the plug barrel.
items.source: MMA/AMEI CA-033, MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update (2014); binder catalogue M16 IP67, series 423/723, contact arrangements (5 contacts stereo, DIN 41524); Switchcraft catalogue, DIN connectors and receptacles (57PC5F PC board layout)

items.name: 6.35 mm (1/4 in) jack, TRS
items.doc: The large 1/4 inch plug of studio and stage equipment, shown from the side with the tip at the left. The same three contacts carry different signals depending on the use: balanced mono, stereo or a mixer insert.
items.notes: Which variant applies is printed at the device, not on the jack: a balanced output into a stereo headphone input, or the reverse, gives wrong channels or phase cancellation. A two-contact TS plug has tip = signal (hot, +) and sleeve = ground or shield; in a balanced TRS input it ties the ring to the sleeve and unbalances the input.
items.source: Rane Corporation, RaneNote 102 Analog I/O Standards, section 1/4 phone jacks; Mackie 1620 owner's manual, appendix B Connections (page 23) and TRS send/receive insert jacks (page 24); Mackie ProFX12 owner's manual, page 28; Yamaha Hub, How to Use Inserts (Steve La Cerra, 2022)

pins.notes: Some mixers swap send and return, so the ring then carries the send. Check the manual of your mixer.

items.name: RCA (cinch) connector
items.doc: The unbalanced audio and video connector with a centre pin inside an outer ring, seen here from the mating face of the plug. The centre pin carries the signal, the shell is ground and shield.
items.notes: The shell is a ring, drawn as one contact on the rim of the face at the largest radius the drawing allows. The face is rotationally symmetric, so there is no key and no mirror question. Colours (white left, red right, yellow video) are a cabling convention, not a property of the pins.
items.source: Mackie 1620 owner's manual, appendix B Connections (page 23); Garmin Primacy S3 Active Loudspeaker installation instructions, RCA or Unbalanced Input; RS Components, A Complete Guide to RCA Connectors (2026)

items.name: XLR, 5-pin (DMX512)
items.doc: The 5-pin XLR connector of DMX512 lighting control. Pin 1 is the common of the data link, pins 2 and 3 carry the primary EIA-485 pair.
items.notes: Female connectors belong on transmitters (controllers) and where loop-through connections are provided, male connectors on receivers (dimmers, fixtures), so outputs are female and inputs male. The drawing shows the male face. The pattern is not symmetric: pins 1 to 4 lie about 50 degrees apart, pin 5 about 58 degrees from pin 4. Pins 4 and 5 are the optional second data link and often not connected; older equipment may use pins 4/5 differently, so check the device manual. The notch in the drawing marks the latch at 12 o'clock; a small polarising rib also sits at the upper right of the male face.
items.source: ESTA/USITT BSR E1.11 working draft, DMX512 Revision 1.1a (1999), table 2.8.2.2 and clauses 1.2.9 and 10.1; Leprecon ULD-360DMX user manual, section 8 DMX 512 Information; Doug Fleenor Design 2322DMX user manual; ETC Gadget setup manual, page 2; Neutrik drawings NC5MAH1 and NC5FAH1

items.name: Eurorack power bus, 16-pin (Doepfer A-100)
items.doc: The 2x8 power header of Eurorack modules and bus boards, as Doepfer draws it: eight rows of two contacts, each row one signal, the -12 V row at the bottom.
items.notes: A ribbon cable plugged in the wrong way round can destroy the module (Doepfer). The coloured (typically red) wire marks -12 V and must point to the bottom row, where the bus board is marked -12V; pin 1 is that wire. Boxed headers have a code gap that can force the cable the wrong way round, so check the red stripe. Both contacts of a row carry the same signal. No source numbers the header in a view, so which column holds the odd pins is not documented; the drawing puts them on the left, which does not change any wiring because both pins of a row are the same signal. The 10-pin variant carries only -12 V, GND and +12 V (pins 1 and 2 = -12V, 3 to 8 = GND, 9 and 10 = +12V): it is the lower five rows of this drawing, a 10-pin plug sits on the -12 V end, and the bus board side is always 16-pin. +5 V, CV and Gate are used by only a few modules.
items.source: Doepfer Musikelektronik, A-100 Technical Details (a100t_e.htm) with figures a100b_e.gif and a100t_3.gif; Doepfer A-100 FAQ, orientation of bus connection cables and boxed pin headers; Elby Designs, EuroSynth Power Distribution

items.name: Arduino Uno R3
items.doc: Arduino Uno R3 from above with the USB socket at the top and the DC jack beside it. The board carries no pin numbers, so each pin is named after its header in the Arduino schematic (POWER, AD, IOH, IOL, ICSP) plus its position there.
items.notes: Logic level 5 V; each I/O pin carries 20 mA at most. The ICSP block is the 6-pin header at the end of the board away from USB and belongs to the ATmega328P. A second 6-pin header near the USB socket, ICSP1, programs the ATmega16U2 and is not listed here. D0 and D1 also reach the USB bridge, so a circuit on them can get in the way of uploads.

items.name: ESP32-DevKitC V4
items.doc: ESP32-DevKitC V4 from the component side, drawn with the Micro-USB socket at the top, so the antenna is at the bottom; Espressif's own figure shows the board the other way up. Numbers are the headers J2 and J3 of Espressif's user guide.
items.notes: GPIO34, 35, 36 and 39 are inputs only and have no pull resistors. GPIO0, 2, 5, 12 and 15 are strapping pins, read at reset, so a circuit on them can change how the board starts. GPIO6 to GPIO11 belong to the SPI flash and cannot serve as regular GPIO. Every other GPIO that can output can also do PWM. Inputs take at most the 3.3 V supply plus 0.3 V. Power the board from one source only (USB, the 5V pin or the 3V3 pin); two at once can do damage.

items.name: NodeMCU DevKit 1.0 (ESP8266)
items.doc: NodeMCU DevKit V1.0 with ESP-12E from the component side, drawn with the Micro-USB socket at the top, so the antenna is at the bottom; the project's own pin map shows the board the other way up. Numbers are the headers J1 and J2 of its schematic.
items.notes: This is the open-hardware V1.0 revision only. Clones differ, so compare with the silk screen before wiring. For a boot D8 (GPIO15) must be low and D4 (GPIO2) high; D3 (GPIO0) high runs the firmware, low enters flash mode. Logic runs at 3.3 V, inputs take 3.6 V at most, an output 12 mA. PWM and I2C are done in software: the NodeMCU firmware accepts the IO indexes 1 to 12, and its examples use a different pair than the Arduino core's default of D2 (SDA) and D1 (SCL).

items.name: Raspberry Pi 40-pin header
items.doc: The 40-pin GPIO header of Raspberry Pi B+ and later and of the Zero models, turned as in Raspberry Pi's figure: header at the right edge, USB and Ethernet at the bottom, pin 1 top left. With the header along the top edge of the board, pin 1 is the lower left corner.

Alternative functions vary with the SoC; the list shows Raspberry Pi's typical ones. Pi models with the old 26-pin header are not covered.

items.name: Arduino Mega 2560 Rev3
items.doc: Arduino Mega 2560 Rev3 from above with the USB-B socket at the top and the DC jack beside it. The board carries no pin numbers, so each pin is named after its header in the Arduino schematic plus its position there. JP6, ADCH, XIO (the 2×18 double row) and ICSP are the schematic's names; POWER, ADCL, PWML and COMM stand for the four 8-pin headers the schematic leaves unnamed and are ours. The double row is drawn as one block in the middle of the board; on the board it lies along the bottom edge, with the +5V pins (XIO.1, XIO.2) at the right end and the even pins XIO.2 to XIO.36 in the lower row at the board edge.
items.notes: Logic level 5 V; each I/O pin carries 20 mA at most, the 3V3 pin 50 mA. VIN: Arduino's pinout says 6–20 V, the datasheet recommends 7–12 V; stay within 7–12 V. PWM is on D2 to D13 and D44 to D46 (15 pins) per the datasheet and the analogWrite reference; the pinout figure also marks D0 and D1 with a tilde, which the other documents do not support. I2C is on D20 (SDA) and D21 (SCL), also on the SDA and SCL pins beside AREF, not on A4 and A5 as on the Uno. SPI is on D50 to D53 and the ICSP block, not on D11 to D13. D0 and D1 also reach the USB bridge. The pinout also prints external-memory names (A8 to A15 on D37 to D30); those are address lines, not the analog inputs A8 to A15. ICSP1 of the ATmega16U2 near the USB socket and the 2×2 JP5 pads are not listed; the RESET-EN solder jumper disables auto-reset.
items.source: Arduino MEGA 2560 REV3 full pinout, SKU A000067 (last update 16/12/2020); Arduino schematic MEGA2560_Rev3e (A000067-schematics.pdf, 23/01/19); Arduino Mega 2560 Rev3 datasheet, SKU A000067 (modified 19/11/2026); Arduino analogWrite() reference; Arduino Mega 2560 product page

items.name: Arduino Leonardo
items.doc: Arduino Leonardo from above in the Uno form factor, with the Micro-USB socket at the top and the DC jack beside it. The board carries no pin numbers, so each pin is named after its header in the Arduino schematic (J3, J4, JP1, J2, ICSP) plus its position there. These names differ from the Uno's although the positions are the same.
items.notes: Logic level 5 V. Current per I/O pin: Arduino's pinout says 20 mA at most, the tech specs say 10 mA; stay at 10 mA. The 3V3 pin gives 50 mA at most. VIN: the pinout says 6–20 V, the tech specs 7–12 V nominal; stay within 7–12 V. I2C is on D2 (SDA) and D3 (SCL) and on the two pins beside AREF, not on A4 and A5. SPI is only on the ICSP block, not on D11 to D13. The USB serial port is native (Serial); D0 and D1 are a separate hardware UART (Serial1), not linked to USB, so a circuit on them does not disturb uploads. A6 to A11 are extra analog inputs on D4, D6, D8, D9, D10 and D12. PWM is on D3, D5, D6, D9, D10, D11 and D13. There is no ATmega16U2 and no second ICSP header on this board.
items.source: Arduino LEONARDO full pinout, SKU A000057 (last update 25/11/2025); Arduino schematic Leonardo_Rev3d (A000057-schematics.pdf, 28/01/19); Arduino Leonardo tech specs and features (docs-content); Arduino Getting Started with the Arduino Leonardo, Leonardo ETH and Micro; ArduinoCore-avr variants/leonardo/pins_arduino.h; Arduino analogWrite() reference

items.name: Arduino Pro Mini
items.doc: Arduino Pro Mini in the layout of the maker SparkFun (PCB v14), seen from the component side with the 6-pin FTDI header at the top edge. The board carries no pin numbers, so each pin is named after its header in the SparkFun schematic: JP1 (FTDI), JP7 (left edge), JP6 (right edge) and the two inner pads JP2 (A4, A5) and JP3 (A6, A7) plus its position there. The drawing places the FTDI header (BLK end at the left, GRN end at the right) and the inner pads, which sit inside the board off the 0.1 inch grid of the edge rows, as small groups in the middle of the board, not at their real places. Clone boards sold as Pro Mini are not covered.
items.notes: One PCB for two models, 5 V / 16 MHz and 3.3 V / 8 MHz: the logic level of every I/O pin is the VCC of the model, so do not drive the pins of the 3.3 V model with 5 V. RAW feeds the on-board regulator (150 mA): Arduino's tech specs give 5–12 V for the 5 V model and 3.35–12 V for the 3.3 V model, SparkFun up to 16 V; stay within 12 V and feed unregulated power to RAW, not to VCC. Current per I/O pin: 40 mA at most (Arduino and SparkFun), 20 mA recommended by SparkFun; use 20 mA. The FTDI header takes a 3.3 V or 5 V FTDI cable or breakout; JP1.6 (marked BLK) is the ground end and JP1.1 (marked GRN) is DTR. TXO and RXI are the board's own TX and RX, which the adapter crosses. The board has no USB. A6 and A7 are analog inputs only.
items.source: Arduino Pro Mini retired product page (Arduino docs-content); SparkFun schematic Arduino-Pro-Mini REV 14 (4/9/2014, hosted by Arduino); SparkFun Eagle board file Arduino-Pro-Mini.brd (Arduino_Pro_Mini_328 repository); SparkFun graphical datasheets Arduino Pro Mini DEV-11113 (16 MHz / 5 V) and DEV-11114 (8 MHz / 3.3 V)

items.name: BBC micro:bit V2
items.doc: Edge connector of the BBC micro:bit V2 in the front view: the side with the LED matrix and the buttons A and B, upright, the connector along the bottom edge and read from left to right. The board prints no pin numbers, so each contact is numbered like the pins of J1 in the V2.2.1 schematic (1 to 40 along the edge): the five large rings are 2 (ring 0), 10 (ring 1), 19 (ring 2), 28 (3V) and 36 (GND), the others are the small strips between them. Every ring is drawn as one position, although it is four strip widths wide. Only the front contacts are listed: the rings on the back are the same nets and the small strips on the back are not connected. The USB socket, marked at the top as an orientation aid, is on the back of the board.
items.notes: All signal contacts are 3.3 V logic and not 5 V tolerant: the pin voltage must stay between −0.3 V and VDD + 0.3 V, and the board supply is 1.7 to 3.6 V. Drive is 1 to 4 mA standard and 6 to 15 mA high. The edge connector may supply 190 mA (300 mA regulator minus the on-board budget); the edge-connector page says 270 mA and marks it as to be confirmed, so use 190 mA. Only three pins can do PWM at the same time. P3, P4, P6, P7 and P10 belong to the LED display: switch the display off in software before using them otherwise. P5 and P11 are the buttons A and B, P12 is reserved for the accessibility mode. P19 and P20 are the external I2C bus with 4.7 kΩ pull-ups; on V2 the motion sensor is on a separate internal I2C bus. Do not connect speakers, motors or piezos directly. To power the board through the 3V ring use a regulated supply and a protection diode.

items.name: WEMOS D1 mini
items.doc: WEMOS D1 mini (V3 and V4, same positions) from the component side, drawn with the USB socket at the top, so the antenna is at the bottom; WEMOS's own figure shows the board the other way up. Numbers are the headers J2 and J3 of the V4.0.0 schematic, pin 1 of both at the antenna end.
items.notes: All I/O pins run at 3.3 V and are not 5 V tolerant (the chip takes 3.6 V at most, an output 12 mA). D3 (GPIO0) and D4 (GPIO2) have a pull-up and D8 (GPIO15) a pull-down on the board; both schematics (V3.0.0 and V4.0.0) show 12 kΩ, while the V3.1.0 pin table says 10k. These three pins select the boot mode at reset, and TX must not be pulled low during power-up. A0 takes 0 to 3.2 V. D0 (GPIO16) has no interrupt, PWM or I2C and wakes the chip from deep sleep when it is linked to RST. The positions are the same on V3 and V4, the 5V pin is not: on V3 it is the 5 V rail behind a diode and a 0.5 A fuse from USB, on V4 it is USB VBUS directly, with no diode or fuse, so feeding 5 V into it while USB is plugged in drives the USB port. The V4 also has a 4-pin I2C socket, not drawn. Clones exist; compare with the silk screen.
items.source: WEMOS/LOLIN D1 mini board pages V4.0.0 and V3.1.0 with pinout figure and board photo; WEMOS/LOLIN schematics D1 mini V4.0.0 and V3.0.0; Espressif, ESP8266EX Datasheet v7.1

items.notes: All GPIOs are 3.3 V only (inputs take VDD plus 0.3 V at most). GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9 are strapping pins, read at reset, so a circuit on them can change how the board starts; GPIO9 low with GPIO8 high enters download mode, which is what the BOOT button does. GPIO8 also drives the RGB LED. GPIO18 and GPIO19 are the chip's own USB pins; the Micro-USB socket of this board goes to the USB-UART bridge on GPIO20 and GPIO21, not to them. items.name: ESP32-CAM
items.doc: ESP32-CAM (Ai-Thinker ESP-32S module with OV2640 camera) from the side with the camera, the microSD socket and the pin labels, drawn with the microSD socket at the top and the camera connector at the bottom. The board has no USB socket. Numbers P1 and P2 follow a copy of the board schematic (Rev 1.6).
items.notes: No maker document: Ai-Thinker's own pages and files could not be opened, so the layout comes from two independent sources (pinout figures of two tutorial sites, confirmed by a copy of the board schematic) and the signal functions from Espressif (ESP32 datasheet, arduino-esp32 camera pin map AI_THINKER). Clones may differ; check the silk screen. All GPIOs are 3.3 V logic. Feed the board through 5V; the 3V3 pin is the regulator output, and VCC is an output too (3.3 V, or 5 V when the 0 Ω link is moved). The camera uses GPIO0 (XCLK), 5, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 32, 34, 35, 36 and 39. The microSD card uses GPIO2, 4, 12, 13, 14 and 15, which are on the headers; GPIO4 also drives the white flash LED, and the red LED is on GPIO33. GPIO16 is the chip select of the PSRAM, GPIO17 its clock. GPIO0, GPIO2, GPIO12 and GPIO15 are strapping pins. Programming needs a USB-serial adapter on U0R and U0T with GPIO0 pulled to GND at reset.
items.source: Espressif, ESP32 Series Datasheet v5.3; Espressif, arduino-esp32 camera_pins.h (CAMERA_MODEL_AI_THINKER); schematic ESP32_CAM Rev 1.6 (copy hosted by Seeed Studio); Random Nerd Tutorials, ESP32-CAM AI-Thinker Pinout Guide; Last Minute Engineers, ESP32-CAM Pinout Reference; no Ai-Thinker document could be opened

items.name: Blue Pill (STM32F103C8)
items.doc: STM32F103C8 Blue Pill from the component side (MCU, crystal, reset button), drawn with the Micro-USB socket at the top. The 4-pin SWD header, which sits at the bottom edge of the real board, is shown as a block in the middle of the drawing. The board carries no header names; H1 (right column) and H2 (left column) and the SWD header follow stm32-base.org, and pin 1 of each is at the SWD end.
items.notes: There is no official maker of the Blue Pill: it is a clone board, and the layout comes from two independent sources (stm32-base.org and the Zephyr Project's figure), the pin functions from ST's STM32F103x8/xB datasheet. Clones differ: regulator (RT9193-33 or TX6211B), USB D+ pull-up (4.7 kΩ or 10 kΩ instead of 1.5 kΩ) and sometimes the chip itself; compare with the silk screen. The chip runs at 2.0 to 3.6 V. Pins marked 5 V tolerant take 5 V; all others, among them PA0 to PA7, PB0, PB1, PB5 and PC13 to PC15, must never see 5 V. PB5 is the one pin of its neighbours that is not 5 V tolerant. PC13 to PC15 sink or source 3 mA at 2 MHz only. PB3, PB4 and PA15 start as JTAG pins. The 5V pin is tied to USB VBUS without protection: do not feed it while USB is plugged in. BOOT0 and BOOT1 are jumpers, not header pins.
items.source: STMicroelectronics, STM32F103x8 STM32F103xB datasheet, DocID13587 Rev 16; stm32-base.org, STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill board page; Zephyr Project, STM32 Minimum Development Board pinout figure; VCC-GND Studio, STM32F103C8T6 core board schematic

items.notes: RX and TX are named from the host's point of view. Pins 1 to 4 are the USB 2.0 contacts, pins 5 to 9 the SuperSpeed contacts. The two rows lie at different depths of the connector, so face-on they are not really above each other; the left-right position is as drawn. The drawn receptacle has its contact tongue in the upper half of the shell. The shell is the shield and mates first. The specification names no wire colours for this connector.
