items.name: USB Type-C
items.doc: The reversible 24-contact USB connector. The contact plan repeats after a half turn, so the plug fits both ways; the CC lines show which way it is in.
items.notes: CC resistors, from tables 4-27 and 4-28 of the Type-C specification. Sink: Rd 5.1 kΩ to GND on CC1 and on CC2 (±10% if it reads the advertised current, otherwise ±20% is allowed). Source: Rp to 4.75–5.5 V on CC1 and on CC2: 56 kΩ ±20% for default USB power, 22 kΩ ±5% for 1.5 A, 10 kΩ ±5% for 3.0 A. With a pull-up to 3.3 V: 36 kΩ ±20%, 12 kΩ ±5%, 4.7 kΩ ±5%. A cable or adapter whose Type-C plug stands for a legacy USB host uses 56 kΩ ±5%. All VBUS contacts are tied together, and so are all GND contacts. A USB 2.0 receptacle leaves A2, A3, A10, A11, B2, B3, B10 and B11 unconnected.

items.name: RJ45 (8P8C)
items.doc: The eight-contact modular connector of twisted-pair Ethernet. T568A and T568B differ only in the wire colours: the green and the orange pair swap places, the signals stay on the same pins.
items.notes: Drawn: a jack seen from the front with the latch notch at the bottom, pin 1 on the left. A plug seen from its tip with the latch at the bottom has pin 1 on the right; with the latch on top, pin 1 is on the left. Signal names are those of an end device; at a switch TX and RX swap. Power over Ethernet: IEEE 802.3af/at Mode A puts the power on the data pairs, pins 1 and 2 as one pole, pins 3 and 6 as the other. Mode B uses the spare pairs, pins 4 and 5 as one pole, pins 7 and 8 as the other. The power source uses only one of the two at a time. Four-pair IEEE 802.3bt can use all four pairs together. The polarity of the data pairs is not the same everywhere, so measure before wiring anything without a rectifier.
items.source: NetAlly PoE reference flyer; Seetronic, RJ45 Color Code: T568A vs T568B; Microchip AN3361 (DS00003361C), table 3-1; Barco Event Master user guide R5905948, A.24; L-com drawing TDG1026-8R; GlobTek, PoE Mode A vs. Mode B; L-com PoE white paper; IEEE 802.3bt contribution darshan_02_0314

items.name: RS-232 (DE-9)
items.doc: The 9-pin serial port of PCs, often called DB9. The DTE (a PC or terminal) has the male connector with pins; the DCE (a modem) has the female connector with sockets.
items.notes: Every signal name and direction is from the DTE's point of view. A pin carries the same signal at both ends, so the DCE drives what the DTE reads: pin 2 is an output on a DCE. The genders are the usual rule and some devices break it, so check the pin directions on the device before you connect a cable. To join two DTEs you need a cable that crosses TXD and RXD. The levels are RS-232 voltages, not logic levels.
items.source: Texas Instruments SLLA037A, Interface Circuits for TIA/EIA-232-F; Moxa NPort 6110 user's manual, Pin assignments; Crypto Museum, D-sub connectors; serial_pinout.txt (xmtel archive, University of Louisville); CS Club Waterloo wiki, Serial Pin-outs

items.name: DVI-I (Dual Link)
items.doc: The combined analogue and digital DVI connector: 24 digital contacts in three rows of eight plus the analogue block C1 to C5, 29 contacts in all. Two TMDS links share the connector: the second link is only used by dual-link devices.
items.notes: DVI-D, the digital-only connector, has the same 24 contacts with the same numbers, but no C1 to C5 and pin 8 is not connected. A single link uses only the TMDS data channels 0 to 2 and the clock: pins 4, 5, 12, 13, 20 and 21 (data channels 4, 3 and 5) belong to the second link alone. The shields 3, 11 and 19 serve a pair of each link and stay in use. The colour words in the data channel names only say which colour of the pixel data a channel carries, they are not wire colours. The drawing is the receptacle on a graphics card or monitor seen onto its mating face, the wide side of the shell at the top and the two chamfered corners at the bottom; the plug is the mirror image with pin 1 at the upper right and the analogue block at the left. DVI-D single-link cables and plugs that leave out the second-link contacts were not verified.
items.source: Digital Display Working Group (DDWG), Digital Visual Interface DVI, Revision 1.0 (2 April 1999), tables 5-1 to 5-3, figures 5-1, 5-3, 5-4 and 5-6, sections 2.2.6, 2.2.9.2, 3.1.5 and 3.2.1; Apple, Xserve G4 Developer Note, Input and Output Devices (DVI connector, tables 3-9 and 3-10, figure 3-6); Euresys, Picolo HD documentation, DVI-I Input connector

items.name: SCART (21-pin)
items.doc: The 21-position audio and video connector of European televisions, video recorders and receivers (SCART, also Péritel or Euro-AV): composite and RGB video, stereo audio and switching lines. The functions are given for a TV.
items.notes: Every device has its outputs on pins 1, 3 and 19 and its inputs on 2, 6 and 20, and a SCART cable crosses 1 with 2, 3 with 6 and 19 with 20 and runs the other pins straight. So RGB (7, 11, 15), pin 8 and pin 16 are inputs at a TV and outputs at a source such as a player or a console. Pins 10, 12, 14, 17 and 18 differ between devices: the catalog shows 17 as the ground of the composite video, 18 as the ground of pin 16 and 14 as a plain ground, see the pin notes. Pin 21 is a contact in the socket and the metal shell of the plug, which has 20 pins. The standard itself (EN 50049-1, IEC 60933-1) was not read: the pins rest on the tables of device manuals. The drawing is the socket on a device, the wide side of the shell at the top and the slanted corner at the lower left; the plug is the mirror image.
items.source: Kycon, catalogue page 134, K-SCART series (K-SCART-021 front view); Pioneer KRP-600A operating instructions, Additional information (SCART pin assignment); Daewoo 2898ST service manual, 21 PIN EURO-SCART table; LG Electronics 32LC2D service manual, tables 1 and 2 (Scart arrangement); AOC L19WA91 service manual, Full Scart Connector Pin Assignments; RND Connect RND 205-01033 SCART male data sheet; Wikipedia, SCART with the figure SCART_Connector_Pinout_Color.svg

items.name: PS/2 (Mini-DIN 6)
items.doc: The 6-pin mini-DIN connector of PS/2 keyboards and mice. Keyboard and mouse ports use the same pins: a data line, a clock line, ground and +5 V; pins 2 and 6 are reserved.
items.notes: Data and clock are bidirectional open-collector lines with a pull-up to +5 V. The shell is the frame (chassis) ground. The drawing is the socket on the computer seen onto its mating face, with the key (notch of the shell) at 12 o'clock; the plug at the cable end is the mirror image. The positions are measured on a generic mini-DIN drawing of a connector maker; the arrangement agrees with the IBM and Dell figures, which are not dimensioned. Pins 2 and 6 are not always free: the combined keyboard and mouse port of the IBM ThinkPad 560 carries Mouse Data on pin 1, Keyboard Data on pin 2, Mouse Clock on pin 5 and Keyboard Clock on pin 6 (for a Y splitter), so leave them unconnected otherwise. No general current limit for +5 V was verified.
items.source: IBM, Hardware Interface Technical Reference, Keyboards (101- and 102-Key), October 1990, figure 22; Dell PowerEdge 1600SC Systems Installation and Troubleshooting Guide, appendix B, figure B-4 and table B-4; Dell PowerEdge 8450 Systems User's Guide, I/O Ports and Connectors, tables 3 and 4 and figure 4; IBM ThinkPad 560/560E technical information, Keyboard/Mouse Connector; Kycon drawing KMDGX-xS-BS, rev C6 (geometry only)

items.name: S-Video (Mini-DIN 4)
items.doc: The 4-pin mini-DIN connector for S-Video (Y/C): luminance on pin 3, chrominance on pin 4 and two ground pins.
items.notes: Neither source says which of the two ground pins 1 and 2 belongs to Y and which to C, so both are named GND here. The drawing is the socket on the device seen onto its mating face, with the notch of the shell at 12 o'clock and the rectangular plastic key at 6 o'clock; the plug at the cable end is the mirror image. A 7-pin S-Video socket, as Apple builds it, accepts the 4-pin plug in the positions of pins 1 to 4. The positions are measured on a generic mini-DIN drawing of a connector maker. No standard text for this connector was read.
items.source: Euresys, MultiCam 6.7 documentation, Picolo handbook, Connectors, S-VIDEO Connector; Apple, Video Product-Specific Details (Hardware Technologies: Video), Power Mac G5, figure 5 and table 31; Kycon drawing KMDGX-xS-BS, rev C6 (geometry only)

items.name: D-Sub 25-pin
items.doc: The 25-way D-subminiature connector (DB-25), two rows of 13 and 12 contacts. Two uses share the same numbering: the PC parallel (printer) port and the EIA-232 serial interface on DB-25.
items.notes: Choose the variant by the use. parallel: the compatibility-mode signals of the PC parallel port in the IEEE 1284 names, directions for the PC (host); on bidirectional (EPP and ECP) ports pins 2 to 9 and several control lines change their roles, and only the compatibility mode is given. rs232: the EIA-232-D/E assignment, signals named from the DTE side, a pin carries the same signal at both ends. An asynchronous PC port uses only pins 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 20 and 22. The PC parallel port is the female connector; an RS-232 DTE such as a PC or terminal usually has the male one, which is the mirror image, and some devices break that rule. IEEE 1284 and TIA-232-F themselves were not read, the pins rest on device manuals and reproductions of EIA-232-D. The drawing is the female connector seen onto its mating face with the wide side of the shell at the top.
items.source: Winford Engineering, PBC25F and PBC25M Physical Layout (DB25 female and male pinout); Black Box Corporation, Technical Reference: Pinouts for Serial Interfaces (1997), section 1A; Datapro Information Services Group, report 2741, ANSI EIA/TIA-232-E Interface Standard (1995), table EIA-232-D Interface Connector Pin Assignments; Dell PowerEdge 8450 Systems User's Guide, I/O Ports and Connectors, figure 3 and table 2; Sun Enterprise 220R Server Service Manual 806-1081-11, A.5.2 Parallel Port Signals; HP 8924E CDMA Mobile Station Test Set User Guide, parallel port

items.name: RJ11 / RJ12 (6P4C, 6P6C)
items.doc: The miniature 6-position modular jack of telephone lines. Line 1 is on positions 3 (ring) and 4 (tip), a second line on 2 (tip 2) and 5 (ring 2). The RJ11 jack usually has four contacts (6P4C), the RJ12 jack all six (6P6C).
items.notes: The line assignment is read from 47 CFR Part 68 (10-1-00 edition): RJ11C carries one line on conductors 3 (ring) and 4 (tip) and reserves 1, 2, 5 and 6 for the telephone company; RJ14C carries two lines, line 1 on 3 and 4, line 2 on 2 (tip 2) and 5 (ring 2). On a single-line installation only 3 and 4 are used. The names follow RJ14C. RJ12 is a trade name for a 6P6C jack, not a code of that text. The positions are counted 1 to 6 across the jack, as the CFR does; whether other makers number the four contacts of a 6P4C part 1 to 4 was not verified. Neither the CFR nor the maker drawing names wire colours, and tip and ring polarity and line voltages are not stated here; the German a/b wire names were not verified. The drawing is the jack seen into its opening with the latch notch at the bottom and position 1 on the left; a plug seen from its tip with the latch at the bottom reads 6 to 1, with the latch on top 1 to 6.
items.source: US Code of Federal Regulations, Title 47, Part 68, Subpart F (10-1-00 edition), section 68.500(b) and figure 68.500(b)(2)(i), section 68.502(a)(1) and (c)(1); Würth Elektronik eiSos, WR-MJ Modular Jack Tab Up 615006138421, revision 001.002, page 1; Aastra TA710i user guide, RJ-11 (Telephone) Cable, table 12

items.name: CAN (D-Sub 9)
items.doc: The 9-pin D-sub connector that CAN and CANopen interfaces use as a de-facto standard: CAN_L on pin 2, CAN_H on pin 7, ground on pins 3 and 6. The other pins are optional or reserved.
items.notes: The pins 2, 3, 6 and 7 are the same in every source read. Pins 1, 5 and 9 vary with the maker: pin 1 is reserved at one maker and not used at another, and one interface can put 5 V on pins 1 and 9 by solder bridges that are not fitted at delivery; pin 5 is an optional shield at some makers and not connected at another; pin 9 is an optional external supply for the transceivers at some makers and not used at another. Measure before you connect anything to pins 1 and 9. The catalog follows the pin table of an interface maker that cites the CiA specification. The CiA documents themselves (CiA 303-1 and its successor CiA 106) need a login and were not read. The drawing is the male connector seen at its pins, wide side of the shell at the top, as for RS-232 on DE-9; the female connector of the cable is the mirror image.
items.source: PEAK-System, PCAN-USB User Manual 3.2.0, section 4.1 and appendix D; HMS Networks (Ixxat), knowledge base article CAN-Steckerbelegung (Sub-D9 after CiA DS 102); Beckhoff CX7050 documentation, D-sub connector X003; Black Box Corporation, Technical Reference: Pinouts for Serial Interfaces (1997), section 1B (front-view numbering); CAN in Automation, CiA 106 overview page (not read beyond the overview)

items.name: microSD card
items.doc: The eight contact pads of a microSD memory card. In SD mode the card has four data lines, a command line and a clock; in SPI mode the same pads carry chip select, data in, clock and data out.
items.notes: Drawn is the contact side of the card (back view, bottom view): the insertion edge with the pads is at the top, the step in the card's edge on the left and the pads read 1 to 8 from the left. Pads 4 (VDD) and 6 (VSS) are the longer ones. The label side is the mirror image: step on the right, 8 to 1 from the left. CD/DAT3 has a 50 kΩ pull-up in the card at power-up for card detection and mode selection; the host pulls it low to select SPI mode, and the pull-up is switched off with ACMD42. The host should pull up all data lines even if only DAT0 is used, otherwise floating DAT1 and DAT2 inputs can draw current. In SPI mode the reserved pads 1 and 8 should be pulled up by the host with 10 to 100 kΩ. DAT1 can be the SDIO interrupt and DAT2 the SDIO read wait. One maker states an operating voltage of 2.7 V to 3.6 V for its card. The microSD addendum of the SD specification is not free and was not read; the UHS-II second-row pads and the full-size SD card are not covered.
items.source: SanDisk, microSD, microSDHC and microSDXC cards OEM Product Manual, revision 3.1 (document 80-36-03335, November 2013), figures 4 and 5 and table 4; Kingston Technology, microSDHC industrial card specification SDCIT 8GB-32GB (document 4900180-001.A00), section 6.1, figure 1 and table 3; Cactus Technologies, Industrial 3D pSLC -295M Series microSD Card Product Manual (2 April 2025), table 3-5

items.doc: 4-pin, 1 mm JST SH connector for I2C modules, used by SparkFun Qwiic and Adafruit STEMMA QT.
items.notes: STEMMA QT is compatible with Qwiic: connector, pin order and wire colours are the same, and Adafruit states that both kinds of device work together. They differ in the supply. Qwiic boards run on 3.3 V only, while STEMMA QT devices accept 3 to 5 V and carry their own regulator and level shifting. So keep V+ at 3.3 V when a Qwiic device is on the bus. Pin numbers are not uniform: the schematics of both makers count GND as pin 1, SparkFun's cable drawing counts the yellow SCL wire as 1. Go by signal and wire colour, not by number.
items.source: SparkFun, Qwiic Connect System page (sparkfun.com/qwiic), Qwiic cable drawing ACCA-1571 and SparkFun-Connectors.lbr (device QWIIC_CONNECTOR); Adafruit, Adafruit STEMMA & STEMMA QT guide (What is STEMMA QT?, Technical Specs, comparison page) and Adafruit QT Py schematic (device STEMMA_I2C)

items.name: Grove (4-pin)
items.doc: The 4-wire, 2.0 mm connector of Seeed's Grove modules. Pins 3 and 4 always carry the supply; the meaning of pins 1 and 2 depends on the interface.
items.notes: Digital: pin 1 is Dn (main line), pin 2 is Dn+1 (second line). Analog: pin 1 is An (main input), pin 2 is An+1. UART: pin 1 is RX and pin 2 is TX, both named from the base unit's side. I2C: pin 1 is SCL, pin 2 is SDA. VCC is 5 V or 3.3 V, and some modules accept only one of them: check the module. Grove is not Qwiic: the pitch differs, and the wires run in the opposite order. Adafruit describes the housing as an HY type and not as a true JST.
items.source: Seeed Studio Wiki, Grove Ecosystem Introduction (Grove_System), interface tables for digital, analog, UART and I2C; Adafruit STEMMA & STEMMA QT guide, STEMMA / Grove comparison

items.name: Hobby servo (3-pin)
items.doc: The usual 3-way, 0.1 inch plug of hobby servos: signal, V+, ground. Makers number these pins differently, so this page calls them S, + and -.
items.notes: V+ sits in the middle. That matters because a plug turned round keeps V+ on V+ and only swaps signal and ground, so the supply is not reversed across the servo; it just gets no usable signal. Avoid it anyway, because the servo's ground then hangs on the controller's signal pin. Truly reversed power, for example from a wrongly built adapter, can destroy a servo at once. Wire colours drawn here: Futaba scheme, white signal, red V+, black ground. JR scheme: orange signal, red V+, brown ground. Hitec scheme: signal on the third wire, usually yellow, red V+, black ground. Exceptions exist: Spektrum's AR6310 manual has the brown negative wire in the middle of its JST micro plug and warns that JST servos differ, and Airtronics is reported to use another order. Check the data sheet of an unknown servo.
items.source: Parallax Standard Servo (#900-00005) product guide v3.0 (2022) and datasheet v2.0, pin tables; Hitec RCD, General Servo Information, Wire Color Meanings; Pololu, Electrical characteristics of servos and introduction to the servo control interface (2011); SparkFun, Hobby Servo Tutorial; Spektrum SPMAR6310 User Manual; ProgressiveRC, JR/Hitec servo extension; RobotPlatform, Major Servo Manufacturers

items.name: OBD-II (SAE J1962)
items.doc: The 16-way diagnostic connector of road vehicles under SAE J1962 and ISO 15031-3. The drawing shows the vehicle's socket, looking into it with the wide side up; the other view is the tester's plug.
items.notes: Pin 16 stays live with the ignition off: nominally 12 V on a type A connector and 24 V on type B. Fuse your own adapter. Pins 2, 6, 7, 10, 14 and 15 carry their listed signal only if the vehicle uses that protocol for OBD; otherwise the manufacturer may use them for something else. A few vehicles are reported to lack pin 5: use pin 4 for ground there.
items.source: Elm Electronics, ELM327 datasheet (ELM327DSK), figures 8 and 9; AESTECHNO, OBD2 pinout (OBD-II port) reference page, citing SAE J1962 table 1, section 6.3 and figure 3; Wikipedia, On-board diagnostics, standard interface section. SAE J1962 and ISO 15031-3 themselves are paywalled and were not read.

items.name: ESP-01 (ESP8266)
items.doc: The 2 × 4 pin, 0.1 inch header of the Ai-Thinker ESP-01 and ESP-01S Wi-Fi modules (ESP8266). Pin 1 is GND and pin 8 is VCC.
items.notes: The numbering runs along the rows, not counter-clockwise like a DIP package: pin 5 lies below pin 1. The module runs on 3.0 to 3.6 V and must not be fed 5 V. Ai-Thinker's boot table: for flashing (download mode) IO0 must be low at reset while IO2 and EN are high; for normal running IO0 is high. IO2 must be high at boot in both modes. The module can draw about 170 mA when transmitting; check that the 3.3 V supply can deliver that. Cheap clones of other makers are not covered.
items.source: Shenzhen Ai-Thinker Technology, ESP-01/07/12 Series Modules User's Manual, version 1.3 (figure 2.1, tables 2.2 and 2.3, tables 3.1 and 3.2, figure 4.1)

items.doc: The common 2 × 4 pin, 0.1 inch header of nRF24L01 radio modules, as documented for the Ebyte E01 modules. The signal names are those of Nordic's chip.
items.notes: This is the pin order that Ebyte documents for its E01 modules. Unbranded nRF24L01 modules have no maker document: check the silkscreen of your board. Supply 3.3 V only: Ebyte states 2.0 to 3.6 V for its modules, Nordic 1.9 to 3.6 V for the chip, and above 3.6 V the module is destroyed. Keep 5 V signal lines away or use series resistors, as Ebyte advises. Modules with a power amplifier draw more than 100 mA when sending (Ebyte: 130 mA at 20 dBm, the supply must deliver more than 300 mA).

items.name: HC-SR04
items.doc: The 4-pin header of the HC-SR04 ultrasonic ranging module: VCC, Trig, Echo, GND. The module prints no pin numbers, so the pins are named by their signals.
items.notes: Echo is a 5 V signal: a 3.3 V controller needs a voltage divider or a level shifter there (this advice follows from the 5 V level, it is not a statement of the vendors). Connect GND first, before VCC, as both vendor documents ask. Both documents are vendor reproductions, no document of the original maker was found; clone boards with another layout exist (the HC-SR04P and RCWL types were not read), so check the silkscreen.
items.source: ElecFreaks, Ultrasonic Ranging Module HC-SR04 (SparkFun copy, pages 1 to 3); Cytron Technologies, Product User's Manual HC-SR04 Ultrasonic Sensor, V1.0 (pages 5 to 7)

items.name: DHT22 / AM2302
items.doc: The 4-pin humidity and temperature sensor of Aosong, also sold as AM2302. Pins 1, 2 and 4 are used (VDD, DATA, GND); pin 3 stays free.
items.notes: Drawn from the front, the side with the perforated grille, pins down, pin 1 at the left. Stay within 3.3 to 5.5 V: one edition of Aosong's datasheet gives 3.3 to 6 V, the other 3.3 to 5.5 V. DATA is a single-bus line (not Dallas/Maxim 1-Wire) with a pull-up to VDD; Aosong draws 1 kΩ. Wait at least 1 s after power-up before the first request and 2 s between readings. Only the 4-pin sensor is covered: breakout boards with 3 pins have their own order. The wired AM2302 in the big case uses red for the supply, black for GND and yellow for data.
items.source: Aosong, Digital-output relative humidity & temperature sensor/module DHT22 (also named AM2302), datasheet edition read at SparkFun (pages 2, 4, 5, 9); Aosong, Digital relative humidity & temperature sensor AM2302/DHT22, datasheet edition read at Adafruit (pages 1, 2, 5)

items.name: mikroBUS
items.doc: The mikroBUS socket of MikroElektronika for add-on (click) boards: two 1 × 8 female headers, 0.1 inch pitch, with SPI, I2C, UART, analog, PWM, interrupt and reset lines and 3.3 V and 5 V supplies.
items.notes: The mikroBUS standard 2.00 defines positions and names, not numbers. The numbers 1 to 16 are those of Microchip's board guides: down the left column, then up the right column, so the two GND pins are 8 and 9. The notch lies at the lower right of the socket, and the two square pads (AN, PWM) mark the top. The columns are 900 mil apart; the gap is not drawn. The UART names follow the socket (mainboard) side: the add-on board's silkscreen is crossed, so a pin printed TX on the add-on board sits on the socket's RX pin. The add-on board prints SDI and SDO where the socket says MOSI and MISO. The standard gives no supply current limit.
items.source: MikroElektronika, mikroBUS Standard specifications, revision 2.00 (pages 6, 7, 9, 11, 12); Microchip, PIC32CK SG01/GC01 Curiosity Ultra User's Guide, section 2.4 (table 2-3); Microchip, PIC32 WFI32E Curiosity Board User's Guide, section 3.5 (table 3-5)

items.name: Pmod (2×6)
items.doc: The generic 12-pin Digilent Pmod connector (2 × 6, 0.1 inch): eight signal pins, two ground pins and two supply pins, two six-pin interfaces stacked.
items.notes: This page shows the generic layout, with the eight signals as general I/O. The Pmod type of the module decides what each signal does (SPI, UART, I2C, H-bridge and others); the type tables differ between the editions of the Digilent specification, so read the manual of the module. For SPI (type 2) both the 2011 specification and Wikipedia give pin 1 CS, 2 MOSI, 3 MISO, 4 SCK. VCC is normally 3.3 V; some hosts can switch it to 5 V, and both VCC pins always carry the same voltage. The pin numbering is mirrored between the host connector and the module. Pin 1 is the square pad, in the column farther from the board edge.
items.source: Digilent, Digilent Pmod Interface Specification, Doc 510-002, revision of November 20, 2011 (pages 1 to 4, 6, 7); Wikipedia, Pmod Interface (generic pin table and list of specification editions)

items.name: TO-92: examples
items.doc: The pin order of a TO-92 part depends on the part, not on the package: this page lists examples only, so check the datasheet of your exact part and maker. Each is drawn from the front, flat side towards you and leads pointing down, and the numbers are positions from left to right.
items.notes: The PN2222A entry is the plastic TO-92 type from onsemi (formerly Fairchild). It does not apply to the round metal-can 2N2222 (TO-18), whose leads form a triangle, and the similarly named onsemi P2N2222A has collector and emitter swapped: collector left, emitter right. The 78L05 runs the opposite way to the L78xx in TO-220: its input is on the right. TI's table numbers the TL431 leads against the positions used here; see its pin notes. The BS170 runs the opposite way to the 2N7000: drain left, source right. The DS18B20 has ground on the left and the supply on the right, the reverse of the LM35. The BC337 and BC557 have the same order as the BC547 (collector left), the 2N3906 the same as the 2N3904 (emitter left).
items.source: onsemi BC546/D Rev. 8 (BC547); onsemi/Fairchild PN2222A Rev. 1.1.0 and onsemi P2N2222A/D Rev. 7; multicomp 2N2222 sheet V1.0 (TO-18); onsemi 2N3903/D Rev. 9 (2N3904); onsemi NDS7002A/D Rev. 11 (2N7000); TI LM35 SNIS159H; TI UA78L SLVS010X and onsemi MC78L00A/D Rev. 21 (78L05); TI TL431 SLVS543S and onsemi TL431/D Rev. 45; Diotec BC337 and BC556 to BC559 (version 2026-03-30); MCC BC337/BC338 Rev.3-3-04162021; onsemi BC556B/D Rev. 3 (BC557); onsemi 2N3906/D Rev. 4; onsemi BS170/D Rev. 7, MMBF170/D Rev. 9 and Vishay 70226 (BS170); Dallas DS18B20 preliminary datasheet (2000, footer 050400)

items.name: SOT-23: examples
items.doc: The pin order of a SOT-23 part depends on the part, not on the package: this page lists examples only, so check the datasheet of your exact part and maker. Each is drawn from above with the marking side up: pin 1 lower left, pin 2 lower right, pin 3 alone at the top.
items.notes: The pin order of a SOT-23 part depends on the part, not on the package: transistors, MOSFETs, diodes and regulators in the same case use different orders. items.name: LM386 (DIP-8)
items.doc: Low-voltage audio power amplifier, drawn as the 8-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: With pins 1 and 8 open the gain is 20; a capacitor from pin 1 to pin 8 bypasses the internal 1.35 kOhm resistor and gives 200; a resistor in series with that capacitor sets any gain between. Both inputs are biased to ground through 50 kOhm inside, and a signal above 0.4 V either way must not reach pins 2 and 3 directly. At high gain the unused input must be bypassed to ground (0.1 uF or a short). Supply 4 V to 12 V (LM386N-4: 5 V to 18 V). Basis of the DIP drawing: TI's pin figure is captioned only for the 8-pin MSOP/SOIC package; the PDIP assignment rests on TI's single pin table plus the PDIP layout example (Figure 11-1), which confirms pins 2 to 6.

items.name: MAX232 (DIP-16)
items.doc: Dual RS-232 driver and receiver with charge pump, drawn as the 16-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: The chip needs four 1 uF capacitors: C1 between pins 1 and 3, C2 between pins 4 and 5, C3 from pin 2 to GND or VCC, C4 from pin 6 to GND, plus a 1 uF bypass on VCC. With polarized capacitors mind the polarity drawn in TI's Figure 8-1 (the plus side of C4 goes to GND). Pins 9 to 12 go to the UART or logic, pins 7, 8, 13 and 14 to the RS-232 connector, whose receiver inputs take up to 30 V. The signals are inverted: a high at TIN gives a negative RS-232 level, and an open receiver input reads as a high at ROUT. Pin 12 (R1OUT) is read from TI's Figure 4-1 and Figure 8-1, because TI's pin table leaves it out. The MAX232I shares this pinout.

items.name: SN74HC165 (DIP-16)
items.doc: 8-bit parallel-load shift register with serial input and complementary serial outputs, drawn as the 16-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: The parallel inputs are split, A to D on pins 11 to 14 and E to H on pins 3 to 6. A low SH/LD loads all eight inputs at once, whatever the clock does. With SH/LD high and CLK INH low, each rising edge of CLK shifts one step: H comes out at QH first, and SER moves into the first stage. CLK and CLK INH are interchangeable; change CLK INH to high only while CLK is high.

items.doc: Octal bus transceiver with 3-state outputs, one direction input and one output-enable input, drawn as the 20-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: The B side is shifted by one row against the A side: A1 (pin 2) faces OE (pin 19), A2 (pin 3) faces B1 (pin 18), and B8 (pin 11) faces GND (pin 10). With OE low, DIR high drives the B side from the A side and DIR low drives the A side from the B side; with OE high both sides are high-impedance. TI advises a pull-up resistor from OE to VCC so that the outputs stay off during power-up.

items.name: SN74HC08 (DIP-14)
items.doc: Quad 2-input AND gate, drawn as the 14-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: gates 1 and 2 run A, B, Y by rising pin number (pins 1 to 6). Gates 3 and 4 are the other way round: the output has the lowest number, 3Y is pin 8 (3A 9, 3B 10) and 4Y is pin 11 (4A 12, 4B 13). The pins sit where the 74HC00 has them.
items.source: Texas Instruments SN54HC08, SN74HC08 datasheet SCLS081J (February 2025), section 4, pin figure and table Pin Functions; cross-checked against onsemi MC74HC08A/D Rev. 17 (September 2026), page 1, logic diagram and pinout

items.name: SN74HC32 (DIP-14)
items.doc: Quad 2-input OR gate, drawn as the 14-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: gates 1 and 2 run A, B, Y by rising pin number (pins 1 to 6). Gates 3 and 4 are the other way round: the output has the lowest number, 3Y is pin 8 (3A 9, 3B 10) and 4Y is pin 11 (4A 12, 4B 13). The pins sit where the 74HC00 has them.
items.source: Texas Instruments SN54HC32, SN74HC32 datasheet SCLS200F (April 2021), section 5, Figure 5-1 and table Pin Functions; cross-checked against onsemi MC74HC32A/D Rev. 15 (September 2026), page 1, Figures 1 and 2

items.name: SN74HC86 (DIP-14)
items.doc: Quad 2-input exclusive-OR gate, drawn as the 14-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: gates 1 and 2 run A, B, Y by rising pin number (pins 1 to 6). Gates 3 and 4 are the other way round: the output has the lowest number, 3Y is pin 8 (3A 9, 3B 10) and 4Y is pin 11 (4A 12, 4B 13). An output is high when its two inputs differ; with one input held high the gate inverts the other.
items.source: Texas Instruments SN54HC86, SN74HC86 datasheet SCLS100F (April 2021), section 5, Figure 5-1 and table Pin Functions; cross-checked against onsemi MC74HC86A/D Rev. 9 (September 2026), pages 1 and 2, Figures 1 and 2

items.name: SN74HC74 (DIP-14)
items.doc: Dual D flip-flop with preset and clear, drawn as the 14-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: flip-flop 2 repeats the order of flip-flop 1 from pin 13 down to pin 8 (CLR, D, CLK, PRE, Q, ~Q), so it sits one row lower: 2CLR on pin 13 faces 1D on pin 2. PRE and CLR act at once, without the clock, and are active low; hold both high for clocked operation. If both are low together, Q and ~Q are both high, and that state does not persist when they return high.
items.source: Texas Instruments SN54HC74, SN74HC74 datasheet SCLS094F (June 2021), section 5, pin figure and table Pin Functions; cross-checked against onsemi MC74HC74A/D Rev. 17 (September 2026), page 2, Figures 1 and 2

pins.function: Flip-flop 1, clear, active low: low forces 1Q low

pins.name: 1CLK
pins.function: Flip-flop 1, clock: a rising edge stores 1D

pins.name: 1PRE
pins.function: Flip-flop 1, preset, active low: low forces 1Q high

pins.function: Flip-flop 2, preset, active low: low forces 2Q high

pins.name: 2CLK
pins.function: Flip-flop 2, clock: a rising edge stores 2D

pins.name: 2CLR
pins.function: Flip-flop 2, clear, active low: low forces 2Q low

items.name: SN74HC139 (DIP-16)
items.doc: Dual 2-to-4 line decoder/demultiplexer, drawn as the 16-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: with G low, B and A pick one output as a binary number, A is the lowest bit, and that output goes low while the other three stay high; with G high all four are high. The second decoder mirrors the first from pin 15 down to pin 9 (2G, 2A, 2B, 2Y0 to 2Y3), one row lower: 2G on pin 15 faces 1A on pin 2. As a demultiplexer, G is the data input.
items.source: Texas Instruments SN54HC139, SN74HC139 datasheet SCLS108E (February 2022), section 4, DIP pin figure; cross-checked against onsemi MC74HC139A/D Rev. 13 (April 2024), pages 1 and 2, pin assignment and Figure 1

items.name: SN74HC161 / SN74HC163 (DIP-16)
items.doc: 4-bit synchronous binary counter with synchronous load (SN74HC161 with asynchronous clear, SN74HC163 with synchronous clear), drawn as the 16-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: the counter counts only while ENP, ENT, LOAD and CLR are all high; each rising edge at CLK then adds one. QA is the lowest bit. A low at LOAD loads A to D at the next rising edge. The SN74HC161 clears as soon as CLR goes low; the SN74HC163 clears only at the next rising clock edge, so a gate that decodes the outputs can shorten the count. Otherwise the two parts are pin-compatible.
items.source: Texas Instruments SN54HC161, SN74HC161 datasheet SCLS297D (September 2003) and SN54HC163, SN74HC163 datasheet SCLS298D (October 2003), page 1, DIP pin figures; cross-checked against onsemi MC74HC161A/D Rev. 14 (May 2024), page 2, Figure 1

pins.function: Ripple-carry output: high at count 15 while ENT is high; enables the next counter

items.name: CD4011B (DIP-14)
items.doc: Quad 2-input NAND gate (CMOS 4000 series), drawn as the 14-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: the outputs sit in the middle of each side, J on pin 3 and K on pin 4, L on pin 10 and M on pin 11; the inputs take the outer pins. Supply and ground are where the 74HC00 has them, but the gates are not: pins 4 and 10 are outputs here and inputs on the 74HC00, pins 6 and 8 the other way round. Tie unused inputs to VSS or VDD.
items.source: Texas Instruments CD4011B, CD4012B, CD4023B datasheet SCHS021D (September 2003), page 1, terminal assignments CD4011B; cross-checked against onsemi MC14001B/D Rev. 13 (November 2025), page 2, pin assignments, and Renesas CD4011BMS FN3079, page 1, pinouts

items.name: CD4013B (DIP-14)
items.doc: Dual D flip-flop with set and reset (CMOS 4000 series), drawn as the 14-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: unlike the 74HC74, SET and RESET are active high: hold both low for clocked operation. If both are high, Q and ~Q are both high. Flip-flop 2 repeats the order of flip-flop 1 from pin 13 down to pin 8 (Q, ~Q, CLOCK, RESET, D, SET), so it sits one row lower: Q2 on pin 13 faces ~Q1 on pin 2. The pinout is not that of the 74HC74. Tie unused inputs to VSS or VDD.
items.source: Texas Instruments CD4013B datasheet SCHS023E (September 2016), section 5, pin figure and table Pin Functions; cross-checked against onsemi MC14013B/D Rev. 11 (July 2025), page 1, pin assignment, and Renesas CD4013BMS FN3080, page 1, pinout

items.name: CD4511B (DIP-16)
items.doc: BCD-to-7-segment latch, decoder and driver (CMOS 4000 series), drawn as the 16-pin PDIP from above.
items.notes: the BCD inputs are scattered: A (lowest bit) is pin 7, B pin 1, C pin 2, D pin 6. The segment outputs a to g are on pins 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 15 and 14. With LT and BL high and LE low, the code on D C B A shows as a digit; codes above 9 blank the display. LT low lights every segment, BL low blanks the display, and LE high holds the last code. The outputs drive common-cathode LED displays with up to 25 mA each; an output that is high must not be shorted to VSS. Pin 4 is called BL in TI's pin figure; onsemi and TI's truth table call it BI.
items.source: Texas Instruments CD4511B datasheet SCHS072B (July 2003), page 1, CD4511B terminal assignment; cross-checked against onsemi MC14511B/D Rev. 13 (March 2022), page 2, pin assignment

pins.name: BL

pins.function: Latch enable: low passes A to D through, high holds the last code

items.name: ATX12V CPU power, 4-pin
items.doc: The small extra 12 V supply of the CPU, a Mini-Fit Jr. housing with two rows of two. The latch sits on the row with the +12 V pins 3 and 4; it is drawn on top.
items.notes: It is the half-size form of the 8-pin EPS12V plug: on an 8-pin header it goes along pins 1 and 5 and meets pins 1, 2, 5 and 6, so ground meets ground. Two wires carry 12 V (18 AWG).
items.source: Intel ATX Version 3 Multi Rail Desktop Platform Power Supply Design Guide (336521) Rev. 2.1a, table 5-8 and figure 5-2; ASRock B450 Steel Legend manual, 8-pin ATX12V1 header (a 4-pin supply goes along pins 1 and 5)

items.name: PCIe power, 12VHPWR / 12V-2x6, 16-pin (12+4)
items.doc: Extra 12 V supply of a graphics card, up to 600 W: two rows of six power contacts and below them four sideband contacts S1 to S4. The latch sits on the row with the ground pins 7 to 12 and is drawn on top.
items.notes: One item for the older 12VHPWR (housing marked H+) and the 12V-2x6 (marked H++): the pins and numbers are the same. The 12V-2x6 header has longer power contacts and sideband contacts 1.5 mm shorter. The drawing shows the four sideband contacts at the size of the power contacts, centred under the middle of the power rows. That is an approximation: the real sideband contacts are smaller and at a finer pitch. Each power pin is rated 9.2 A with all twelve contacts in use, so no contact may be left out.
items.source: Intel ATX Version 3 Multi Rail Desktop Platform Power Supply Design Guide (336521) Rev. 2.1a, tables 3-5, 3-6 and 5-7, sections 3.3.1 to 3.3.3 and 5.2.2.4.3, figures 5-4 to 5-6; Corsair, Evolving Standards: 12VHPWR and 12V-2x6

pins.function: Power good from the card, open drain: low = a card rail is out of limits (optional)
pins.notes: Optional. In the supply a 4.7 kΩ pull-up to +3.3 V; open = card rails within limits, driven low for at least 100 ms = fault.

pins.notes: SENSE0, SENSE1 and the permitted power (initial / sustained, 12V-2x6): Ground, Ground 375 W / 600 W; Open, Ground 225 W / 450 W; Ground, Open 150 W / 300 W; the two shorted to each other 100 W / 150 W; Open, Open 0 W. A card must read both pins before it draws power through the plug.

items.name: Front panel header, 2x5
items.doc: The 2x5 header at 2.54 mm pitch for the power switch, the reset switch and the two LEDs of the case. It is drawn from above as the manuals draw it: pin 1 at the bottom left, the odd pins in the bottom row. Position 10 has no pin.
items.notes: Both switches are momentary and normally open: shorting the pulled-up pin (6 or 7) to its ground pin (8 or 5) is a press, and the power switch should hold for at least 50 ms. The names are the board makers'; Intel calls the pins HD_LED_P and HD_LED_N, FP PWR/SLP, PWR_SW_P and PWR_SW_N, RST_SW_P and RST_SW_N, RSVD_DNU.
items.source: Intel Front Panel I/O Connectivity Design Guide (600569) Rev. 1.1, section 2.2.2, table 2-4 and figure 2-1; Intel Front Panel I/O Connectivity Design Guide Version 1.2 (A29286-004), table 5 and figure 1; MSI B450 TOMAHAWK user guide, JFP1; ASRock B450 Steel Legend manual, PANEL1

items.doc: The 2x5 header at 2.54 mm pitch for two USB 2.0 ports of the case. It is drawn from above as the manuals draw it: pin 1 at the bottom left, the odd pins in the bottom row. Position 9 has no pin.
items.notes: Each header serves two ports. The power is +5 V, or on some boards +5 V dual, which switches between +5 V and standby with the state of the board. The fuse belongs on the board; the header is not for devices outside the case.
items.source: Intel Front Panel I/O Connectivity Design Guide (600569) Rev. 1.1, section 3.2, figure 3-1 and table 3-1; Intel Front Panel I/O Connectivity Design Guide Version 1.2 (A29286-004), figure 7 and table 8; MSI B450 TOMAHAWK user guide, JUSB1~2; ASRock B450 Steel Legend manual, USB_1_2

items.doc: The shrouded 2x10 header at 2.00 mm pitch for two USB 3.x ports of the case, with the pin removed at position 20. It is drawn from above: the key slot of the shroud sits on top, over the row 1 to 10.
items.notes: RX and TX are seen from the host: SSRX is what the board receives. Each Vbus pin carries at least 1.5 A and each signal pin 0.5 A. Some manuals mark pin 1 at the other end, at the pin the Intel specification calls pin 10; follow the key slot and the Vbus pin next to the removed pin.

items.name: HD Audio front panel header, 2x5
items.doc: The 2x5 header at 2.54 mm pitch for the headphone and microphone jacks of the case. It is drawn from above as the manuals draw it: pin 1 at the bottom left, the odd pins in the bottom row. Position 8 has no pin.
items.notes: The two RETURN pins and SENSE_SEND report which front jack holds a plug. Check what the panel is before plugging it in.

items.doc: The 4-pin header at 2.54 mm pitch for a 12 V RGB LED strip, drawn from above with pin 1 at the left. There is no standard: the order 12V, G, R, B is the board makers' convention.
items.notes: For 5050 RGB LED strips (12V/G/R/B) up to 3 A at 12 V and 2 m. Note the order: green comes before red. Match the arrow or mark of the plug to pin 1. Never put a 5 V addressable strip on this header: the 12 V would destroy it.

items.name: Peripheral power, 4-pin (Molex)
items.doc: The 4-pin peripheral power connector of older drives and accessories, AMP Mate-N-Lok 1-480424-0 or Molex 8981 type. The two cut corners are drawn at the bottom.
items.notes: Hold it with the cut corners on top and the order flips: the cable connector then reads 1, 2, 3, 4 from the left and the drive connector 4, 3, 2, 1. The pin numbers of the smaller floppy connector are different.
items.source: Intel ATX Version 3 Multi Rail Desktop Platform Power Supply Design Guide (336521) Rev. 2.1a, table 5-2 and figure 5-2; Maxtor DiamondMax 17 product manual, figure 3-5 and table 3-3; Wikipedia, Molex connector

items.name: Fan, 3-pin
items.doc: Three-wire fan connector with a speed signal and no PWM input. The notch stands for the guide rails on the plug, which take the wall of the header.
items.notes: It fits pins 1 to 3 of a 4-pin header. The colours are the makers' habit, not a standard: the third wire can also be white, and on 4-wire fans yellow is +12 V. Go by position.
items.source: Noctua FAQ, What pin configuration do Noctua fans use?; Sunon, Fan 3rd Wire Signal (PMD1212PTB3-A datasheet); ASRock B450 Steel Legend manual, fan connectors; Intel 4-Wire PWM Controlled Fans Specification Rev. 1.2, figures 6 and 7 (key and view of the family)

items.name: Fan, 4-pin PWM
items.doc: Four-wire fan connector to Intel's PWM specification, 2.54 mm pitch. The notch stands for the guide rails on the plug; they span pins 1 to 3 and take the wall of the header.
items.notes: A 3-pin fan fits pins 1 to 3 of the header and has no control input. Without a control signal a 4-wire fan runs at full speed. Some boards also vary the voltage on pin 2.
items.source: Intel 4-Wire Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) Controlled Fans Specification Rev. 1.2 (July 2004), table 1, sections 2 and 3, figures 6 and 7; Noctua FAQ, What pin configuration do Noctua fans use?; Gigabyte B450M K and ASRock B450 Steel Legend manuals

pins.notes: Target 25 kHz, allowed 21 to 28 kHz; at most 5.25 V open circuit and 5 mA short circuit.

items.name: Trailer socket, 7-pin (ISO 1724, 12N)
items.doc: The 7-pin 12 V trailer socket of ISO 1724 (type N, 12N): direction indicators, brake, tail and fog lights on one common return, drawn from the socket face.
items.notes: Work on mains and vehicle electrics only if you are qualified, and check the actual connector before wiring. This is the 12 V socket of ISO 1724 (12N), not the white 12S socket of ISO 3732, which uses the same contact numbers for other functions. Contact 3 is the common return of all lamps. Contacts 5 and 7 are the two sides of the tail lights, so no lamp may be connected to both. The core colours are given for information. The makers' documents do not show a key position, so none is drawn; the radius of the outer ring is a drawing value, not a dimension from the standard.
items.source: Erich Jaeger, ISO 1724: The international standard for 7-pin trailer connectors (scope and application, contact table and the figures of socket, rear view and plug); M&K catalogue pages 14 and 15, 7-polige 12-Volt-Steckvorrichtung ISO 1724 / ISO 3732 (Conrad item 808849), Kontaktbelegung Connector N-type

items.name: Trailer socket, 13-pin (ISO 11446)
items.doc: The 13-pin 12 V trailer socket of ISO 11446 (Jaeger system): contacts 1 to 7 as on the 7-pin socket, plus reversing light, permanent and ignition-switched supply with their own returns, drawn from the socket face.
items.notes: Work on mains and vehicle electrics only if you are qualified, and check the actual connector before wiring. The drawing follows Jaeger's figure and the angles are approximate (within about 7 degrees of the maker's rendering, rounded to a 36 degree pattern); the contact numbers are exact. Contacts 9 (permanent +) and 10 (ignition +) each have their own return, 13 and 11: do not use contact 3 for them. Contact 9 is live with the ignition off; Jaeger states no current rating for 9 and 10. No key is drawn because it rests on a render only. This is the 12 V version; the 24 V version is not covered.
items.source: Erich Jaeger, ISO 11446 scope and application (contact table, nominal voltage and the figures of socket, rear view and plug); Erich Jaeger, ISO 11446 overview; Erich Jaeger and M&K ISO 1724 tables for contacts 1 to 7

items.name: Charging connector Type 2 (IEC 62196-2)
items.doc: The Type 2 connector of IEC 62196-2 for AC charging of electric vehicles: five power contacts (PE, N, L1 to L3) and the two signal contacts CP and PP, drawn on the pin face.
items.notes: Work on mains and vehicle electrics only if you are qualified, and check the actual connector before wiring. Never bridge CP or PP to fake a vehicle and never apply power outside a charging station. Single-phase cables and inlets use L1 and N only. Contact sequence when plugging in: PE first, then N, the phases, and CP and PP last; unplugging runs in reverse (TE table 4-11). The Rc values of PP follow TE table 4-7 (from IEC 61851-22 Annex B). The voltages and currents in TE's document (250 V AC, 20 A three-phase, 32 A single-phase, 2 A 30 V for CP and PP) are TE's assembly ratings, not the limits of the Type 2 system. CP signalling (the PWM levels) is not covered. The angles are rounded from a small render (about 5 degrees).
items.source: TE Connectivity, Product Specification 108-94323 Rev A (01 FEB 16), IEC 62196 Electric Vehicle Charge Connector Assembly (Type 2 for Mode 2 and 3), pages 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11 to 13

items.name: Car radio connector ISO 10487, part A (power)
items.name_en: Car radio connector ISO 10487, part A (power)
items.doc: Part A of the ISO 10487 car radio connector: battery positive, ground, illumination and the antenna supply, as the standard draws it from the rear of the radio.
items.notes: Work on mains and vehicle electrics only if you are qualified, and check the actual connector before wiring. The standard makes A7 the main supply (permanent, or switched in the vehicle only when A4 is not switched) and A4 a switched positive of at most 0.3 A, which differs from the common folklore of A4 permanent and A7 ignition: some vehicles and radios use their own split, so measure both contacts in the car before connecting a radio. A5 is an output of the radio for an antenna amplifier (max. 0.3 A), not a supply into the radio. Contacts 9 and 10 do not exist in part A. The standard gives no wire colours.
items.source: ISO 10487-1:1992, Passenger car radio connections, Part 1: Dimensions and general requirements (official preview with the complete normative text: clauses 3 and 4, figure 1, table 1)

items.name: Car radio connector ISO 10487, part B (speakers)
items.name_en: Car radio connector ISO 10487, part B (speakers)
items.doc: Part B of the ISO 10487 car radio connector: the four loudspeaker channels, each with its own positive and negative contact, as the standard draws it from the rear of the radio.
items.notes: Work on mains and vehicle electrics only if you are qualified, and check the actual connector before wiring. Each speaker has its own negative line: never join the negative lines or connect them to ground, because ISO 10487-1 (table 1, footnote 2) does not allow common negative wiring in the vehicle, and a negative line on ground can damage the output stage of a bridged amplifier. Each positive contact sits directly above its negative contact. Contacts 9 and 10 do not exist in part B. The standard gives no wire colours.
items.source: ISO 10487-1:1992, Passenger car radio connections, Part 1: Dimensions and general requirements (official preview with the complete normative text: figure 1 and table 1, part B, footnote 2)
